I have learned that the fastest traveler goes on foot. Let us see who arrives first, I tell my friend. The journey is thirty miles, the fare ninety cents, nearly a day’s pay. I remember laborers on this very railroad earning sixty cents daily. I can set out walking now and arrive before night; I have maintained that pace for weeks at a time. Meanwhile you will earn your fare and arrive tomorrow, perhaps this evening if you find work promptly. Instead of traveling to Fitchburg, you will spend most of the day working here. Even if the railroad circled the globe, I believe I would stay ahead. As for seeing the countryside and gaining that sort of experience, I would have to stop counting you among my acquaintances altogether.

That universal law outwits everyone; even the railroad is as broad as it is long. Making a round-the-world railroad available to all humanity amounts to grading the planet’s entire surface. People vaguely suppose that enough activity with joint stocks and spades will eventually carry everyone somewhere almost instantly and for nothing. A crowd rushes to the station, the conductor calls “All aboard!” But once the smoke clears and steam condenses, a few will be riding and everyone else run over. It will be called—and truly be—“A melancholy accident.” Those who earn their fares can doubtless eventually ride, if they live long enough, but by then they will probably have lost their spring and desire to travel. This habit of spending the best and most valuable part of one’s life earning money to enjoy a questionable liberty during the least valuable part of it reminds me of the Englishman who first went to India to make a fortune, intending to return to England and live as a poet. He should have gone straight upstairs to his attic. “What!” cry a million Irishmen springing from shanties across the country. “Isn’t the railroad we built a good thing?” Yes, I answer, _comparatively_ good: you could have done worse. But because you are my brothers, I wish you could have spent your time better than digging this dirt.

Before finishing the house, I wanted to earn ten or twelve dollars honestly and pleasantly to meet my unusual expenses. I planted about two and a half acres of nearby light, sandy ground, mostly with beans, with smaller amounts of potatoes, corn, peas, and turnips. The whole eleven-acre lot, largely growing up in pines and hickories, had sold the previous season for eight dollars and eight cents an acre. A farmer pronounced it “good for nothing but to raise cheeping squirrels on.” Being merely a squatter, not the owner, and not expecting to cultivate so much again, I used no manure and did not quite hoe the whole area even once. Plowing brought up several cords of stumps, providing fuel for a long time and leaving little circles of virgin earth where especially luxuriant beans marked the spots all summer. Dead wood behind my house, mostly unsaleable, and driftwood from the pond supplied the rest of my fuel. I hired a man and team for plowing, though I held the plow. My first season’s spending on tools, seed, labor, and so on was $14.72½. Someone gave me seed corn; unless you plant too much, it costs practically nothing anyway. My harvest was twelve bushels of beans, eighteen of potatoes, and some peas and sweet corn. Yellow corn and turnips went in too late to produce anything. My total farm income was as follows.

$23.44.
Subtract the expenses: $14.72½.
The balance remaining is $8.71½.

That excludes produce already eaten or still on hand when I made this calculation, valued at $4.50. What remained more than offset a little grass I had not grown myself. Considering everything—the importance of a man’s soul and of today—despite the experiment’s brevity, indeed partly because it was temporary, I believe I did better that year than any farmer in Concord.

The following year I did better still, digging by spade all the land I needed, about a third of an acre. The experience of both years taught me something, undaunted as I was by celebrated farming books, including Arthur Young’s. Live simply, eat only what you grow, grow no more than you eat, and avoid exchanging it for inadequate quantities of costlier luxuries: then only a few rods of ground need cultivation. Digging that with a spade costs less than plowing with oxen; selecting a fresh plot occasionally costs less than manuring the old one. You could do all necessary farming almost with your left hand, in spare summer hours, without tying yourself to an ox, horse, cow, or pig as people now do. I want to speak impartially here, without a stake in the success or failure of current economic and social arrangements. I was more independent than any Concord farmer, anchored to neither house nor farm, free every moment to follow my genius’s bent, crooked though that bent is. Besides already being better off than they were, I would have remained almost equally well off had the house burned or the crops failed.

I often think that herds keep people more than people keep herds: the herds are so much freer. People and oxen exchange work, but if we count only necessary work, the oxen have decidedly the better bargain; their farm is much bigger. Six weeks of haymaking supplies part of the human share, and it is no child’s play. Surely a nation living simply in every respect, a nation of philosophers, would never make the great mistake of employing animals’ labor. Admittedly no such nation has existed or is likely soon to exist, and I am not certain it would be desirable. But _I_ would never have broken in a horse or bull and boarded it for the work it could do, fearing I would become merely a horse-man or herds-man. If society seems to gain by this arrangement, can we be certain one person’s gain is not another’s loss, and the stable boy has as much reason for satisfaction as his master? Grant that certain public works could not have been built without animals; let people share that glory with horses and oxen. Does it follow they could not otherwise have accomplished still worthier works? When animals assist with work not merely unnecessary or artistic but luxurious and idle, a few people inevitably perform all the exchanged labor for the oxen—in other words, become slaves of the strongest. A man thus labors for the animal outside him as an emblem of his labor for the animal within. Despite our substantial brick and stone houses, a farmer’s prosperity is still measured by how far his barn overshadows his home. This town reportedly has the district’s largest houses for oxen, cows, and horses and keeps up in public buildings; yet this county has very few halls for free speech or free worship. Why should nations commemorate themselves by architecture instead of, say, their capacity for abstract thought? The Bhagvat-Geeta is far more admirable than all the East’s ruins! Towers and temples are princes’ luxuries. A simple, independent mind does not toil at a prince’s command. Genius serves no emperor and works scarcely at all in silver, gold, or marble. Why, pray, hammer so much stone? When I visited Arcadia, I saw no stone hammering. Nations madly want to perpetuate their memory through quantities of hammered stone. What if they spent equal effort smoothing and polishing their manners? A single instance of good sense would outlast in memory a monument reaching the moon. I prefer stones where they belong. Thebes’ grandeur was vulgar. A rod of stone wall around an honest man’s field makes more sense than hundred-gated Thebes wandering far from life’s true purpose. Barbarous, heathen religion and civilization build splendid temples; what you might call Christianity does not. Most national stonework contributes only to a tomb: the nation buries itself alive. The Pyramids’ greatest marvel is that so many people could be found degraded enough to spend their lives building a tomb for an ambitious booby. Drowning him in the Nile and giving his body to dogs would have been wiser and manlier. I might invent an excuse for them and him, but have no time. The builders’ religion and love of art are much the same worldwide, whether building an Egyptian temple or the United States Bank. The result costs more than it is worth. Vanity drives it, helped by an appetite for garlic, bread, and butter. Promising young architect Mr. Balcom draws the design with hard pencil and ruler on the back of his Vitruvius, and Dobson & Sons, stonecutters, receive the contract. Only when thirty centuries look down upon it does humanity start looking up. As for lofty towers and monuments, a madman here once dug toward China until, he said, he heard Chinese pots and kettles rattling. I shall not go out of my way to admire his hole. Many ask who built the monuments of East and West. For my own part, I would rather know who in those days did not build them—who rose above such trifles. But back to my figures.

Meanwhile, surveying, carpentry, and other day work in the village earned me $13.34; I have as many trades as fingers. My food costs for eight months, July 4 to March 1, when I made these calculations—although I lived there more than two years—were as follows. This excludes potatoes, a little green corn, and some peas I grew, and takes no account of provisions remaining at the final date:

Rice: $1.73½.
Molasses: $1.73. The cheapest way to buy sweetness.
Rye meal: $1.04¾.
Indian meal: $0.99¾. Less expensive than rye.
Pork: $0.22.

These experiments all failed:
Flour: $0.88. More expensive than Indian meal in money and trouble alike.
Sugar: $0.80.
Lard: $0.65.
Apples: $0.25.
Dried apple: $0.22.
Sweet potatoes: $0.10.
One pumpkin: $0.06.
One watermelon: $0.02.
Salt: $0.03.

Yes, I ate $8.74 altogether. I would not publish my guilt so shamelessly if I did not know most readers were equally guilty, and their deeds would look no better in print. The following year I sometimes caught enough fish for dinner. Once I even killed a woodchuck plundering my bean-field—effected its transmigration, as a Tartar might say—and ate it, partly as an experiment. Despite a musky taste, it gave me momentary pleasure. Yet I saw that no length of practice would make this a good habit, whatever impression the village butcher’s ready-dressed woodchucks might give.
Clothing and a few incidental expenses over the same period, though this item tells little by itself, were as follows.

$8.40¾.
Oil and several household utensils cost another $2.00.

Thus the full sum of my cash expenditures was as follows, apart from washing and mending, which were mostly done outside my house and for which the bills had not yet arrived. These cover all, and more than all, the necessary ways money goes out in this part of the world:

House: $28.12½.
Farm, for one year: $14.72½.
Food, for eight months: $8.74.
Clothing and incidentals, for eight months: $8.40¾.
Oil and other items, for eight months: $2.00.
Grand total: $61.99¾.
I am speaking now to readers who must earn their living. Against these expenses, my receipts for farm produce sold were as follows.

$23.44.
Income from work by the day: $13.34.
Total receipts: $36.78.

Subtracting those receipts from the expenditures leaves $25.21¾ on one side of the account. That was almost exactly my starting capital and the measure of the expenses I needed to incur. On the other side stand the leisure, independence, and health I gained, along with a comfortable house for as long as I care to live in it.

However incidental and therefore uninformative these figures may seem, their completeness gives them some value. I received nothing without accounting for it in some way. The calculation shows that food alone cost me about twenty-seven cents weekly in cash. For nearly two years afterward my diet was unleavened rye and Indian meal, potatoes, rice, very little salt pork, molasses, and salt; I drank water. Living chiefly on rice suited someone so fond of India’s philosophy. To answer habitual faultfinders, I should add that I sometimes dined out, as I always had and hope to have opportunities to do again. Often this disrupted my household arrangements. But since dining out was a constant element, as I have said, it does not affect a comparison of this kind at all.

Those two years taught me how astonishingly little trouble obtaining necessary food requires, even at this latitude. A person can eat as simply as animals and remain healthy and strong. I have made a satisfying dinner, satisfying in several respects, from nothing but purslane (_Portulaca oleracea_) gathered in my cornfield, boiled, and salted. I supply the Latin for the savor of its scientific name. On an ordinary midday in peaceful times, what more, pray, should a reasonable person want than enough ears of boiled young sweet corn, with salt? Even my limited variety yielded to appetite’s demands rather than health’s. Yet people have reached the point of frequently starving through lack of luxuries rather than necessities. I know a good woman convinced her son died because he took to drinking water alone.

Readers will see that I approach this subject chiefly as a matter of economy, rather than nutrition. They will not attempt to test my abstinence themselves unless they have a well-stocked pantry behind them.

At first I made bread from Indian meal and salt alone, genuine hoe-cakes baked before my outdoor fire on a shingle or on the end of timber cut off while building. They often acquired smoke and a pine flavor. I also tried flour, but eventually found rye mixed with Indian meal the pleasantest and most convenient. In cold weather baking several small loaves in succession amused me considerably; I tended and turned them as carefully as an Egyptian watching hatching eggs. These were true cereal fruits ripening under my care, with a fragrance to my senses like other noble fruits’. I wrapped them in cloth to preserve it as long as possible. I studied the ancient, indispensable craft of breadmaking, consulting whatever authorities I found. My studies began with the first unleavened bread, when people passed from the wildness of nuts and meats to this milder, more refined food. Then I followed the dough’s accidental souring, supposedly the discovery of leavening, and subsequent fermentations, down to “good, sweet, wholesome bread,” the staff of life. Some regard leaven as bread’s soul, the _spiritus_ filling its cellular structure, preserved religiously like the Vestal fire. I suppose a precious bottle brought on the Mayflower began America’s supply, its influence still rising, swelling, and spreading in waves of grain across the country. Faithfully I fetched this seed from the village until one morning I forgot the rules and scalded my yeast. The accident taught me that even yeast was unnecessary: I made discoveries by analysis, not synthesis. Ever since I have happily omitted it, although most housewives earnestly insisted that safe, wholesome bread without yeast was impossible, and elderly people predicted my vital powers would quickly decline. I find it no essential ingredient; after a year without it I remain among the living. I am glad to avoid the petty business of carrying a bottle in my pocket that sometimes popped and discharged its contents to my embarrassment. Leaving it out is simpler and more respectable. Humanity adapts to climates and circumstances better than almost any animal. Nor did I add sal soda or any other acid or alkali. Apparently my bread followed Marcus Porcius Cato’s recipe from about two centuries before Christ: “Panem depsticium sic facito. Manus mortariumque bene lavato. Farinam in mortarium indito, aquæ paulatim addito, subigitoque pulchre. Ubi bene subegeris, defingito, coquitoque sub testu.” I understand this as: “Make kneaded bread this way. Wash your hands and trough thoroughly. Put meal in the trough, gradually add water, and knead thoroughly. Once it is well kneaded, shape it and bake beneath a cover”—in other words, a baking kettle. Not a word of leaven. But I did not always use this staff of life. Once my empty purse kept all bread from my sight for more than a month.

In this land so well suited to rye and Indian corn, every New Englander could readily grow all his bread grains instead of depending on distant, unstable markets. Yet we are so far from simple independence that Concord shops seldom sell fresh, sweet meal, and hardly anyone uses hominy or still coarser forms of corn. Generally farmers feed their own grain to cattle and hogs, then buy costlier flour at the store, although it is certainly no healthier. I saw how easily I could grow my bushel or two of rye and Indian corn—the former grows on the poorest soil, the latter needs less than the best—and grind them by hand, dispensing with rice and pork. If concentrated sweetness was necessary, experiments showed that pumpkins or beets made very good molasses. I knew planting a few maples would eventually provide it more easily still; while they grew, various substitutes besides those already named were available. “For,” sang the Forefathers.

“We can make liquor to sweeten our lips
From pumpkins and parsnips and walnut-tree chips.”

Finally, obtaining salt, the most basic grocery, might supply a suitable reason for a seaside visit. Doing without it altogether would probably make me drink less water. I have never learned that the Indians troubled themselves to go in search of it.

In this way I could dispense with buying and bartering for food. Already having shelter, I would need only clothes and fuel. The trousers I wear now were woven in a farmer’s household—thank Heaven humanity retains that much virtue. I consider the fall from farmer to factory worker as great and memorable as the fall from man to farmer. In a newly settled country, fuel is an encumbrance. As for a home site, if squatting were no longer permitted, I could buy an acre at the price fetched by my cultivated land: eight dollars and eight cents. As things stood, however, I believed my squatting increased the land’s value.

Some unbelievers occasionally ask whether I think I can live entirely on vegetables. To reach the root of the question at once—and faith is that root—I usually tell them I can live on board nails. If they cannot understand that, they cannot understand much of what I have to say. I welcome reports of such experiments: for example, a young man living for two weeks on hard, raw corn straight from the ear, using his teeth as his only mortar. Squirrels attempted the same experiment successfully. All humanity has an interest in these trials, even if they alarm a few old women unable to undertake them or holding their widow’s thirds in mills.

I made some of my furniture myself; the rest cost nothing I have not accounted for. It consisted of a bed, table, desk, three chairs, a mirror three inches across, tongs and andirons, a kettle, skillet, frying pan, dipper, washbasin, two knives and forks, three plates, one cup, one spoon, an oil jug, a molasses jug, and a japanned lamp. Nobody is so poor he must sit on a pumpkin; that is lack of resourcefulness. Village attics hold plenty of the chairs I like best, free to anyone who carries them away. Furniture! Thank God I can sit down and stand up without a furniture warehouse’s assistance. Who but a philosopher would not feel ashamed to see his furniture loaded onto a cart and driven upcountry under heaven’s light and human eyes, a beggarly inventory of empty boxes? There goes Spaulding’s furniture. Examining such a load, I could never tell whether it belonged to a supposedly rich man or a poor one; the owner always seemed poverty-stricken. Indeed, possessing more of these things makes you poorer. Every load seems to contain a dozen shanties’ contents; if one shanty means poverty, this means poverty multiplied by twelve. Why, pray, do we ever _move_, unless to shed furniture, our _exuviæ_, our cast skins—finally to leave this world for another newly furnished one, letting this one burn? It is as though all these traps were buckled to a man’s belt, forcing him to drag them across the rough country where our lot is cast, dragging his trap. Lucky the fox that left its tail behind in the trap. A muskrat gnaws off its third leg to escape. No wonder people lose their spring. How often they reach a dead stop! “Sir, if I may ask so boldly, what do you mean by a dead stop?” With a seer’s eyes, you will see behind everyone you meet all he owns, and much he claims to disown: even kitchen furnishings and the rubbish he hoards and refuses to burn. He appears harnessed to it, struggling forward as best he can. A man reaches a dead stop, I think, when he gets through a knothole or gateway too narrow for the sledge of furniture behind him. I cannot help pitying a trim, compact-looking fellow, seemingly free, equipped and ready, when he mentions his “furniture” and whether he has insured it. “But what shall I do with my furniture?” My bright butterfly has become caught in a spiderweb. Even those who long seem to own none prove, on closer inquiry, to have some stored in another person’s barn. England today resembles an old gentleman traveling with heaps of baggage, rubbish accumulated over years of housekeeping that he dares not burn: big trunk, small trunk, hatbox, bundle. Throw away at least the first three. Nowadays picking up his bed and walking would exceed a healthy man’s strength; I would certainly advise a sick man to put down his bed and run. When I meet an immigrant staggering under a bundle containing everything he owns, like an enormous swelling grown from the back of his neck, I pity him not because it is all he has, but because he must carry all _that_. If I must drag a trap, I will choose a light one that does not pinch a vital part. Perhaps wisest of all would be never putting a paw into it.

Incidentally, curtains cost me nothing: the only watchers I might exclude are sun and moon, and I welcome their looking in. Moonlight will neither sour my milk nor spoil my meat; sunlight will neither damage my furniture nor fade my carpet. When the sun’s friendship grows too warm, retreating behind Nature’s curtains remains better economy than adding another housekeeping item. A lady once offered a mat. I declined because I had no spare room indoors and no spare time, indoors or out, to shake it. I preferred wiping my feet on the turf before my door. It is best to avoid even the beginnings of evil before they take hold.
Not long ago I attended the auction of a deacon’s effects, for his life had not, after all, been without effects:—
“The evil that men do lives after them.”

As usual, much of it was rubbish, accumulating since his father’s time. Among the objects was a dried tapeworm. After half a century in the attic and other dusty corners, these things were not burned. Instead of a _bonfire_, a cleansing destruction, came an _auction_, an increase. Neighbors eagerly gathered to inspect them, bought everything, and carefully carried it to their own attics and dust holes. There it will remain until their estates are settled and the journey begins again. When a man dies, he kicks up the dust.

We might usefully imitate certain savage peoples’ customs. At least they make a show of shedding their skin annually: they possess the idea, whether or not the reality follows. Would we not benefit from celebrating a “busk,” or “feast of first fruits,” like the Mucclasse Indians’ custom described by Bartram? He says: “When a town celebrates the busk, the people first supply themselves with fresh clothes, pots, pans, other household utensils, and furniture. They gather their worn-out clothes and other worthless objects, sweep and clean their houses, squares, and the entire town, and heap all the filth together with the remaining grain and old provisions. They burn this common pile. After taking medicine and fasting for three days, they extinguish every fire in town. Throughout the fast they abstain from satisfying every appetite and passion. They proclaim a general amnesty: all wrongdoers may return to the town.—”
“On the fourth morning the high priest rubs dry pieces of wood together to kindle a fresh fire in the public square. Every household in town receives its supply of new, pure flame from there.”

Next they feast on fresh corn and fruit, singing and dancing for three days. “For the next four days they welcome visits and rejoice with friends from neighboring towns, who have likewise purified and prepared themselves.”
The Mexicans performed a similar purification at the close of each fifty-two-year period, believing the time had come for the world to end.

I have rarely heard of a truer sacrament, an “outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace,” as the dictionary defines it. I am sure their original inspiration came directly from Heaven, although no biblical account records their revelation.

For over five years I supported myself entirely by hand labor in this way, discovering that about six weeks’ work each year paid every living expense. All winter and most of summer remained wholly free for study. I tried schoolkeeping thoroughly and found my expenses proportionate—or rather disproportionate—to my income. I had to dress and behave accordingly, not to mention think and believe, and lost my time into the bargain. Since I taught for a living rather than humanity’s benefit, it failed. I tried trade, but found it would take ten years to get started; by then I would probably be heading toward the devil. I actually feared that I might then be conducting what people call a good business. Earlier, while considering how to earn a living, some unhappy experiences of following friends’ wishes were fresh enough to challenge my ingenuity. I often seriously considered picking huckleberries. Surely I could do that, and the small earnings might suffice, since my greatest talent was needing little. It required so little capital and, I foolishly thought, so little disturbance of my usual moods. While acquaintances entered commerce or professions without hesitation, I contemplated the occupation as most resembling theirs: roaming hills all summer, picking whatever berries I met and disposing of them afterward without concern, thus tending Admetus’s flocks. I also dreamed of gathering wild herbs or bringing evergreens, by hay-cart loads, to villagers—even city dwellers—who liked reminders of the woods. Since then I have learned that trade curses everything it touches. Even a trade in messages from heaven bears the entire commercial curse.

Because I preferred some things to others, especially my own freedom, and could live roughly yet thrive, I did not wish to spend my time earning rich carpets, fine furniture, delicate cooking, or a Grecian or Gothic house just yet. If there are people for whom acquiring these things interrupts nothing they value, and who know how to use them once acquired, I am content to relinquish this pursuit entirely to them. Some are “industrious,” apparently loving work for itself, or perhaps because it keeps them from worse mischief; I have nothing to say to them now. Those unable to imagine using more leisure might work twice as hard, I suggest, until they have paid for themselves and obtained their freedom papers. For myself, day labor proved the most independent occupation, especially since thirty or forty working days yearly could support a person. Sunset ends the laborer’s day, leaving him free for his chosen pursuit, independent of his job. His employer, speculating month after month, enjoys no break throughout the entire year.

In short, faith and experience both convince me that supporting yourself on earth can be recreation rather than hardship if you live wisely and simply. Simpler peoples’ everyday pursuits remain more artificial societies’ sports. It is not necessary for anyone to earn his living by the sweat of his brow unless he sweats more readily than I do.

A young acquaintance who inherited several acres told me he thought he would live as I did _if he had the means_. Under no circumstances would I want anyone to adopt _my_ way of living. Before he had properly learned it, I might have discovered another; besides, I want as many different people in the world as possible. I want everyone to discover and carefully follow _his own_ way, rather than his father’s, mother’s, or neighbor’s. Let the young man build, plant, or sail; only let nothing prevent him from doing what he says he wants to do. Our wisdom rests on a mere mathematical point, as sailors and escaping slaves keep the pole star in view. Yet that suffices to guide an entire life. We may not reach port within a calculable time, but we will maintain the true course.

Here, undoubtedly, what holds for one holds still more for a thousand. A large house costs proportionately less than a small one, since several apartments can share roof, cellar, and dividing walls. Personally, however, I preferred a solitary home. Besides, building everything yourself will usually cost less than persuading someone else of a common wall’s advantages. Even after persuasion, the partition must be thin to save much, and the other person may prove a bad neighbor who neglects repairs on his side. Usually only extremely partial, superficial cooperation is possible. The little true cooperation existing might as well not exist, its harmony being inaudible to people. Someone with faith will cooperate wherever equal faith exists; someone without it will keep living like everyone else, whatever company he joins. In the highest and lowest senses alike, cooperation means _getting our living together_. Recently I heard a proposal that two young men travel the world together. One would go penniless, earning his way before the mast and behind the plow; the other would carry a bill of exchange. Plainly they could not cooperate or remain companions long, since one would not _operate_ at all. Their first interesting crisis would separate them. Above all, as I have suggested, someone traveling alone can begin today; with a companion he must wait until the other is ready, and their departure may be long delayed.

I have heard townsmen call all this very selfish. I admit to indulging very little in charitable enterprises so far. Among the sacrifices I have made to duty is the sacrifice of that pleasure. Some have used every persuasive art to induce me to support a poor local family. If I had nothing to do—for the devil employs the idle—I might try that sort of pastime. Yet when I considered indulging myself, putting their Heaven in my debt by making certain poor people as comfortable in every respect as I make myself, and even ventured to offer, every one promptly preferred remaining poor. My fellow townsmen and women devote themselves to others’ welfare in so many ways that surely at least one of us may be spared for other, less humane occupations. You must possess a genius for charitable work just as you must possess a genius for any other undertaking in life. As for Doing-good, that profession is already crowded. I have also given it a fair trial and, strangely enough, find it disagrees with my constitution. Probably I would not knowingly abandon my particular calling to perform society’s prescribed good even to prevent the universe’s destruction. I believe a similar but infinitely greater steadfastness elsewhere is all that currently preserves it. Still, I would never obstruct anyone’s genius. To whoever gives heart, soul, and life to the work I decline, I say: persist, even if the world calls it evil, as it most likely will.

I do not imagine my situation unusual; many readers would doubtless offer the same defense. For doing something—I cannot promise my neighbors would call it good—I can confidently recommend myself as an excellent person to hire. But exactly what that particular something is, and where my abilities would be useful, are matters for my employer to discover for himself. Whatever _good_ I do in the ordinary sense must lie off my principal path and usually be entirely unintended. In practice people say: start where and as you are, without chiefly trying to become worthier, and with deliberate kindness go about doing good. If I preached in that vein, I would instead say: begin by being good. Imagine the sun stopping after kindling itself only to the brightness of the moon or a sixth-magnitude star, then wandering like Robin Goodfellow, peeping through cottage windows, inspiring lunatics, spoiling meat, and making darkness visible. Instead it steadily increases its kindly heat and generosity until no mortal can look directly at its brilliance. Then—and meanwhile—it travels its own orbit doing the world good, or, as truer philosophy discovered, the world travels around it receiving good. Phaeton, wanting to prove his heavenly birth through beneficence, drove the sun’s chariot for only a day. Leaving the proper track, he burned several blocks in heaven’s lower streets, scorched the earth, dried every spring, and created the Sahara. Finally Jupiter struck him headlong to earth with a thunderbolt, and the sun, grieving his death, refused to shine for a year.

No smell is worse than spoiled goodness: human, divine carrion. If I knew someone was coming with the deliberate purpose of doing me good, I would run for my life. I would flee as from the simoom, that parching African desert wind filling eyes, ears, nose, and mouth with dust until you suffocate. I would be afraid of having some of that intended good actually done to me, and of finding some of its poisonous infection mingled with my own blood. No: I would rather suffer evil in the natural way. Feeding me when I starve, warming me when I freeze, or pulling me from a ditch does not by itself make someone a good _man_. I can find a Newfoundland dog that does as much. Philanthropy is not love of humanity in its broadest sense. Howard was undoubtedly remarkably kind and worthy in his way, and receives his reward. But what, comparatively, are a hundred Howards to _us_ if their charity cannot help _us_ at our best, when we most deserve help? I have never heard of a charitable meeting sincerely proposing anything beneficial for me or anyone like me.

The Jesuits found themselves completely baffled by Indians who, burning at the stake, suggested fresh tortures to their tormentors. Their superiority to bodily suffering sometimes placed them beyond any comfort missionaries could offer. The command to treat others as you would be treated sounded less persuasive to people who did not particularly care how others treated them, who loved their enemies in a new fashion and came close to freely forgiving everything done to them.

Be certain to give poor people the help they need most, even if it is an example that leaves them far behind. When giving money, give yourself with it rather than merely abandoning it to them. We sometimes make curious mistakes. Often a poor man is less cold and hungry than dirty, ragged, and coarse, partly from taste rather than misfortune alone. Money may only buy him more rags. I used to pity the awkward Irish laborers cutting pond ice in shabby, torn clothes while I shivered in my tidier, somewhat more fashionable ones. Then, on a bitter day, a man who had fallen in came to warm himself at my house. I watched him remove three pairs of trousers and two pairs of stockings before reaching skin. Dirty and ragged they certainly were, but his many _inner_ garments let him refuse the _extra_ ones I offered. A ducking was exactly what he needed. I began pitying myself: giving me a flannel shirt would have been greater charity than giving him an entire secondhand clothing shop. A thousand people hack at evil’s branches for every one striking its root. The person giving the most time and money to the needy may, through his way of living, contribute most to the misery he vainly tries to relieve. He resembles the pious slave-breeder using every tenth slave’s proceeds to buy the others a Sunday’s freedom. Some demonstrate kindness by employing poor people in their kitchens. Would employing themselves there not be kinder? You boast of donating a tenth of your income; perhaps you should give the other nine-tenths that way and finish the matter. Society then recovers only a tenth of its property. Does that reflect generosity in the person possessing it, or negligence among the officers of justice?

Philanthropy is almost the only virtue humanity appreciates enough. Indeed, we greatly overvalue it, prompted by our own selfishness. One sunny Concord day a strong, poor man praised a fellow townsman to me for kindness to the poor—meaning himself. Humanity esteems its kindly uncles and aunts more than its real spiritual fathers and mothers. I once heard a learned, intelligent clergyman lecture on England. After listing her scientific, literary, and political greats—Shakespeare, Bacon, Cromwell, Milton, Newton, and others—he turned to Christian heroes. As though professional duty required it, he placed them far above everyone else, greatest of the great: Penn, Howard, and Mrs. Fry. Surely everyone must feel the falseness and cant. These were not England’s finest men and women, but perhaps her finest philanthropists.

I would take nothing from philanthropy’s rightful praise, but ask justice for everyone whose work and life bless humanity. Uprightness and benevolence are not what I chiefly value in someone; they are, so to speak, his stem and leaves. Plants whose dried greenery makes sick people’s herb tea perform a humble service, chiefly employed by quacks. I want a person’s flower and fruit, some fragrance drifting from him toward me, some ripeness flavoring our intercourse. His goodness should be no isolated, temporary act but an unceasing surplus, costing him nothing and escaping his notice. Such charity covers a multitude of sins. Too often philanthropists surround humanity with an atmosphere of remembered troubles they themselves have discarded, calling it sympathy. We should communicate courage rather than despair, health and ease rather than illness, taking care not to spread illness by contagion. From which southern plains rises that wailing? In what latitudes live the heathens we want to enlighten? Who is the drunken, brutal man we want to redeem? Let someone suffer any ailment that impairs his functions—even a bowel pain, for sympathy has its seat there—and immediately he starts reforming the world. A miniature world himself, he discovers—truly, and he is the very man to discover it—that the world has been eating green apples. Indeed, he sees the globe itself as a huge green apple, in terrible danger of being nibbled by humanity’s children before ripening. His drastic philanthropy promptly seeks the Esquimaux and Patagonian and embraces crowded Indian and Chinese villages. A few years of such charitable activity, during which the powers doubtless use him for their own purposes, cures his indigestion. The globe develops a faint blush on one or both cheeks, seemingly beginning to ripen; life loses its rawness and becomes sweet and wholesome again. I have never imagined a greater enormity than one I have committed. I never have known, and never shall know, anyone worse than myself.

I believe reformers’ deep sadness comes not from sympathy with suffering neighbors but from a private ailment, however holy a son of God a reformer may be. Cure that; let spring reach him and morning rise over his couch, and he will abandon his generous companions without apology. My excuse for not lecturing against tobacco is that I never chewed it: such lectures are the penalty reformed chewers pay. I have, however, chewed plenty of other things I could lecture against. If ever tempted into one of these philanthropies, keep your left hand ignorant of your right hand’s actions: they are not worth knowing. Rescue a drowning person and tie your shoelaces. Take your time and undertake some freely chosen labor.

Association with saints has corrupted our manners. Our hymnbooks melodiously curse God and endure him forever. Even prophets and redeemers seem to have soothed human fears more than strengthened human hopes. Nowhere is a simple, irrepressible delight in life’s gift recorded, any memorable praise of God. All health and success benefit me, however remote and secluded they seem; every illness and failure saddens and harms me, however sympathetically we regard each other. If we truly want to restore humanity by Indian, botanical, magnetic, or natural methods, let us first become as simple and healthy as Nature ourselves. Clear the clouds from our own foreheads and absorb a little life through our pores. Do not linger as an overseer of the poor; try instead to become one of the world’s worthy people.

In Sheik Sadi of Shiraz’s Gulistan, or Flower Garden, I read: “They asked a wise man: Among the many celebrated trees the Most High God created tall and shady, why is only the fruitless cypress called azad, or free? What is the mystery? He answered: Each tree has its proper produce and appointed season, when it stands fresh and flowering; outside that season it grows dry and withered. The cypress undergoes neither condition, always flourishing. Such are the azads, the religious independents. Set no heart on passing things: the Dijlah, or Tigris, will still run through Bagdad when the line of caliphs is extinct. If your hand holds plenty, give generously like the date tree; if it has nothing to give, be an azad, a free man, like the cypress.”
COMPLEMENTARY VERSES
The Pretensions of Poverty

“You presume too much, poor needy wretch,
To claim a place among the stars
Because your humble cottage, or your tub,
Nurtures some idle or pedantic virtue
In cheap sunshine or beside shaded springs,
With roots and garden herbs; where your right hand,
Tearing those human passions from the mind
On whose stocks virtues bloom so beautifully,
Degrades our nature and numbs our senses,
And, like a Gorgon, turns active people into stone.
We do not need the dreary company
Of your temperance imposed by want,
Or that unnatural numbness
That knows neither joy nor sorrow; nor your forced
Passive endurance falsely raised
Above the active kind. This low, abject brood,
Settling themselves in mediocrity,
Suits your servile minds; but we promote
Only those virtues that allow excess:
Brave, generous deeds, royal magnificence,
All-seeing prudence, greatness of soul
Knowing no limit, and that heroic virtue
For which antiquity left us no name,
Only examples: Hercules,
Achilles, Theseus. Back to your hated cell;
And when you see the newly lighted sphere,
Study merely to learn what those worthies were.”
T. CAREW

chapters.title: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For
paragraphs: At a certain stage of life we tend to look at every place as a possible spot for a house. In this way I have surveyed the countryside in every direction for a dozen miles around my home. In my imagination I have bought every farm, one after another; all were for sale, and I knew their prices. I walked over each farmer’s land, sampled his wild apples, talked farming with him, and bought his farm at his price—at any price—mortgaging it back to him in my mind. I even put a higher value on it. I took everything except the deed, taking his word for his deed instead, for I dearly love conversation. I cultivated the farm, and, I hope, cultivated the farmer a little too. When I had enjoyed it long enough I withdrew, leaving him to carry on. These experiences gave my friends grounds to regard me as a sort of real-estate broker. Wherever I sat could be my home, and the landscape spread outward from me accordingly. What is a house but a _sedes_, a seat? Better still, a country seat. I found many places for a house that nobody was likely to develop soon. Some people might have considered them too far from the village; to my eyes the village was too far from them. Well, I could live there, I said. And there, for an hour, I did live through summer and winter, watching how I might let the years pass, weather the winter, and welcome the spring. Wherever future inhabitants of this region put their houses, they may be sure I have been there before them. An afternoon was enough to divide the land into orchard, woodlot, and pasture, choose which fine oaks or pines should remain before the door, and decide the best viewpoint for each blasted tree. Then I left it alone, perhaps lying fallow. A man’s wealth is in proportion to the number of things he can afford to leave alone.

My imagination took me so far that I even secured first refusal on several farms; refusal was all I wanted. But actual ownership never burned my fingers. The closest I came was buying the Hollowell place. I had begun sorting seeds and gathering materials for a wheelbarrow to carry it on—or off—with. Before the owner handed over the deed, however, his wife—every man has such a wife—changed her mind and wanted to keep it. He offered me ten dollars to let him out of the bargain. Now, in truth, I possessed only ten cents in the world. It was beyond my arithmetic to decide whether I was the man with ten cents, with a farm, with ten dollars, or with all of them together. Anyway, I let him keep both the ten dollars and the farm: I had carried it far enough. Or, to put it generously, I sold him back the farm for exactly what I had paid, and, since he was not wealthy, gave him ten dollars as a present. I still had my ten cents, my seeds, and my wheelbarrow materials. So I found I had been rich without doing any damage to my poverty. I did keep the landscape, though, and every year since I have carried away its harvest without a wheelbarrow. As for landscapes:—

“I am monarch of all I _survey_,
My right there is none to dispute.”

I have often watched a poet leave a farm after enjoying its most valuable part, while the sour old farmer imagined he had taken only a few wild apples. Why, years may pass before an owner discovers that a poet has put his farm into verse, the finest sort of invisible fence. He has thoroughly impounded it, milked it, skimmed it, taken all the cream, and left the farmer nothing but skimmed milk.

What really drew me to the Hollowell farm was its seclusion. It lay about two miles from the village and half a mile from the nearest neighbor, with a wide field separating it from the highway. It bordered the river, whose fogs, the owner said, protected it from spring frosts, although that did not matter to me. The gray, ruined house and barn and the broken-down fences put a comforting distance between me and the last occupant. Hollow apple trees, covered in lichens and gnawed by rabbits, showed me what neighbors I would have. Above all, I remembered it from my earliest trips upriver, when a thick grove of red maples hid the house and I could hear the house-dog barking through the trees. I wanted to buy before the owner finished removing some rocks, felling the hollow apple trees, and digging out young birches that had sprung up in the pasture—in short, before he made any more improvements. To enjoy these advantages, I was willing to run the farm, to shoulder the world like Atlas—I never heard what he was paid for that—and to do all the things that had no purpose or excuse except to pay for it and secure my undisturbed possession. All the while I knew it would produce the richest possible crop of what I wanted if only I could afford to leave it alone. But the outcome was as I have described.

All I could claim, then, about farming on a large scale—I have always kept a garden—was that I had my seeds ready. Many people believe seeds grow better with age. I do not doubt that time separates good ones from bad, so when I finally plant mine I shall be less likely to suffer disappointment. But let me tell my fellows once and for all: remain free and uncommitted as long as you possibly can. There is little difference between being committed to a farm and being committed to the county jail.

Old Cato, whose “De Re Rusticâ” serves as my “Cultivator,” says the following; the only translation I have seen turns the passage into complete nonsense: “When you think of getting a farm, turn it thus in your mind, not to buy greedily; nor spare your pains to look at it, and do not think it enough to go round it once. The oftener you go there the more it will please you, if it is good.” I believe I shall avoid buying greedily. Instead I will keep walking round it throughout my life, and be buried in it first, so that at last it may please me all the more.

The experiment I now describe was my next attempt of this kind. I intend to tell it at greater length, gathering two years of experience into one for convenience. As I have said, I am not setting out to compose an ode to misery. I mean to crow as vigorously as a cock on his morning roost, if only to wake my neighbors.

When I first moved into the woods—began sleeping there as well as spending my days there—my house was not ready for winter. This happened, by chance, on Independence Day, the Fourth of July, 1845. The house was only a shelter against rain, without plaster or chimney. Rough, weather-stained boards formed its walls, with broad gaps between them that made the nights cool. Its upright, freshly hewn white studs and newly planed door and window frames gave it a clean, airy appearance, especially in the morning when dew soaked the timbers. I imagined that by noon they might ooze some fragrant gum. To my eyes the house kept something of that dawnlike quality all day, recalling a mountain house I had visited the previous year. It was an airy, unplastered cabin, fit to receive a traveling god, a place where a goddess might let her garments trail. The winds over my home were like those sweeping mountain ridges, carrying broken phrases of earthly music, or only its heavenly parts. The morning wind never stops blowing; creation’s poem continues without a break, though few ears hear it. Everywhere, Olympus is simply the earth’s outer surface.

Apart from a boat, the only house I had owned before was a tent, which I sometimes took on summer excursions. It still lies rolled up in my attic, but the boat passed from owner to owner and has drifted down the stream of time. Now that a more solid shelter surrounded me, I had made some progress toward settling in the world. Its lightly covered frame was a sort of crystallization around me, and it acted in turn upon its builder. Like an outline drawing, it left room for suggestion. I had no need to step outside for fresh air: the air indoors had lost none of its freshness. Even in the wettest weather, I was sitting less indoors than behind a door. The Harivansa says, “An abode without birds is like a meat without seasoning.” My home was not like that, for suddenly I found myself a neighbor of the birds, not by imprisoning one, but by putting myself in a cage near them. I was closer not only to birds that regularly visit gardens and orchards, but also to the forest’s wilder, more thrilling singers, who seldom or never serenade villagers: the wood-thrush, veery, scarlet tanager, field-sparrow, whippoorwill, and many others.

My seat was beside a small pond, about a mile and a half south of Concord village and a little above it. It lay in a large wood between Concord and Lincoln, about two miles south of our only field known to fame, Concord Battle Ground. Yet I was so low among the trees that my farthest horizon was the opposite shore, half a mile away and wooded like all the rest. Throughout the first week, each view of the pond suggested a mountain tarn lying high on a mountainside, its bottom well above the surface of other lakes. As the sun rose, I watched it shed its nighttime covering of mist. Here and there its gentle ripples or smooth, reflecting surface gradually appeared, while the mists slipped like ghosts into the woods in every direction, as though a secret midnight assembly were breaking up. Even the dew seemed to linger on the trees later than usual, as it does on mountainsides.

The little lake was most valuable as a neighbor during pauses in a gentle August rainstorm. Air and water would both be utterly still beneath an overcast sky, and midafternoon had all the calm of evening. Wood-thrushes sang nearby and could be heard from one shore to the other. A lake like this is never smoother than at such moments. With only a shallow layer of clear air above it, darkened by clouds, its bright, reflecting water becomes a lower heaven, all the more important for that. A nearby hilltop, recently cleared of trees, offered a lovely southward view across the pond through a broad gap in the surrounding hills. Their facing slopes suggested a stream flowing that way through a wooded valley, although no stream existed. In that direction I could look between and over the close green hills toward higher, more distant ones, blue on the horizon. Standing on tiptoe, I could even glimpse peaks of the still bluer and more distant mountain ranges to the northwest—those true-blue coins struck in heaven’s own mint—and a little of the village too. In other directions, however, even from this height I could not see above or beyond the woods surrounding me. It is good to have water nearby, to buoy up the earth and set it afloat. Even the smallest well has this value: looking into it, you discover that the earth is an island, not a continent. That matters as much as keeping the butter cool. From this height I looked across the pond toward the Sudbury meadows. When flooded, they seemed raised in their seething valley, perhaps by a mirage, like a coin seen in a basin. All the land beyond the pond appeared a thin crust, cut off and floated even by this small sheet of water between us. It reminded me that the ground I lived on was only _dry land_.

Although the view from my door was narrower still, I never felt cramped or shut in. My imagination had plenty of grazing room. The opposite shore rose to a low plateau of scrub oaks, stretching away toward the western prairies and the steppes of Tartary, with abundant space for all humanity’s wandering families. When his herds needed fresh, more extensive pastures, Damodara said, “There are none happy in the world but beings who enjoy freely a vast horizon.”

Place and time had both altered. I lived closer to the regions of the universe and the periods of history that had always drawn me most strongly. My home was as remote as many of the regions astronomers study each night. We tend to imagine rare and delightful places tucked into some distant, more heavenly corner of the system, beyond the constellation of Cassiopeia’s Chair, far from noise and disruption. I discovered that my house really did stand in just such a secluded part of the universe, forever fresh and unprofaned. If it was worthwhile to settle near the Pleiades or the Hyades, Aldebaran or Altair, then that was where I really was—or at an equal distance from the life I had left. To my nearest neighbor I had dwindled to a tiny, delicate ray of twinkling light, visible only on moonless nights. Such was the corner of creation where I had squatted:—

“There lived a shepherd once,
Who kept his thoughts as high
As the mountains where his flocks
Would feed beside him hour by hour.”
What would we think of a shepherd’s life if his sheep always reached higher pastures than his thoughts did?

Each morning cheerfully invited me to make my life as simple, and I may say as innocent, as Nature herself. I have worshipped Aurora as sincerely as the Greeks did. I rose early and bathed in the pond, a religious observance and one of the best things I did. They say that king Tching-thang’s bathing tub bore an inscription meaning: “Renew thyself completely each day; do it again, and again, and forever again.” I understand that. Morning restores the heroic ages. Sitting at earliest dawn with door and windows open, I was moved by a mosquito’s faint hum as it traveled its invisible, unimaginable circuit through my room as deeply as by any trumpet that ever proclaimed fame. It was Homer’s requiem, an Iliad and an Odyssey of its own in the air, singing its own anger and wanderings. Something cosmic lived in it: a standing announcement, to remain until forbidden, of the world’s unending energy and fertility. Morning, the day’s most memorable season, is the hour of waking. We are least sleepy then; for at least an hour, a part of us wakes that sleeps through the rest of the day and night. Little can be expected from a day—if it deserves the name—when some servant’s mechanical nudging wakes us instead of our Genius. We should wake through fresh strength and aspirations rising within us, to the swell of heavenly music rather than factory bells, with fragrance filling the air, and enter a life higher than the one from which we fell asleep. Then darkness bears its fruit and proves as good as light. Whoever does not believe that every day holds an earlier, more sacred hour of dawn than any he has yet profaned has despaired of life and taken a descending road into darkness. After our life of the senses has partly rested, the human soul—or rather its organs—gains fresh vigor each day, and its Genius tries once more to see what noble life it can create. I would say that every memorable event happens at morning, in a morning atmosphere. The Vedas say, “All intelligences awake with the morning.” Poetry, art, and the finest and most memorable human deeds originate in such an hour. Like Memnon, all poets and heroes are Aurora’s children, sounding their music at sunrise. For someone whose supple, vigorous thought keeps pace with the sun, the day remains morning forever. Clocks, human postures, and human occupations make no difference. Morning comes when I am awake and a dawn rises within me. Moral reform is an effort to shake off sleep. Why do people give such a poor account of their day, unless they have been dozing? Their arithmetic is not that bad. Had drowsiness not overcome them, they would have accomplished something. Millions are awake enough to work with their bodies; only one in a million is awake enough for effective work of the mind, and only one in a hundred million for a poetic or divine life. Being awake is being alive. I have never met anyone completely awake. How could I have looked such a person in the face?

We must learn to wake again and stay awake through an endless expectation of dawn that remains with us even in our deepest sleep, rather than through mechanical assistance. Nothing I know is more encouraging than the undeniable human ability to raise the quality of life by deliberate effort. Being able to paint a picture or carve a statue, making a few objects beautiful, is an achievement. But how much more glorious to paint and carve the very atmosphere, the medium through which we see. Morally, we can do that. The highest art is to change the quality of the day. Each person’s task is to make his life, down to its details, worthy of consideration in his loftiest and most discerning hour. If we rejected—or, better, exhausted—the scraps of information we receive, the oracles would tell us clearly how to do it.

I went into the woods because I wanted to live deliberately, facing only life’s essential facts, to discover what it could teach me, so that when I came to die I would not discover I had never lived. Life is too precious to spend on something that is not life; nor did I want to practice resignation unless it was absolutely necessary. I wanted to live deeply and suck all the marrow out of life, to live with such sturdy Spartan discipline that everything that was not life would be driven out. I wanted to mow a broad swath and shave close, force life into a corner, and reduce it to its simplest terms. If it turned out to be mean, I wanted to grasp its whole, authentic meanness and announce it to the world. If it was sublime, I wanted to know that firsthand and give a truthful account of it on my next excursion. Most people, it seems to me, remain strangely unsure whether life belongs to the devil or to God. They have decided _somewhat hastily_ that humanity’s chief purpose here is to “glorify God and enjoy him forever.”

Yet we go on living meanly, like ants, although the fable says we were transformed into people long ago. Like pygmies, we battle cranes. We pile error on error and patch on patch; even our finest virtue arises from unnecessary misery that could have been avoided. Details fritter our lives away. An honest man scarcely needs to count beyond his ten fingers; in an emergency he can add his ten toes and bundle the rest together. Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity! Keep your affairs to two or three, I say, instead of a hundred or a thousand. Count half a dozen instead of a million, and fit your accounts onto your thumbnail. Civilized life is such a choppy sea, with so many clouds, storms, quicksands, and a thousand and one other matters to reckon with, that anyone hoping to reach port instead of foundering and sinking must navigate by dead reckoning. Whoever succeeds must be a prodigious calculator. Simplify, simplify. If necessary, eat one meal a day instead of three, five dishes instead of a hundred, and cut everything else down in proportion. Our lives resemble a German Confederacy made up of petty states, with borders forever shifting so that not even a German can tell you their position at any given moment. The nation itself, with its so-called internal improvements—which, incidentally, are entirely outward and superficial—is as cumbersome and overgrown as the million households that compose it. It is stuffed with furniture, trips over its own traps, and is ruined by luxury, careless spending, poor calculation, and the absence of a worthy goal. For the nation as for its households, the only remedy is strict economy, a stern simplicity beyond even the Spartans’, and a higher purpose. It lives too fast. People are certain that the _Nation_ must trade, export ice, communicate by telegraph, and travel thirty miles an hour, whether _they_ do or not. Whether we ought to live as baboons or as human beings remains a little uncertain. If we stop cutting sleepers and forging rails, stop working day and night, and start tinkering with our _lives_ to improve _them_, who will construct the railroads? Without railroads, how will we reach heaven in time? But if we stay home and attend to our own affairs, who will need railroads? We do not ride upon the railroad; it rides upon us. Have you ever considered what the sleepers underneath the rails are? Each is a man, an Irishman or a Yankee. Rails are laid across them, sand covers them, and the cars roll smoothly overhead. They are sound sleepers, I assure you. Every few years another set is laid down and run over: some enjoy riding on a rail, while others suffer being ridden upon. When the cars run over a man walking in his sleep—an extra sleeper lying the wrong way—and wake him, they suddenly stop and raise a tremendous outcry, as though something exceptional had happened. I am glad it already takes a gang of men for every five miles to keep the sleepers down and level in their beds. That suggests they may rise again someday.

Why rush through life and waste it this way? We insist on starving before we are hungry. People say a stitch in time saves nine, so they sew a thousand stitches today to save nine tomorrow. As for _work_, we have none of real importance. We have Saint Vitus’ dance and cannot possibly hold our heads still. If I merely tugged the parish bell-rope a few times as a fire alarm, without setting the bell swinging, scarcely a farmer on Concord’s outskirts would fail to drop everything and follow the sound, despite the urgent business he had pleaded so often that morning. I could almost say the same of every boy and woman. Their chief aim would not be saving property from the flames. Let us admit it: they would much rather watch it burn, since burn it must, and everyone should understand that we did not start the fire. Or they might watch it being put out and lend a hand, if that offered an equally fine performance—even if the building were the parish church. Hardly anyone wakes from a half-hour nap after dinner without raising his head and asking, “What’s the news?” as though everyone else had stood guard for him. Some order themselves wakened every half hour, surely for this purpose alone; to repay the service, they recount their dreams. After a night’s sleep, news is as indispensable as breakfast. “Pray tell me any thing new that has happened to a man any where on this globe,” he asks, and over coffee and rolls reads that someone had his eyes gouged out that morning on the Wachito River. It never occurs to him that he himself inhabits this world’s dark, unfathomed mammoth cave and possesses only the beginnings of an eye.

For myself, I could readily dispense with the post office. Very little of importance, I think, passes through it. Judging strictly, I have received only one or two letters in my life worth their postage—I wrote this some years ago. The penny-post generally lets you make in earnest the offer you can so safely make in jest: a penny for someone’s thoughts. I am also certain I have never found memorable news in a newspaper. Read once about a man robbed, murdered, or accidentally killed; a house burned; a ship wrecked; a steamboat exploded; a cow run over on the Western Railroad; a rabid dog killed; or grasshoppers appearing in winter, and there is no need to read another example. Once is enough. If you understand the principle, why bother with thousands of instances and applications? To a philosopher, everything called _news_ is gossip, and its editors and readers are old women over their tea. Yet many people hunger for this gossip. I hear that the other day people pressed so eagerly into a newspaper office to learn the foreign news from the latest arrival that they broke several large panes of plate glass. I honestly believe a quick-witted person could write that news a year, or twelve years, ahead with sufficient accuracy. Take Spain: scatter Don Carlos and the Infanta, Don Pedro, Seville, and Granada in the right proportions from time to time—the names may have changed a little since I last read the papers—and supply a bullfight when other entertainments run short. The result will be true to the letter and show Spain’s exact condition or ruin as well as the clearest, most concise newspaper reports. As for England, almost the last significant news from there was the revolution of 1649. Once you know the history of her crops in an average year, you need never attend to the subject again, unless your speculations are purely financial. If someone who rarely reads newspapers may judge, nothing new ever happens abroad, not even a French revolution.

News indeed! How much more important to discover what has never grown old! “Kieou-he-yu (great dignitary of the state of Wei) sent a man to Khoung-tseu to know his news. Khoung-tseu caused the messenger to be seated near him, and questioned him in these terms: What is your master doing? The messenger answered with respect: My master desires to diminish the number of his faults, but he cannot come to the end of them. The messenger being gone, the philosopher remarked: What a worthy messenger! What a worthy messenger!” Instead of tormenting sleepy farmers’ ears with yet another bedraggled sermon on their day of rest at the week’s end—for Sunday appropriately concludes a badly spent week rather than freshly and bravely beginning a new one—the preacher should thunder, “Pause! Avast! Why so seeming fast, but deadly slow?”

We prize frauds and illusions as the most reliable truths, while reality seems a fable. If people steadily attended to realities alone and refused to be deceived, life would resemble, to compare it with things we know, a fairy tale or the Arabian Nights’ Entertainments. If we honored only what is inevitable and has a right to exist, music and poetry would echo in the streets. When we are calm and wise, we see that only great, worthy things possess a lasting, absolute existence; little fears and little pleasures merely cast reality’s shadow. Seeing this is always exhilarating and sublime. By shutting their eyes, dozing, and agreeing to be fooled by appearances, people everywhere establish and reinforce their daily round of habits and routines, still resting on wholly imaginary foundations. Children playing at life understand its true laws and relationships better than adults who fail to live it worthily, yet think experience—that is, failure—has made them wiser. In a Hindoo book I read that “there was a king’s son, who, being expelled in infancy from his native city, was brought up by a forester, and, growing up to maturity in that state, imagined himself to belong to the barbarous race with which he lived. One of his father’s ministers having discovered him, revealed to him what he was, and the misconception of his character was removed, and he knew himself to be a prince. So soul,” the Hindoo philosopher continues, “from the circumstances in which it is placed, mistakes its own character, until the truth is revealed to it by some holy teacher, and then it knows itself to be _Brahme_.” I see that we New Englanders live such a mean life because our sight does not reach beneath the surface. We suppose that what _appears_ to be _is_. If someone walked through this town seeing only reality, what do you think would become of the “Mill-dam”? If he described the realities he saw there, we would never recognize the place. Look at a meeting-house, courthouse, jail, shop, or home, and describe what it actually is to a truthful gaze: in that description every one would fall to pieces. People imagine truth to be far away, on the system’s outskirts beyond the farthest star, before Adam and after the last human being. Eternity does indeed hold something true and sublime. But all these times, places, and occasions are here and now. God himself reaches his height in the present moment and will never become more divine throughout all the ages. We can perceive anything sublime or noble only because surrounding reality continually seeps into us and drenches us. The universe answers our conceptions constantly and obediently. Fast or slow, we travel on a track laid for us. Let us devote our lives, then, to conceiving. No poet or artist has imagined a design so beautiful and noble that at least some of his descendants could not carry it out.

Let us live one day with Nature’s deliberation, refusing to be derailed by every nutshell or mosquito wing that lands on the track. Let us rise early and fast—or break our fast—quietly and untroubled. Let visitors come and go, let bells ring and children cry: we will make a day of it. Why surrender and drift with the current? Let us not capsize and drown in that dreadful rapid and whirlpool called dinner, lying in the shallows of midday. Survive that danger and you are safe; the rest of the journey runs downhill. With nerves still firm and morning energy unspent, sail past looking the other way, bound to the mast like Ulysses. Let the engine whistle itself hoarse if it likes. Why run because a bell rings? We can consider what sort of music these sounds resemble. Let us stand firmly and work our feet downward, wedging through the mud and slush of opinion, prejudice, tradition, delusion, and appearance—the sediment covering the globe. Down through Paris and London, New York and Boston and Concord; through church and state, poetry and philosophy and religion; down until we reach a solid bottom and bedrock we can call _reality_, and say: This is, beyond mistake. Then we can begin, with a _point d’appui_, a firm support beneath flood, frost, and fire, where we could build a wall or a state, plant a lamp-post securely, or perhaps place a gauge. Not a Nilometer but a Realometer, so future ages could measure how deep the floods of sham and appearance had risen from time to time. Stand directly before a fact, face to face, and you will see sunlight glint on both its surfaces as on a scimitar. You will feel its sweet edge divide you through heart and marrow, bringing your mortal career to a happy close. In life or death, reality alone is what we crave. If we are truly dying, let us hear the rattle in our throats and feel our hands and feet grow cold. If we are alive, let us get on with our business.

Time is only the stream where I fish. I drink from it, yet as I drink I see the sandy bottom and notice its shallowness. Its slender current passes away; eternity stays. I would drink from deeper waters and fish in the sky, whose bed is strewn with the pebbles of stars. I cannot count even one. I do not know the alphabet’s first letter. I have always regretted being less wise than I was on the day of my birth. The intellect is a cleaver: it sees into things and splits its way to their secret. I want to do no more work with my hands than necessary. My head serves as hands and feet; I feel all my finest powers gathered there. Instinct tells me my head is a digging organ, like the snout and forepaws of certain creatures. With it I would tunnel and mine through these hills. I believe the richest vein lies somewhere nearby; that is what the divining rod and the thin, rising vapors tell me. Here I shall start to mine.

chapters.title: Reading
paragraphs: If people took a little more care in choosing what to do with their lives, perhaps everyone would become, in essence, a student and an observer. Surely our nature and our destiny interest us all equally. When we gather property for ourselves or our descendants, establish a family or a state, or even win fame, we are mortal. But when we engage with truth, we are immortal, and need fear neither change nor accident. The earliest Egyptian or Hindoo philosopher lifted a corner of the veil covering the statue of the divinity. That trembling robe is still lifted, and the glory I look upon is as fresh as the glory he saw: it was I within him who dared to lift it then, and it is he within me who now looks at the vision again. Not a speck of dust has settled on that robe; no time has passed since the divinity was revealed. The time we truly put to use, or can put to use, belongs neither to the past, the present, nor the future.

The place where I lived suited serious reading, as well as thinking, better than a university would have. Although I was out of reach of the ordinary lending library, I had come more fully than ever within the reach of those books that travel around the world: books whose sentences were first inscribed on bark and are now simply copied onto linen paper from time to time. The poet Mîr Camar Uddîn Mast says, “Being seated to run through the region of the spiritual world; I have had this advantage in books. To be intoxicated by a single glass of wine; I have experienced this pleasure when I have drunk the liquor of the esoteric doctrines.” All summer I kept Homer’s Iliad on my table, although I turned to its pages only occasionally. At first the unceasing work of my hands left no room for further study: I had to finish building my house and hoe my beans at the same time. Still, the thought of reading like this in the future sustained me. During breaks in my work I read one or two superficial travel books, until spending my time that way made me ashamed of myself, and I began to ask where, after all, _I_ was living.

A student can read Homer or Æschylus in Greek without the danger of becoming dissipated or self-indulgent. Such reading asks him, to some extent, to follow the example of their heroes and to devote his mornings to their pages. Heroic books will always speak a language dead to degraded times, even when they are printed in the letters of our native tongue. We must work patiently to discover the meaning of every word and line, drawing on whatever wisdom, courage, and generosity we possess to imagine a meaning beyond the one ordinary usage allows. With all its translations, today’s cheap and prolific printing press has brought us little closer to the heroic writers of antiquity. They remain as solitary as ever, and the type in which we find them seems as rare and strange. Days of youth and precious hours are well spent if all you gain is a few words of an ancient language, lifted above the trivial talk of the street to become lasting suggestions and challenges. The farmer who remembers and repeats the few Latin words he has heard does not do so in vain. People sometimes talk as though the classics must eventually give way to more modern and practical subjects. But an adventurous student will always study the classics, whatever their language and however old they are. What are classics, after all, but the noblest human thoughts ever set down? They alone are oracles that have not fallen into decay, and they offer answers to our most modern questions such as Delphi and Dodona never gave. We might as sensibly stop studying Nature because she is old. Reading well—reading true books in a truthful spirit—is a noble exercise, and it demands more of the reader than any exercise honored by the habits of our time. It calls for the kind of discipline athletes underwent, for a steady dedication to this purpose through almost a whole lifetime. We must read books with the same deliberation and restraint with which they were written. Even speaking the language of the nation that produced them is not enough. A remarkable distance separates spoken language from written language, the language we hear from the language we read. The first is usually fleeting: a sound, a tongue, a mere dialect, almost animal; like animals, we learn it unconsciously from our mothers. The second is that language grown mature and experienced. If the first is our mother tongue, the second is our father tongue: a restrained and chosen expression, too full of meaning for the ear to take in, which we must be born again to speak. The multitudes who merely _spoke_ Greek and Latin during the Middle Ages did not acquire, by the accident of birth, the ability to _read_ the works of genius in those languages. Those works were written not in the Greek or Latin they knew, but in the chosen language of literature. They had never learned the nobler dialects of Greece and Rome. Even the materials on which these works were written were waste paper to them; they preferred cheap literature of their own day. Learning first revived when the separate nations of Europe developed distinct written languages of their own, rough though they were, sufficient for their emerging literatures. From that distance, scholars could at last recognize the treasures of antiquity. What the Greek and Roman multitudes could not _hear_, a few scholars _read_ after centuries had passed; and only a few scholars are still reading it.

However much we admire a public speaker’s occasional flights of eloquence, the noblest written words usually lie as far beyond or above passing speech as the starry heavens lie beyond the clouds. _There_ the stars stand, for anyone able to read them. Astronomers continually observe them and write their commentaries. They are no passing vapors like our daily conversations and the mist of our breath. What passes for eloquence in a public assembly generally turns out to be mere rhetoric when examined in the study. The speaker gives himself to the inspiration of a passing occasion and addresses the crowd in front of him, the people who can _hear_ him. The writer’s occasion is his own more even life; the event and the crowd that inspire the speaker would distract him. He addresses the intelligence and soundness of humanity, everyone in every age who can _understand_ him.

It is hardly surprising that Alexander took the Iliad on his campaigns in a precious casket. A written word is the finest relic we possess.
