There were men with one idea, like hens with a single chick that turns out to be a duckling; men with a thousand ideas and untidy heads, like hens entrusted with a hundred chicks all chasing one insect, twenty lost in every morning’s dew, leaving the hens frizzled and mangy. There were people with ideas for legs, intellectual centipedes that made your skin crawl. Someone suggested a visitors’ book for signatures, as at the White Mountains. Alas! my memory is too good to require one.

Certain features of my visitors were impossible to miss. Boys, girls, and young women generally enjoyed the woods, looking into the pond, noticing flowers, and using their time well. Businessmen, even farmers, thought only of isolation, occupation, and how far I lived from one thing or another. Although they claimed to enjoy occasional woodland walks, plainly they did not. Restless men tied to commitments spent all their time earning or preserving a living. Ministers spoke as though God were their exclusive subject and could not tolerate every sort of opinion. Doctors, lawyers, anxious housekeepers inspecting my cupboard and bed while I was away—how did Mrs. —— discover my sheets were less clean than hers?—and young men no longer young, convinced the professions’ beaten path was safest: all generally said my position prevented doing as much good. Ah, there was the difficulty! The old, infirm, and timid of any sex or age thought chiefly of illness, sudden accidents, and death. Life seemed perilous to them—what danger exists if you think of none?—and prudence meant choosing the safest spot, with Dr. B. available at a moment’s notice. The village was literally their _com-munity_, an alliance for mutual defense. You would suppose they required a medicine chest to pick huckleberries. The whole matter comes to this: as long as a person remains alive there is always a _danger_ that he may die, though admittedly that danger becomes smaller in proportion as he was already half dead and half alive to begin with. A person sits as many risks as he runs. Finally came self-declared reformers, the worst bores, imagining I sang continually:—

This is the house I have built;
This is the man living in the house I have built.
But they never knew what the third line said.

These are the people who trouble the man
Who lives in the house I have built.
Since I kept no chickens, hen-harriers did not frighten me; it was the men-harriers I feared instead.

Other visitors cheered me more than these. Children picking berries, railroad workers walking on Sunday mornings in clean shirts, anglers and hunters, poets and philosophers—in short, every honest pilgrim entering the woods for freedom and truly leaving the village behind—received my ready greeting: “Welcome, Englishmen! welcome, Englishmen!” For I had communicated with that race.

chapters.title: The Bean-Field
paragraphs: Meanwhile my planted bean rows, seven miles long altogether, clamored for hoeing. The earliest had grown considerably before the last went into the ground; postponement was not easy. I did not know what this steady, self-respecting little Herculean labor meant. I grew fond of the rows and their beans, far more than I needed. They bound me to the earth and gave me strength like Antæus. But why grow them? Heaven alone knows. All summer this was my peculiar task: to make ground formerly producing cinquefoil, blackberries, johnswort, and other sweet wild fruits and pleasant flowers produce this legume instead. What would beans teach me, or I teach beans? I nurture and hoe them, watching them early and late; that is my day’s work. Their broad leaves are handsome. Dew and rain watering the dry ground assist me, along with whatever fertility remains in its generally lean, exhausted soil. My enemies are worms, cold days, and above all woodchucks, which have nibbled a quarter-acre bare. Yet what right had I to displace johnswort and its companions, breaking up their ancient herb garden? Soon, however, the surviving beans will be too tough for woodchucks and advance to confront fresh enemies.

I clearly remember being brought from Boston to my native town at four years old, through these same woods and this field to the pond. It is among the earliest scenes impressed on my memory. Tonight my flute has awakened echoes across that very water. Pines older than I still stand; where some have fallen, their stumps have cooked my supper. New growth rises everywhere, preparing a fresh view for new infant eyes. Almost the same johnswort sprouts from the same perennial roots here. Even I have finally helped clothe that fabulous landscape of childhood dreams: these bean leaves, corn blades, and potato vines show something of my presence and influence.

I planted roughly two and a half acres of upland. Since it had been cleared only fifteen years earlier, and I myself had removed two or three cords of stumps, I added no manure. But arrowheads turned up by my hoe that summer revealed that a vanished people had lived here long before white settlers cleared the land. They had grown corn and beans, already exhausting the soil to some degree for precisely this crop.

Before woodchuck or squirrel crossed the road, before the sun rose above the scrub oaks, while dew still covered everything, I began overthrowing the proud ranks of weeds and heaping dust on their heads. Farmers warned against it; I advise doing all your work in the dew, if possible. Early I worked barefoot, dabbling like a sculptor in damp, crumbling sand; later sunlight blistered my feet. The sun lit my hoeing as I paced slowly back and forth along fifteen-rod green rows on the yellow, gravelly upland. One end reached scrub-oak thickets offering shade; the other a blackberry field, where green berries deepened in color by the time I made another circuit. Pulling weeds, drawing fresh earth around bean stems, encouraging the weed I had planted, persuading yellow soil to express its summer thoughts in bean flowers and leaves rather than wormwood, piper, and millet grass—making the earth say beans instead of grass—filled my days. Because I had very little assistance from horses or cattle, from men or boys hired to work beside me, or from improved farming implements, my progress was much slower than usual, and I became correspondingly more intimately acquainted with my own beans than farmers ordinarily do. Hand labor, even near drudgery, may never be the worst idleness. It carries an enduring moral and yields the scholar a classical result. To travelers heading west through Lincoln and Wayland toward nobody knows where, I was a true _agricola laboriosus_. They lounged in gigs, elbows on knees, reins hanging in loose loops; I was the hardworking, homebound native of the soil. Soon my homestead vanished from sight and thought. As the only cultivated clearing along a great stretch of either roadside, it received their full attention. Sometimes the worker heard more comments and gossip than intended: “Beans so late! Peas so late!” I was still planting when others began hoeing, unsuspected by the ministerial farmer. “Corn, my boy, for fodder; corn for fodder.” A black bonnet asks a gray coat, “Does he _live_ there?” A hard-faced farmer reins in his grateful dobbin to ask what you are doing without manure in the furrow, suggesting chip dirt, any waste material, or perhaps ashes or plaster. Here, though, were two and a half acres of furrows, a hoe for a cart, and two hands to pull it—I disliked other carts and horses—with chip dirt far away. Passing travelers compared it aloud to other fields, teaching me my standing in the agricultural world. Mr. Coleman’s report omitted this field. Incidentally, who values Nature’s crops in wilder fields untouched by people? _English_ hay is carefully weighed, its moisture, silicates, and potash calculated. Yet hollows and pond holes in woods, pastures, and swamps produce rich, varied crops that people alone leave unharvested. My field linked the wild and cultivated. As some states are civilized, others partly so, and others savage or barbarous, mine was half-cultivated, without disparagement. My beans cheerfully returned toward their wild, primitive condition while my hoe played them the _Ranz des Vaches_.

Nearby, on a birch’s highest twig, the brown-thrasher—or red mavis, as some prefer—sings all morning, enjoying your company. Without your field he would seek another farmer’s. As you plant, he calls, “Drop it, drop it,—cover it up, cover it up,—pull it up, pull it up, pull it up.” Mine was not corn, however, and was safe from his kind. You might wonder what this rigmarole, this amateur Paganini performance on one string or twenty, contributes to planting, yet prefer it to leached ashes or plaster. It was inexpensive top-dressing in which I had complete faith.

As I used my hoe to draw still fresher soil around the planted rows, I disturbed the ashes of peoples whose histories have never been recorded, nations that lived beneath these same heavens in the world’s earliest years. Their small implements for war and hunting were brought up again into the light of our modern day. They mingled with ordinary stones, some marked by Indian fires and some by sun, and with pottery and glass left by recent cultivators. The hoe’s tinkle against stones echoed into woods and sky, accompanying my work with an immediate, immeasurable harvest. I was no longer hoeing beans, nor was it I who hoed. If I remembered acquaintances attending city oratorios at all, pity mingled equally with pride. On sunny afternoons—for sometimes I worked all day—a nighthawk circled overhead like a speck in the eye, or heaven’s eye. Occasionally it swooped, sounding as though the sky tore into rags and tatters, yet leaving a seamless cloak. These little imps fill the air and lay eggs on bare sand or hilltop rocks where few find them. Slender and graceful, they seem ripples lifted from the pond, like leaves carried heavenward by wind: such kinship joins Nature. The hawk is the aerial brother of the wave it sails above and surveys, its perfect air-filled wings corresponding to the sea’s elementary, unfeathered pinions. Sometimes two hen-hawks circled high above, rising and falling in turn, approaching and separating, embodiments of my thoughts. Or wild pigeons hurried from wood to wood like messengers, with a soft quivering, winnowing sound. Or my hoe uncovered beneath a rotten stump a sluggish, strange, portentous spotted salamander, a trace of Egypt and the Nile yet living in our time. Pausing to lean on my hoe anywhere along a row, I encountered these sounds and sights, part of the countryside’s inexhaustible entertainment.

On festive days the town fires large guns that echo here like popguns, and stray scraps of military music sometimes reach the woods. In my bean-field at the town’s other end, the cannon sounded like a bursting puffball. During military gatherings I knew nothing about, I sometimes felt all day a vague itching or sickness on the horizon, as though scarlet fever or canker-rash were about to erupt there. Eventually a favorable gust hurried over fields and up the Wayland road, announcing the “trainers.” The distant hum suggested swarming bees, with neighbors following Virgil’s advice by softly ringing a _tintinnabulum_ on their most resonant household utensils to call them back into the hive. When the sound had faded completely away, the humming had entirely ceased, and even the most favorably directed breezes had no further story to tell me, I knew they had safely brought the very last drone of the whole company into the Middlesex hive. Now all their thoughts turned to the honey smeared within it.

I felt proud that Massachusetts’s liberties and those of our fatherland were guarded so securely. Returning to my hoe, I was filled with confidence beyond expression, and continued working cheerfully, with quiet faith in the future.

Several bands playing together made the entire village sound like enormous bellows, every building noisily swelling and collapsing in turn. Sometimes, though, a truly noble, inspiring melody reached the woods, a trumpet singing of fame. I felt ready to skewer a Mexican with real relish—why must we always hesitate over trifles?—and looked for a woodchuck or skunk on which to practice my chivalry. Those martial airs seemed as distant as Palestine, suggesting crusaders marching along the horizon amid faint galloping sounds and tremors in the village’s overhanging elm tops. This was one of the _great_ days. Yet from my clearing the sky wore its usual everlasting greatness, and I could detect no change.

Cultivating so long an acquaintance with beans was a peculiar experience: planting, hoeing, harvesting, threshing, sorting, and selling—the hardest part. I might add eating, since I did taste them. I was determined to know beans. During their growth I usually hoed from five in the morning until noon, devoting the afternoon to other affairs. Consider the curious intimacy one acquires with different weeds. Some repetition in telling is justified by the labor’s considerable repetition. Ruthlessly one disturbs their delicate structures and makes hostile distinctions with the hoe, destroying whole ranks of one species while carefully tending another. That is Roman wormwood, that pigweed, that sorrel, that piper-grass: attack, chop it, turn its roots toward the sun, leave no fiber shaded. Otherwise it will turn itself right side up and be green as a leek within two days. It was a long war against weeds instead of cranes, those Trojans aided by sunshine, rain, and dew. Daily the beans watched their rescuer arrive armed with a hoe, thinning enemy ranks and filling trenches with weedy corpses. Many a vigorous Hector, crest waving a foot above his crowded comrades, fell to my weapon and rolled in dust.

Thus I joined New England’s farmers in dedicating summer days to husbandry, while contemporaries devoted theirs to Boston’s or Rome’s fine arts, contemplation in India, or commerce in London or New York. I did not want beans for food. Where beans are concerned, whether porridge or voting, I am naturally a Pythagorean, and traded them for rice. Perhaps, though, someone must work the fields for metaphors and expressions, serving a future maker of parables. Overall it was rare amusement that might have become dissipation if prolonged. Although I used no manure and never finished hoeing the entire field once, what I did hoe I hoed exceptionally well, and it paid. As Evelyn says, “there is truly no compost or fertilization comparable to continually moving, redigging, and turning the soil with a spade.” Elsewhere he adds, “The earth, especially fresh earth, has a certain magnetism that draws the salt, power, or virtue—call it what you will—which gives it life. This explains all our labor and disturbance of it to sustain ourselves; manuring and other dirty mixtures are merely substitutes for this improvement.” Besides, as one of those “worn-out and exhausted fallow fields enjoying their sabbath,” it may, as Sir Kenelm Digby considered likely, have attracted “vital spirits” from the air. My harvest was twelve bushels of beans.
To give more detail, since people complain that Mr. Coleman chiefly reports gentlemen farmers’ costly experiments, here is exactly what I spent:—

One hoe: $0.54.
Plowing, harrowing, and making furrows: $7.50. Too much.
Seed beans: $3.12½.
Seed potatoes: $1.33.
Seed peas: $0.40.
Turnip seed: $0.06.
White cord for a crow fence: $0.02.
Horse cultivator and boy for three hours: $1.00.
Horse and cart to collect the crop: $0.75.
Total expenditure: $14.72½.
My receipts were as follows (patrem familias vendacem, non emacem esse oportet):

Nine bushels and twelve quarts of beans sold: $16.94.
Five bushels of large potatoes: $2.50.
Nine bushels of small potatoes: $2.25.
Grass: $1.00.
Stalks: $0.75.
Total income: $23.44.
The resulting cash profit, as I mentioned elsewhere, was $8.71½.

Here is what growing beans taught me. Around June 1, plant ordinary small white bush beans three feet between rows and eighteen inches apart, choosing fresh, round seed of an unmixed kind. First watch for worms and replant empty spots. Then, in exposed places, watch for woodchucks: they nibble the earliest tender leaves almost completely away as they pass. When young tendrils appear, they notice those too and sit upright like squirrels, shearing them off along with buds and young pods. Above all, harvest as early as you can to avoid frost and secure a sound, saleable crop. This precaution can save considerable loss.

I gained another piece of experience. Next summer, I told myself, I will plant beans and corn less diligently and instead sow sincerity, truth, simplicity, faith, innocence, and similar seeds—if their seed has not been lost. Perhaps with less labor and manure they will grow here and sustain me; surely these crops have not exhausted the soil. Alas! I told myself this, but another summer has passed, and another, and another. I must confess, Reader, that what I planted, if they truly _were_ those virtues’ seeds, had been worm-eaten or had lost vitality, and never sprouted. People generally remain brave—or timid—only as their fathers were. Each year this generation reliably plants beans and corn exactly as Indians did centuries ago and taught the first settlers, as though fate commanded it. The other day I astonishingly saw an old man hoeing holes for at least his seventieth time, and not holes to lie down in! Why should a New Englander not attempt new adventures, place less emphasis on grain, potatoes, grass, and orchards, and cultivate other crops? Why worry so much over seed beans and so little over a new human generation? Meeting someone would truly nourish and cheer us if we could be sure some of these qualities had taken root and grown in him—qualities we all value above those other products, yet which mostly remain scattered abroad, floating in the air. Imagine truth or justice, subtle and indescribable, however small an amount or fresh a variety, coming down the road. Our ambassadors should be instructed to send such seeds home, and Congress should help spread them throughout the land. We should stand on no ceremony with sincerity. With a kernel of worth and friendliness present, we would not cheat, insult, and exclude one another through meanness, or meet so hastily. Most people I never meet at all: apparently they lack time, being busy with beans. We would not deal with a perpetually plodding man leaning between tasks on hoe or spade as a staff, nor with a mushroom, but with someone partly risen from earth, more than upright, like swallows landing and walking on the ground:—

“And as he spoke, his wings would now and then
Open as if to fly, then close again,”

making us suspect we were talking with an angel. Bread does not always nourish us. But recognizing generosity in people or Nature, sharing any pure, heroic joy, always benefits us, even loosening stiff joints and making us supple and buoyant when we had not known what was wrong.

Ancient poetry and mythology at least suggest that farming was once a sacred art. We pursue it hastily and irreverently, heedless of anything beyond large farms and large yields. No festival, procession, or ceremony—not even our Cattle-shows or so-called Thanksgivings—expresses a farmer’s sense of his calling’s holiness or recalls its sacred origin. It is the prospect of receiving a prize and enjoying the feast, rather than any sense of holiness, that tempts him to attend. His sacrifices go not to Ceres and the Terrestrial Jove but rather to the underworld’s Plutus. Greed, selfishness, and the groveling habit we all share of regarding soil chiefly as property or a means to more property disfigure the landscape and degrade husbandry. The farmer lives the meanest life, knowing Nature only as a robber. Cato calls agricultural profit especially pious or just, (_maximeque pius quæstus_). According to Varro, ancient Romans “called the same earth Mother and Ceres, believing its cultivators led pious, useful lives and alone survived from King Saturn’s race.”

We tend to forget that sunlight treats our cultivated fields, prairies, and forests without distinction. They all reflect and absorb its rays alike. Cultivated fields form only a small part of the glorious picture the sun sees during its daily journey. To its eyes, the whole earth is equally cultivated, one garden. We should accept its warmth and light with corresponding trust and generosity. What if I prize these beans’ seed and harvest it in autumn? This broad field I have watched so long does not recognize me as its chief cultivator. It looks beyond me toward kinder influences that water it and make it green. Beans produce results I do not harvest. Do they not grow partly for woodchucks? A wheat ear—Latin _spica_, formerly _speca_, from _spe_, hope—should not be a farmer’s only hope; its grain, _granum_, from _gerendo_, bearing, is not everything it bears. How, then, can the harvest fail? Should I not also rejoice in plentiful weeds whose seeds supply birds’ granary? Whether fields fill the farmer’s barns matters comparatively little. A true husbandman will stop worrying, as squirrels show no concern whether the woods will produce chestnuts this year. Each day he will finish his labor, surrender all claim to his fields’ produce, and mentally sacrifice not merely his first fruits but his last as well.

chapters.title: The Village
paragraphs: After spending the morning hoeing, or perhaps reading and writing, I generally bathed in the pond again, swimming across one of its coves for exercise. I washed the dust of work off my body, or smoothed away the last wrinkle study had left on me, and had the afternoon entirely free. Every day or two I wandered into the village to hear a little of its ceaseless gossip, passed from mouth to mouth or newspaper to newspaper. In homeopathic doses it was really as refreshing, in its own way, as rustling leaves and peeping frogs. Just as I walked in the woods to observe birds and squirrels, I walked in the village to observe men and boys. Instead of wind in the pines, I heard rattling carts. In one direction from my house a colony of muskrats lived in the river meadows; beneath the grove of elms and buttonwoods on the opposite horizon stood a village of busy people. They interested me as much as prairie dogs would have, each sitting at the entrance to his burrow or running over to a neighbor’s to gossip. I often went to watch their habits. The village seemed one great newsroom, with nuts and raisins, or salt, meal, and other groceries sold on the side to support it, as they once were at Redding & Company’s on State Street. Some people have such enormous appetites for the first commodity—the news—and such healthy powers of digestion that they can sit motionless forever on public thoroughfares, letting it simmer and whisper through them like the Etesian winds. It is as if they were breathing ether: the news merely numbs them and deadens pain without disturbing consciousness; otherwise, hearing it would often be painful. On my walks through the village I almost invariably saw a row of these worthies. Sometimes they sat sunning themselves on a ladder, leaning forward and occasionally casting their eyes up and down the line with a voluptuous expression. Sometimes they leaned against a barn, hands in pockets, like caryatides supposedly holding it up. Since they were generally outdoors, they heard whatever was in the wind. They were the coarsest mills, where all gossip first received its rough grinding or cracking before being poured into the finer, more delicate hoppers indoors. I found that the village’s vital organs were the grocery, barroom, post office, and bank. As necessary parts of its machinery, it had a bell, a large gun, and a fire engine placed at convenient points. The houses were arranged in lanes facing one another so as to make the most of humanity: every traveler had to run the gauntlet, giving every man, woman, and child a chance to strike at him. Naturally, those nearest the head of the line, where they could see and be seen most and get in the first blow, paid the highest prices for their positions. The scattered inhabitants on the outskirts paid very little in ground or window tax. There the gaps in the line grew long enough for travelers to climb walls or turn into cow paths and escape. Signs hung on every side to entice the passerby. Taverns and basement eating houses caught him by his appetite; dry-goods shops and jewelers by his fancy; barbers, shoemakers, and tailors by his hair, feet, or coat-tails. Worse still, he had a standing invitation to call at every house, and visitors were expected about this time. I usually escaped these dangers remarkably well. Either I marched straight to my destination, boldly and without pausing, as people running the gauntlet are advised to do, or I fixed my mind on lofty things, like Orpheus, who, “loudly singing the praises of the gods to his lyre, drowned the voices of the Sirens, and kept out of danger.” Sometimes I made a sudden dash and nobody knew where I had gone. I cared little about looking graceful and never hesitated before a gap in a fence. I would even burst into certain houses, where I was hospitably received. After hearing the kernels and final siftings of the news—what had settled out, the prospects for war or peace, and whether the world might hold together much longer—I was shown out by the back ways and escaped into the woods again.

When I stayed late in town, how pleasant it was to launch myself into the night, especially a dark, stormy one. With a sack of rye or Indian meal on my shoulder, I would set sail from some bright village parlor or lecture room toward my snug woodland harbor. Having made everything secure on deck, I withdrew below with a merry crew of thoughts, leaving only my outward self at the helm, or even lashing the helm in place when the sailing was easy. Many a cheerful thought came to me beside the cabin fire “as I sailed.” No weather ever wrecked or seriously troubled me, although I met some fierce storms. Even on an ordinary night, the woods are darker than most people imagine. Often I had to look up at the strip of sky between the trees above the path to find my way. Where no cart track existed, my feet felt out the faint trail I had worn, or my hands touched particular trees whose positions I knew, letting me steer between them. Thus I would always pass between two pines in the middle of the woods, scarcely eighteen inches apart, on the darkest night. Sometimes, arriving home late on a dark, damp night, I could not remember a single step of the journey. My feet had followed the path my eyes could not see while I dreamed and wandered in my thoughts, until raising my hand to lift the latch woke me. I thought perhaps my body could find its own way home if its master abandoned it, just as a hand finds the mouth unaided. Several times, when a visitor stayed into the evening and the night turned dark, I had to lead him to the cart track behind my house and point out his direction, telling him to trust his feet more than his eyes in keeping to it. On one particularly dark night I sent two young men on their way like this after they had been fishing in the pond. They lived about a mile away through the woods and knew the route perfectly well. A day or two later, one told me they had wandered near their own home for most of the night and arrived only toward morning. Several heavy showers had fallen meanwhile; the leaves were drenched, and so were they, right through to their skin. I have heard of many people losing their way even in the village streets when the darkness was, as the saying goes, thick enough to cut with a knife. People from the outskirts who had driven their wagons into town to shop have had to stay overnight. Gentlemen and ladies making a social call have strayed half a mile, feeling the sidewalk only with their feet and failing to notice when they turned. Getting lost in the woods at any time is a surprising, memorable, and valuable experience. Even in daylight, during a snowstorm, you may come onto a familiar road and be unable to tell which direction leads to the village. You know you have traveled it a thousand times, yet recognize nothing; it seems as strange as a road in Siberia. At night, of course, the confusion is infinitely greater. On even our most ordinary walks we unconsciously steer like pilots, using familiar beacons and headlands. If we stray beyond our usual course, we still hold in mind the bearing of some nearby cape. Only when we are utterly lost or turned around do we appreciate Nature’s vastness and strangeness—and in this world, a man need only be turned around once with his eyes shut to lose his way. Every time we wake, whether from sleep or from absorption in thought, we must learn the compass points again. Only after we lose our way—after we lose the world, that is—do we begin to find ourselves, to understand where we stand and how infinitely far our connections extend.

One afternoon toward the end of my first summer, I went into the village to collect a shoe from the cobbler and was arrested and jailed. As I have related elsewhere, I refused to pay a tax to, or acknowledge the authority of, a state that buys and sells men, women, and children like cattle at the very door of its senate-house. I had gone to the woods for other reasons. But wherever a man goes, other men will hunt him down and paw at him with their dirty institutions, forcing him, if they can, into their desperate society of odd fellows. Certainly I could have resisted with force, more or less successfully, and run “amok” against society. I preferred to let society run “amok” against me, since it was the desperate party. At any rate, I was freed the following day, collected my repaired shoe, and went back to the woods in time to dine on huckleberries on Fair-Haven Hill. Nobody ever bothered me except representatives of the state. The only lock or bolt I owned was on the desk containing my papers. I had not even a nail to secure my door latch or windows. Day or night, I never fastened the door, even when I would be away for several days—not even when I spent two weeks in the Maine woods the following autumn. Yet people respected my house more than if a line of soldiers had surrounded it. A weary walker could rest and warm himself at my fire; a reader could enjoy the few books on my table; a curious visitor could open my cupboard and inspect the remains of my dinner and the prospects for my supper. Although people of every class passed this way to the pond, none of this seriously inconvenienced me. The only thing I ever missed was a small volume of Homer, perhaps too richly gilded; by now, I trust, some soldier of our camp has found it. I am convinced that, if everyone lived as simply as I did then, theft and robbery would be unknown. They occur only where some people have more than they need and others have too little. The Pope’s Homers would soon find their proper distribution.—

“Nec bella fuerunt,
Faginus astabat dum scyphus ante dapes.”

“Nor did wars trouble men,
When beechwood bowls alone were wanted.”

“You who manage public affairs, why do you need to use punishments? Love virtue, and the people will become virtuous. The virtues of a superior man are like wind; those of a common man are like grass. When the wind moves across it, the grass bends.”

chapters.title: The Ponds
paragraphs: Sometimes, tired of human company and gossip and having exhausted all my village friends, I wandered farther west than my usual dwelling, into still less visited parts of town, “to fresh woods and pastures new.” Or, as the sun went down, I supped on huckleberries and blueberries on Fair Haven Hill and gathered enough for several days. Fruit does not give its true flavor to the person who buys it, or to the person who grows it for market. There is only one way to get that flavor, and few follow it. To learn the taste of huckleberries, ask the cow-boy or the partridge. Thinking you have tasted huckleberries when you have never picked them is a common vulgar mistake. No huckleberry ever reaches Boston; none has been known there since they grew on her three hills. The fruit’s heavenly essence disappears with the bloom rubbed away in the market cart, leaving mere feed. While Eternal Justice rules, no innocent huckleberry can be carried there from the country’s hills.

Now and then, after finishing my day’s hoeing, I joined an impatient companion who had fished on the pond since morning, still and silent as a duck or a floating leaf. Having tried several philosophies, he had usually decided by my arrival that he belonged to the ancient sect of Cœnobites. One older man, an excellent fisherman versed in every kind of woodcraft, liked to regard my house as a building put up for fishermen’s convenience. I was just as pleased to have him sit in my doorway arranging his lines. Sometimes we sat on the pond together, at opposite ends of the boat. We exchanged few words, for age had made him deaf, but he occasionally hummed a psalm that agreed well enough with my philosophy. Our fellowship was therefore one of unbroken harmony, far pleasanter to remember than any spoken conversation. When I had nobody to commune with, as usually happened, I struck the boat’s side with my paddle to wake the echoes. Sound circled and widened through the surrounding woods. I roused them as a menagerie keeper rouses his wild beasts, until every wooded valley and hillside gave me a growl.

On warm evenings I often played my flute while sitting in the boat, watching perch hover around me as though enchanted, and the moon move across the ribbed bottom, littered with the forest’s wreckage. In earlier days I had sometimes ventured here with a companion on dark summer nights. We lit a fire at the water’s edge, thinking it drew the fish, and caught pouts with worms bunched on a thread. When we finished, late in the night, we flung the burning sticks high like skyrockets. They fell into the pond and went out with a loud hiss, leaving us suddenly groping in complete darkness. Whistling a tune, we made our way through it back to the places where men lived. Now, though, I had made my own home beside the pond.

Sometimes I stayed in a village parlor until the whole family went to bed, then returned to the woods and spent the midnight hours fishing from a boat in moonlight, partly thinking of tomorrow’s dinner. Owls and foxes serenaded me; now and then an unidentified bird nearby gave a creaking call. These experiences remain memorable and precious: anchored in forty feet of water, twenty or thirty rods offshore, sometimes surrounded by thousands of little perch and shiners whose tails dimpled the moonlit surface, I communicated through a long flaxen line with mysterious night fish living forty feet below. At other times I drifted in the soft night wind, trailing sixty feet of line around the pond. An occasional faint vibration told of some life prowling at its end, dull and uncertain in its blundering purpose, slow to decide. At last, drawing in the line hand over hand, you slowly bring a horned pout squeaking and writhing into the upper air. On dark nights especially, when your thoughts have strayed to immense questions of worlds and their creation in other spheres, that slight tug feels very strange. It interrupts your dreams and connects you with Nature again. I felt I might next cast upward into the air as readily as downward into this scarcely denser element. Thus, as it were, I caught two fishes with one hook.

Walden’s scenery is modest in scale. Beautiful though it is, it has no grandeur, and can mean little to anyone who has not often visited it or lived along its shore. Yet the pond’s extraordinary depth and purity deserve a detailed description. It is a deep, clear green well, half a mile long, a mile and three quarters around, covering about sixty-one and a half acres: a perennial spring among pine and oak woods, with no visible inlet or outlet except clouds and evaporation. The surrounding hills rise steeply from the water, forty to eighty feet high. To the southeast they reach about one hundred feet within a quarter of a mile; to the east, about one hundred and fifty within a third. All are wooded. Every body of water in Concord has at least two colors: one seen from a distance and another, more truly its own, close by. The first depends chiefly on light and follows the sky. In clear summer weather the waters look blue from a short distance, particularly when disturbed; from far away they all look alike. Stormy weather sometimes makes them dark slate. Yet the sea is said to be blue one day and green the next without any noticeable atmospheric change. I have seen our river when snow covered the landscape and both water and ice were nearly grass-green. Some believe blue “to be the color of pure water, whether liquid or solid.” But look straight down from a boat into our waters and their colors differ greatly. Even from one viewpoint Walden is sometimes blue, sometimes green. Between earth and heaven, it borrows the color of both. From a hilltop it reflects the sky. Close by, where sand shows near shore, it looks yellowish, then pale green, deepening gradually into an even dark green across the pond’s body. In certain light, even from a hilltop, the water near shore is brilliantly green. Some attribute this to reflected foliage. But it is just as green beside the railroad sand-bank and in spring before the leaves open; perhaps it is simply the prevailing blue mingled with the sand’s yellow. That is the color of its iris. Here too the ice melts first in spring. The sun’s heat reflects from the bottom and passes through the earth, warming the ice and opening a narrow channel around the still-frozen center. Like our other waters, when greatly stirred in clear weather it looks from a little way off darker blue than the sky. Perhaps the waves reflect the sky at the proper angle, or more light mingles with the water. At such times, on the pond and looking with divided vision to catch the reflection, I have seen a peerless, indescribable pale blue, suggested by watered or changeable silks and sword blades, more cerulean than the sky itself. It alternated with the original dark green on the waves’ opposite sides, making that green seem muddy by comparison. As I remember it, this was a glassy greenish blue, like patches of winter sky glimpsed through openings in western clouds before sunset. Yet hold one glass of the water to the light, and it is as colorless as the same volume of air. A large sheet of glass notoriously has a greenish tint, caused, its makers say, by its “body”; a small piece of that glass has none. I have never tested how large a body of Walden water is needed to show green. Look directly down into our river and its water is black or very dark brown. Like most pond water, it gives a bather’s body a yellowish tinge. Walden’s crystalline purity instead makes the bather alabaster-white, an even less natural sight. Together with the enlarged, distorted limbs, this creates monstrous figures fit for Michael Angelo’s studies.

The water is clear enough to show the bottom easily at twenty-five or thirty feet. As you paddle, schools of perch and shiners appear many feet down, perhaps only an inch long. The perch are still easy to distinguish by their crosswise bars. You imagine fish living there must be ascetics. Many winters ago I had been cutting holes in the ice to catch pickerel. Stepping ashore, I tossed my axe back onto the ice. As though guided by an evil genius, it slid four or five rods straight into a hole over twenty-five feet of water. Curious, I lay down and looked through the opening until I spotted the axe slightly to one side, standing on its head. Its upright handle swayed gently with the pond’s pulse. It might have stood swaying there until the handle rotted away if I had left it alone. With my ice chisel I made another hole directly above it, then used my knife to cut the longest birch I could find nearby. I fastened a slip-noose to the tree’s end, lowered it carefully over the knob of the axe handle, tightened it with a line running along the birch, and pulled the axe up again.

Except for one or two short sandy beaches, the shore is a belt of smooth, rounded white stones like paving stones. It drops so steeply that in many places one leap puts you in water over your head. Without its extraordinary clarity, you would see no more of the bottom until it rose on the opposite shore. Some call it bottomless. There is no mud anywhere, and a casual visitor would say there are no weeds. Look closely and, apart from the recently flooded little meadows that do not properly belong to the pond, you find no flag or bulrush, not even a yellow or white lily. There are only a few small heart-leaves and potamogetons, perhaps a water-target or two, easily missed by a bather. The plants are as bright and clean as the water they inhabit. Stones continue a rod or two underwater; beyond them the bottom is clean sand. Only the deepest places usually hold a little sediment, probably decayed leaves blown onto the pond over so many autumns. Even in midwinter anchors bring up a vivid green weed.

One other pond resembles this one: White Pond, at Nine Acre Corner, about two and a half miles west. Though I know most ponds within a dozen miles of this center, I know no third so pure and well-like. Perhaps nation after nation has drunk from it, admired it, sounded it and vanished, while its water remains as green and transparent as ever. No intermittent spring! Perhaps Walden already existed on the spring morning when Adam and Eve were expelled from Eden. Perhaps even then its ice was breaking under a gentle spring rain, mist and a south wind, while countless ducks and geese covered it, ignorant of the fall and still content with such pure lakes. Already it had begun its rises and falls, cleared its waters, given them their present hue, and secured heaven’s patent to be the world’s only Walden Pond and distiller of celestial dews. Who knows how many forgotten nations’ literatures made this their Castalian Fountain, or which nymphs ruled it in the Golden Age? Concord wears this gem of the first water in her coronet.

Perhaps the earliest visitors to this well did leave traces of their feet. I have been surprised to discover a narrow, shelf-like path circling the pond’s steep hillside, even where dense shore woods have just been cut. It rises and falls, nearing and leaving the water, probably as old as mankind’s presence here. Aboriginal hunters wore it with their feet, and the land’s present occupants still occasionally follow it without knowing. Stand in the middle of the frozen pond just after a light snowfall and it becomes especially clear: a wavering white line, free of concealing weeds and twigs. In many places you can plainly see it a quarter-mile away, though in summer you can scarcely find it at your feet. Snow reprints it, as it were, in crisp white alto-relievo type. The landscaped grounds of villas built here one day may still keep some trace of it.

The pond rises and falls, but nobody knows whether it follows a regular cycle or how long that cycle lasts, though many, as usual, claim to know. It is generally higher in winter and lower in summer, without following overall wet or dry conditions. I remember it a foot or two lower than when I lived there, and at least five feet higher. A narrow sand-bar reaches into it beside very deep water. Around 1824 I helped boil chowder on that bar, some six rods from the main shore, something impossible for twenty-five years now. On the other hand, my friends scarcely believed me when I said that a few years later I fished from a boat in a sheltered woodland cove, fifteen rods beyond the only shoreline they knew, in a place long since turned to meadow. But for two years the pond has risen steadily. Now, in the summer of ’52, it stands exactly five feet above its level when I lived there, as high as thirty years ago, and people fish in the meadow again. At most, this amounts to six or seven feet of change. Runoff from the surrounding hills is very slight, so causes affecting the deep springs must account for the overflow. This same summer it has started falling again. Remarkably, this fluctuation, regular or not, seems to take many years to complete. I have watched one rise and parts of two falls, and expect that twelve or fifteen years from now it will again be as low as I have ever seen it. Flint’s Pond, a mile east, allowing for its inlets’ and outlets’ effects, and the smaller ponds between it and Walden follow Walden’s changes. Recently they reached their highest levels together. As far as I have observed, White Pond does the same.

Walden’s slow rises and falls serve at least one purpose. When the water stays high for a year or longer, it makes walking around the pond difficult but kills the growth that has sprung up along the edge since the last rise: pitch-pines, birches, alders, aspens and other shrubs and trees. When it falls, the shore is clear. Unlike many ponds and all waters with daily tides, Walden’s shore is cleanest at low water. Near my house, a row of fifteen-foot pitch pines has been killed and tipped over as though with a lever, ending their encroachment. Their size shows how many years have passed since the water last reached this height. Through these changes the pond asserts its ownership of a shore: the _shore_ is _shorn_, and the trees cannot claim it by possession. These are the lake’s beardless lips. From time to time it licks its chops. At high water, alders, willows and maples struggle to survive by putting out masses of red, fibrous roots several feet long, from every side of their submerged stems up to three or four feet above the ground. I have also known the high-blueberry bushes along the shore, ordinarily fruitless, to yield abundant crops in these conditions.

Some people cannot explain the shore’s regular paving. Every one of my townsmen has heard the tradition, which the oldest inhabitants tell me they already knew in their youth. Long ago, Indians held a pow-wow on a hill here, rising as high into heaven as the pond now sinks into earth. According to the tale, they used much profanity, although the Indians were never guilty of that vice. As they did so, the hill shook and suddenly sank. Only one old squaw, Walden, escaped, and the pond took her name. Some suppose the shaking sent these stones rolling down to form today’s shore. At any rate, it is certain that once no pond existed here and now one does. This Indian fable does not contradict the account of that ancient settler I mentioned. He vividly remembers first arriving with his divining rod, seeing a faint vapor rise from the turf, feeling the hazel point steadily down, and deciding to dig a well. Many still think waves acting on these hills can hardly explain the stones. But I notice the hills are full of the very same stones: along the railroad cutting nearest the pond they had to be piled into walls on both sides. The steepest shore also has the most stones. Unfortunately, then, the mystery has left me. I recognize the paver. Unless the name came from an English place—Saffron Walden, for example—we might imagine the original name was _Walled-in_ Pond.

The pond gave me a well already dug. For four months each year its water is as cold as it is always pure; then, I think, it equals any water in town, if it is not the best. In winter, water open to the air is colder than springs and wells sheltered from it. On March 6, 1846, pond water that had stood in my room from five the previous afternoon until noon measured 42°. The room had sometimes reached 65° or 70°, partly from sunshine on the roof. Yet the water was still one degree colder than water freshly drawn from one of the village’s coldest wells. That day the Boiling Spring measured 45°, warmest of all I tested, although in summer it is the coldest I know; in summer, too, shallow stagnant surface water does not mix with it. Walden’s depth also keeps it from becoming as warm in summer as most sun-exposed water. In the hottest weather I generally put a pailful in my cellar, where it cooled overnight and stayed cool all day, although I also used a nearby spring. After a week it was as good as when dipped, without any pump flavor. Anyone camping for a summer week beside a pond need only bury a pail of water several feet down in the camp’s shade to dispense with the luxury of ice.

Walden has yielded pickerel, including one of seven pounds, not counting another that raced away with a reel and could safely be judged eight pounds by the fisherman because he never saw it. There are perch and pouts, some of each exceeding two pounds, shiners, chivins or roach (_Leuciscus pulchellus_), a very few breams, and two eels, one weighing four pounds. I am exact about this because a fish usually gains fame only by its weight, and these are the only eels I have heard of here. I also dimly remember a small fish about five inches long, silver-sided and green-backed, somewhat like a dace; I mention it chiefly to connect my facts with fable. Still, the pond does not abound in fish. Its greatest pride is its pickerel, though they are not plentiful. I have seen at least three kinds lying together on the ice: a long, shallow-bodied, steel-colored fish most like the river’s; a bright gold kind with greenish gleams and a remarkably deep body, the commonest here; and a similarly shaped golden fish whose sides were sprinkled with little dark-brown or black spots and a few faint blood-red ones, much like a trout. That one does not deserve the specific name _reticulatus_; _guttatus_ would suit it better. All are very firm fish, heavier than their size suggests. The shiners, pouts and perch—indeed every fish here—are cleaner, handsomer and firmer-fleshed than those of the river and most other ponds, just as their water is purer, and are easily told apart from them. Many ichthyologists would probably classify some as new varieties. A clean race of frogs and tortoises lives here too, with a few muscels. Muskrats and minks leave their marks, and a wandering mud-turtle occasionally visits. Sometimes when launching my boat in the morning I disturbed a great mud-turtle that had hidden beneath it overnight. Ducks and geese visit in spring and fall. White-bellied swallows (_Hirundo bicolor_) skim the water, and peetweets (_Totanus macularius_) “teter” along the stones all summer. I have sometimes startled a fishhawk perched in a white-pine above the water, but doubt that a gull’s wing ever profanes it as at Fair Haven. It permits at most one loon each year. These are all the important animals now frequenting the pond.

In calm weather, from a boat near the sandy eastern shore, you can see circular piles of little stones in eight or ten feet of water. They occur elsewhere too. Each heap is about six feet across and a foot high, with stones smaller than hens’ eggs, surrounded by bare sand. At first you wonder whether Indians piled them on the ice for some purpose and they sank when it melted. But they are too regular, and some clearly too recent, for that. They resemble heaps in rivers. Yet neither suckers nor lampreys live here, so I cannot tell which fish might build them. Perhaps they are chivin nests. They give the bottom a pleasant mystery.

The shoreline varies enough to avoid monotony. I picture its deeply bayed western side, the bolder northern side, and the beautifully scalloped south, where cape overlaps cape, suggesting undiscovered coves between. A forest has no finer setting, no more distinct beauty, than the view from the center of a small lake surrounded by hills rising from its edge. The reflecting water supplies the best possible foreground, and the winding shore the most natural, pleasing border. Here the forest’s edge has none of the raw incompleteness left where axes clear a tract or farmland meets the woods. Trees have room to spread toward the water, each sending its strongest branch that way. Nature has woven her own selvage, and the eye climbs in proper stages from low shore shrubs to the tallest trees. Hardly any human handiwork is visible. The water washes the shore just as it did a thousand years ago.

No feature of a landscape is more beautiful or expressive than a lake. It is earth’s eye: whoever looks into it sounds the depth of his own nature. The water-loving trees along the shore fringe it like slender eyelashes; the wooded hills and cliffs above form its overhanging brows.

On a still September afternoon, standing on the smooth sand at the pond’s east end while a slight haze blurs the opposite shoreline, I have understood the phrase “the glassy surface of a lake.” Turn your head upside down and it becomes the finest gossamer thread stretched across the valley, shining against distant pine woods and dividing one layer of atmosphere from another. You might imagine walking dry beneath it to the opposite hills, or swallows landing on it as they skim past. Sometimes they dip below that line, apparently by mistake, and learn better. Looking west across the pond, you need both hands to shield your eyes from the actual sun and its equally brilliant reflection. Examine the surface between them and it is literally smooth as glass. Only the skater insects, evenly scattered everywhere, move in the sunlight to make sparks of unimaginable delicacy; perhaps a duck preens, or a swallow brushes it in passing. A distant fish may trace a three- or four-foot arc in the air, flashing once as it rises and once as it strikes the water; sometimes the whole silver curve shows. Here and there a floating thistle-down draws a darting fish and another dimple. The pond resembles molten glass cooled without hardening, its few motes pure and lovely as flaws in glass. Often a patch looks smoother and darker still, separated from the rest as though an invisible cobweb lay on it, a boom stretched by the water nymphs. From a hilltop you can see a fish jump almost anywhere. No pickerel or shiner plucks an insect from that smoothness without visibly disturbing the whole lake’s balance. How elaborately this simple event is announced—this piscine murder will out. From my distant perch I can see its expanding rings when they span six rods. Even a water-bug (_Gyrinus_), tirelessly moving a quarter-mile away, can be detected. It makes a slight furrow, a visible ripple bounded by two diverging lines, whereas skaters glide without a noticeable wake. Neither appears when the surface is much disturbed. On quiet days they apparently leave their shelters and venture from shore in short glides until they cover the pond. On a fine autumn day, when every bit of the sun’s warmth is welcome, it is soothing to sit on a stump at such a height and watch the circles endlessly drawn among reflected skies and trees on the otherwise unseen surface. Across that whole expanse, every disturbance is immediately softened and smoothed away, as trembling rings in a jarred vase of water travel to its sides and leave it smooth again. Every leaping fish and falling insect is reported in these circling dimples, these lines of beauty: the fountain’s continual rising, the gentle beat of its life, the breathing of its breast. Thrills of pleasure and pain cannot be told apart. How peaceful the lake’s phenomena are! Human works shine again as in spring. Yes, in mid-afternoon every leaf, twig, stone and cobweb sparkles as though dew-covered on a spring morning. Each moving oar or insect strikes a flash of light, and when an oar falls, how sweet the echo!

On such a September or October day, Walden is a flawless forest mirror, framed with stones as precious to me as if they were few and rare. Perhaps nothing on earth’s surface is at once so lovely, pure and large as a lake. Sky water. No fence is needed. Nations arrive and vanish without polluting it. This mirror cannot be cracked by a stone; its quicksilver never wears away, and Nature constantly restores its gilding. Neither dust nor storms can dull its always-fresh surface. Every impurity offered to it sinks. The sun sweeps and dusts it with its hazy brush—this light dust-cloth. It keeps no breath breathed upon it, but sends its own aloft as clouds to be reflected once more in its breast.

A stretch of water reveals the spirit moving in the air. Fresh life and motion reach it continually from above. Its nature stands between earth and sky. On land, grass and trees alone wave; on water, the wind ripples the substance itself. Streaks and flakes of light show me where a breeze races across. It is remarkable that we can look down on this surface. Perhaps eventually we shall look down on the surface of air in the same way, observing where a finer spirit still sweeps over it.

Hard frosts finally drive away the skaters and water-bugs in late October. After that, and usually through November, calm days leave nothing at all to ripple the pond. One November afternoon, in the quiet following several days of rain, the sky was still completely clouded and mist filled the air. The pond was so smooth I could hardly make out its surface. It reflected not October’s bright colors now, but the surrounding hills’ somber November hues. I moved as gently as I could, yet my boat’s small waves reached almost as far as I could see, ribbing the reflections. Looking farther, I noticed faint glimmers here and there, perhaps skaters that had survived the frost gathering together, or springs rising from the bottom and betraying themselves on the glassy water. I paddled quietly toward one and found, to my surprise, countless small perch around me. About five inches long and richly bronze in the green water, they played and kept rising to dimple the surface, sometimes leaving bubbles. In water so clear and seemingly bottomless, reflecting clouds, I felt I was floating in a balloon through the air. Their swimming looked like flight or hovering: a close flock of birds passing just below me to right or left, with fins spread like sails around them. Many such schools filled the pond, apparently taking advantage of the brief time before winter shut an icy shutter across their broad skylight. Sometimes they made the surface look touched by a slight breeze or scattered raindrops. If I approached carelessly and frightened them, their tails splashed and rippled suddenly, as though someone had slapped the water with a leafy bough, and they instantly vanished into the depths. Eventually wind rose, mist thickened and waves began running. The perch jumped higher than before, half out of water, a hundred black points three inches long appearing at once. One year, as late as December fifth, I saw dimples and thought heavy rain was about to begin, since the air was full of mist. I hurried to the oars and rowed home. The apparent rain increased rapidly, although none touched my cheek, and I expected a thorough soaking. Suddenly the dimples stopped. Perch had made them, and my oars had frightened them down; I faintly saw their schools disappearing. After all, I spent a dry afternoon.

An old man who visited this pond nearly sixty years ago, when surrounding forests darkened it, tells me he sometimes saw it alive with ducks and other water fowl, with many eagles nearby. He fished from an old log canoe he found on shore: two hollowed white-pine logs pinned together, squared at the ends. Though very awkward, it lasted years before becoming water-logged and perhaps sinking. He never knew its owner; it belonged to the pond. For an anchor cable he tied together strips of hickory bark. An old potter who lived beside the pond before the Revolution once told him of an iron chest on the bottom that he had seen himself. Sometimes it floated to shore, but if anyone approached it retreated into deep water and disappeared. I was delighted by the old log canoe. It replaced an Indian canoe made from the same material with a more graceful shape—a tree, perhaps, that first stood on the bank and then, as it were, fell into the water to float for a generation, the lake’s most fitting vessel. When I first looked into these depths, I remember dimly seeing many great trunks on the bottom, either blown down long before or left on the ice at the last timber cutting, when wood was cheaper. Most have now disappeared.

When I first took a paddle boat onto Walden, tall, dense pine and oak woods ringed it completely. In some coves grape vines covered the waterside trees, making bowers a boat could pass beneath. The shore hills were so steep and their trees then so tall that, looking down from the western end, you saw an amphitheatre waiting for some woodland spectacle. In my younger days I spent hours drifting wherever the zephyr wished. On a summer morning I paddled to the middle and lay on my back across the seats, dreaming awake, until the boat touched sand. Then I rose to see which shore my fates had chosen. Those were days when idleness was the most tempting and productive industry. Many mornings I slipped away, choosing to spend the day’s most prized hours in this way. Though not rich in money, I owned sunny hours and summer days and spent them freely. I do not regret failing to waste more of them in a workshop or at a teacher’s desk. Since I left, however, woodcutters have devastated the shores still further. For many years to come there will be no wandering the woodland aisles, catching occasional views of water through openings. My Muse deserves pardon if she falls silent now. How can you expect birds to sing after cutting down their groves?

The trunks on the bottom, the old log canoe and the dark encircling woods have all gone. Villagers who hardly know the pond’s location no longer think of coming here to drink or bathe. Instead they propose to pipe its water into the village—water that should be at least as sacred as the Ganges—to wash their dishes! To earn their Walden by turning a cock or pulling a plug! That infernal Iron Horse, whose piercing neigh tears through the whole town, has muddied the Boiling Spring with his foot and grazed away every wood along Walden’s shore: a Trojan horse with a thousand men in his belly, brought in by mercenary Greeks! Where is the country’s champion, the Moore of Moore Hill, to confront him at the Deep Cut and drive a vengeful lance between the ribs of that swollen pest?

Still, of all the characters I have known, Walden perhaps wears best and keeps its purity longest. Many men have been compared with it; few deserve the compliment. Woodcutters have stripped one shore and then another, the Irish have put up their sties beside it, the railroad has invaded its edge, and ice-men have skimmed it once. Yet it remains unchanged: the same water my young eyes first saw. All the change belongs to me. After all its rippling, not one lasting wrinkle has formed. Forever young, it still lets me stand and watch a swallow dip, apparently to pick an insect from the surface, as long ago. Tonight it struck me anew, as though I had not seen it almost daily for over twenty years: why, here is Walden, the very woodland lake I discovered so long ago. Where trees fell last winter, new forest rises beside it as vigorously as ever. The same thought wells up to the surface, the same liquid joy and happiness for itself and its Maker—and it _may_ be so for me. Surely a brave man without guile made this! His hand rounded the water; his thought deepened and purified it; his will left it to Concord. Its face tells me the same reflection still visits it, and I can almost ask, Walden, is it you?

It is no dream of mine,
To ornament a line;
I cannot come nearer to God and Heaven
Than I live to Walden even.
I am its stony shore,
And the breeze that passes over;
In the hollow of my hand
Are its water and its sand,
And its deepest resort
Lies high in my thought.

The trains never stop to admire it. Yet I suspect their engineers, firemen and brakemen, and the season-ticket passengers who often see it, are better men for the sight. At night the engineer does not forget—or his nature does not—that at least once that day he saw this vision of peace and purity. A single glimpse helps wash away State-street and the engine’s soot. Someone suggests naming it “God’s Drop.”

I have said that Walden has no visible inlet or outlet. Yet on one side a chain of little ponds coming from that direction connects it remotely and indirectly with the higher Flint’s Pond. On the other, a similar chain connects it plainly and directly with the lower Concord River. Through these ponds it may have flowed in another geological age; a little digging, God forbid, could send it there again. If its long, secluded, austere life, like a woodland hermit’s, has given it this wonderful purity, who would not grieve to see Flint’s comparatively impure water mixed with it, or Walden itself pouring its sweetness away into an ocean wave?

Flint’s, also called Sandy Pond, in Lincoln, is our largest lake and inland sea, about a mile east of Walden. It is much larger—reportedly one hundred and ninety-seven acres—and richer in fish, but comparatively shallow and not especially pure. I often walked through the woods to it for recreation. The trip was worthwhile simply to feel the wind freely on my cheek, watch the waves run and remember sailors’ lives. On windy autumn days I gathered chestnuts there as they fell into the water and washed to my feet. Once, creeping along the sedgy shore with fresh spray in my face, I found a rotting boat wreck. Its sides had vanished; among the rushes hardly anything remained except the outline of its flat bottom. Yet the shape stood out sharply, like a large decayed leaf-pad with its veins. It was as impressive as any wreck on a seashore and taught as good a lesson. By now it is only vegetable mould, indistinguishable from the pond’s shore, pierced by growing rushes and flags. I used to admire the rippled sand at the north end, packed hard beneath a wader’s feet by the water’s pressure. Rushes grew in Indian file along the ripples, waving row after row as though planted by the waves. I also found many curious, perfectly round balls, half an inch to four inches across, apparently made of fine grass or roots, perhaps pipewort. They roll back and forth over sandy shallows and sometimes wash ashore. Some are grass throughout, others have a little sand at the center. At first they seem rounded by waves like pebbles. Yet even the smallest contain equally coarse material half an inch long, and they form only at one season. Besides, I suspect the waves wear down material already bound together rather than construct it. Once dry, the balls keep their shape indefinitely.

_Flint’s Pond!_ How impoverished our naming is. What right had a dirty, stupid farmer, whose land bordered this sky water and who mercilessly stripped its shores, to name it after himself? Some skin-flint who preferred the reflecting face of a dollar or a shiny cent, where he could admire his own brazen face; who counted even visiting wild ducks as trespassers; whose fingers had become crooked, horny claws through long harpy-like grasping—that is not its name for me. I do not come here to see or hear about him. He never _saw_ the pond, bathed in it, loved it, protected it, spoke kindly of it, or thanked God for making it. Name it instead after its fish, its visiting wild fowl or four-footed creatures, its shoreline wild flowers, or some wild man or child whose history is woven through its own. Not after someone whose only claim was a deed from a like-minded neighbor or legislature; who thought only of its cash value, perhaps cursed the entire shore by his presence, exhausted the land around it and would gladly have exhausted the water too. His sole regret was that it was not English hay land or cranberry meadow—nothing else could redeem it in his eyes—and he would have drained it and sold its bottom mud. It powered no mill of his, and seeing it gave him no _privilege_. I have no respect for his labors or his farm where everything carries a price; for a man who would market the landscape, even his God, if anyone would pay, and who already goes to market _for_ his god. Nothing on his farm grows freely. Fields bear no crops, meadows no flowers, trees no fruit except dollars. He does not love his fruit’s beauty; to him it ripens only when converted to dollars. Give me poverty that enjoys genuine wealth. Farmers interest me and deserve my respect in proportion to their poverty—poor farmers. A model farm! A house like a fungus on a muck-heap, with adjoining rooms for men, horses, oxen and swine, clean and unclean! Stocked with men! An enormous grease-spot smelling of manure and buttermilk! Cultivated to perfection, fertilized with men’s hearts and brains! As though you grew potatoes in the church-yard! Such is a model farm.

No, no. If we name the landscape’s loveliest features after people, choose only the noblest and most worthy. Let our lakes at least have names as true as the Icarian Sea, where “still the shore” a “brave attempt resounds.”

The small Goose Pond lies on my route to Flint’s. Fair-Haven, a widening of Concord River said to cover about seventy acres, is a mile southwest; White Pond, about forty acres, lies another mile and a half beyond it. Here is my lake country. These waters and Concord River are my water privileges. All night and day, year after year, they grind whatever grist I bring.

Since the woodcutters, the railroad and I myself have profaned Walden, White Pond may now be our most attractive lake, if not our most beautiful: the woods’ gem. Its name is commonplace and poor, whether it refers to the water’s exceptional purity or the sand’s color. In these respects and others it is Walden’s smaller twin. So closely do they resemble each other that you might suppose an underground connection. The same stones line the shore; the water has the same hue. In sultry dog-day weather, as at Walden, look through the woods down into bays shallow enough for reflected light from the bottom to color them: the water is a hazy bluish-green, or glaucous. Years ago I went there for cart-loads of sand to make sand-paper, and have visited ever since. One regular visitor suggests Virid Lake. Perhaps Yellow-Pine Lake would suit, for this reason. About fifteen years ago a pitch-pine’s top could be seen above deep water many rods offshore. Such pines are called yellow-pines here, though not a separate species. Some believed the pond had sunk and the tree belonged to the original forest growing there. As early as 1792, I find, a local author’s “Topographical Description of the Town of Concord,” in the Collections of the Massachusetts Historical Society, mentions Walden and White Ponds, then says: “In the middle of the latter may be seen, when the water is very low, a tree which appears as if it grew in the place where it now stands, although the roots are fifty feet below the surface of the water; the top of this tree is broken off, and at that place measures fourteen inches in diameter.” In spring ’49 I spoke with the man living nearest the pond in Sudbury. He told me he had removed the tree ten or fifteen years earlier. As he remembered, it stood twelve or fifteen rods offshore in thirty or forty feet of water. One winter morning he was taking out ice and decided to fetch the old yellow-pine that afternoon with his neighbors’ help. He sawed an ice channel toward shore and used oxen to haul the tree over, along it and onto the ice. Early in the work he was surprised to find it upside down: branch stumps pointed downward and the narrow end was fixed firmly in sand. The larger end was about a foot across. He had expected a good saw-log, but it was so rotten it scarcely suited even fuel. Some still lay in his shed. Axe and woodpecker marks showed on the butt. He thought it might have stood dead on shore before blowing into the pond. Its top became waterlogged while its butt stayed dry and light; then it drifted out and sank upside down. His eighty-year-old father could remember no time without it. Several fairly large logs remain visible on the bottom, where wavering water makes them look like huge moving water snakes.

Boats have seldom profaned this pond; little here tempts fishermen. Instead of white lilies, which need mud, or common sweet flag, scattered blue flag (_Iris versicolor_) rises through pure water from the stony bottom all around the shore. Humming birds visit it in June. The bluish blades and blossoms, and above all their reflections, blend in an extraordinary harmony with the glaucous water.

White Pond and Walden are enormous crystals on earth’s surface, Lakes of Light. If frozen forever and small enough to grasp, they might be carried away by slaves like jewels for emperors’ heads. But because they are liquid, spacious and secured forever to us and those who follow us, we overlook them and chase the diamond of Kohinoor. Their purity leaves them no market price; they contain no muck. How much lovelier than our lives, how much clearer than our characters they are! They never taught us meanness. How much fairer than the pool by the farmer’s door where his ducks swim! Clean wild ducks come here. No human inhabitant appreciates Nature. Birds in feather and song harmonize with flowers, but what young man or woman joins in Nature’s luxuriant wild beauty? She flourishes best alone, far from their towns. Talk of heaven! You disgrace earth.

chapters.title: Baker Farm
paragraphs: Sometimes I wandered into pine groves that stood like temples, or like fleets at sea under full sail, their branches waving and their light rippling. They were so soft, green, and shady that the Druids would have left their oaks to worship there. Sometimes I went into the cedar wood beyond Flint’s Pond, where trees laden with blue berries in a gray bloom rise in higher and higher spires, worthy to stand before Valhalla, and creeping juniper spreads fruit-laden wreaths across the ground. Or I went to swamps where usnea lichen hangs in garlands from white spruces and toadstools—the swamp gods’ round tables—cover the earth. Still lovelier fungi decorate the stumps like butterflies or shells, vegetable winkles. There swamp-pink and dogwood grow; red alder berries gleam like imps’ eyes; waxwork vines cut grooves in the toughest woods and crush them in their coils. The beauty of wild holly berries makes an observer forget home, while countless other nameless, wild, forbidden fruits dazzle and tempt him, too beautiful for mortal taste. Instead of visiting a scholar, I often called on particular trees of species uncommon here. They stood far off in the middle of a pasture, deep in woods or swamps, or on a hilltop. There was the black birch, of which we have fine examples two feet across, and its cousin the yellow birch, dressed in a loose golden vest and scented like the first. There was the beech, with its clean, lovely trunk painted in lichens and perfect in every detail. Apart from scattered trees, I know of only one small grove of large beeches remaining in the township; some suppose pigeons planted it, since people once baited them nearby with beech nuts. Splitting this wood is worth the trouble just to see its silvery grain sparkle. There were the bass and the hornbeam; the _Celtis occidentalis_, or false elm, of which we have only one fully grown specimen; a pine rising like an exceptionally tall mast; a shingle tree; or an unusually perfect hemlock standing like a pagoda in the forest. I could name many more. These were the shrines I visited in winter as well as summer.

Once I happened to stand at the very foot of a rainbow’s arch. It filled the lower layer of air, coloring the grass and leaves around me and dazzling my eyes as though I were looking through colored crystal. For a little while I lived like a dolphin in a lake of rainbow light. Had it lasted longer, it might have colored my occupations and my life. Walking along the railroad causeway, I used to marvel at the luminous halo around my shadow and liked to imagine myself among the elect. One visitor declared that the shadows of certain Irishmen ahead of him had no halos: only natives received that distinction. In his memoirs Benvenuto Cellini tells us that, after a terrible dream or vision during his imprisonment in the castle of St. Angelo, a brilliant light appeared over the shadow of his head in the morning and evening. It followed him in Italy and France alike and shone particularly clearly when dew wet the grass. This was probably the same phenomenon I have described. It is most noticeable in the morning, but appears at other times too, even in moonlight. Though it occurs continually, people seldom notice it, and it would give an excitable imagination like Cellini’s plenty of foundation for superstition. Besides, he says he showed it to very few people. But are those who know they are regarded at all not distinguished indeed?

One afternoon I set off through the woods to fish at Fair-Haven, hoping to supplement my meager vegetable diet. The route took me through Pleasant Meadow, part of the Baker Farm, that retreat a poet has since celebrated in a song that begins:—

“Your entrance is a pleasant field,
Which mossy fruit trees yield
Partly to a ruddy brook,
Where gliding musquash swim,
And quicksilver trout,
Darting about.”

Before going to Walden I had considered living there. I “hooked” the apples, jumped across the brook, and frightened the musquash and trout. It was one of those afternoons that seem to stretch endlessly ahead, leaving room for any number of events—a large share of our natural lives—though it was already half over when I set out. A shower caught me on the way and forced me to stand beneath a pine for half an hour, piling branches above my head and using my handkerchief as a little roof. At last, standing waist-deep in water, I made a cast over the pickerel-weed. Suddenly a cloud’s shadow covered me, and thunder began rumbling so emphatically that I could do nothing but listen. How proud the gods must be, I thought, to drive off one poor, defenseless fisherman with such forked lightning. I hurried for shelter to the nearest hut. It stood half a mile from any road, but that much closer to the pond, and had long been empty:—

“And here a poet built,
In years now past and gone,
For see a little cabin
That toward destruction goes.”

That is the Muse’s version. But, as I discovered, John Field, an Irishman, now lived there with his wife and several children. They ranged from the broad-faced boy who helped his father work, and now ran beside him from the bog to escape the rain, to a wrinkled, sibyl-like infant with a cone-shaped head. The baby sat on its father’s knee as though in a nobleman’s palace, gazing inquisitively at the stranger from its home amid hunger and damp. With infancy’s privilege, it had no reason to know it was not the last of a noble line, the world’s hope and center of attention, instead of John Field’s poor half-starved brat. We sat together beneath the least leaky part of the roof while rain and thunder continued outside. I had often sat there in earlier days, before the ship that carried his family to America was even built. John Field was plainly honest and hardworking, but unable to manage his affairs. His wife also showed courage, cooking so many dinners one after another in the recesses of that tall stove. Round-faced, greasy, and bare-breasted, she still hoped to better her circumstances someday. A mop was always in one hand, though its effects could be seen nowhere.
