The chickens had come in out of the rain too and strutted about like members of the family. I thought them too humanized to roast well. They stood looking me in the eye or giving my shoe significant pecks. Meanwhile my host told me his story. He worked hard at “bogging” for a neighboring farmer, turning meadow soil with a spade or bog hoe for ten dollars an acre and a year’s use of the land with manure. His little broad-faced son worked cheerfully beside him, unaware of the poor bargain his father had struck. I tried to make my experience useful to him. I explained that he was one of my nearest neighbors and that I, who came here to fish and looked like an idler, also earned my own living. I lived in a snug, bright, clean house that had cost scarcely more than a year’s rent for a ruin like his; if he wished, in a month or two he could build a palace of his own. I took no tea, coffee, butter, milk, or fresh meat, so I did not have to work to obtain them. Since I did not work hard, I did not have to eat heavily, and my food cost very little. He, however, began by requiring tea, coffee, butter, milk, and beef. To pay for them he had to work hard; after working hard he had to eat heavily again to replace what his body had used up. So he ended where he began—indeed, worse off, because he was dissatisfied and threw away his life into the bargain. Yet he counted it an advantage of coming to America that here he could have tea, coffee, and meat every day. The only true America, though, is the country where you are free to choose a life that lets you do without these things, and where the state does not try to force you to support the slavery, war, and other needless expenses arising directly or indirectly from their use. I deliberately spoke to him as though he were a philosopher, or wished to become one. I would gladly see every meadow on earth return to the wild if that were the result of people beginning to redeem themselves. A man need not study history to discover the best means of cultivating himself. But alas! cultivating an Irishman is a task that requires a sort of moral bog hoe. I told him that his hard bogging work required heavy boots and stout clothes, which quickly grew dirty and wore out anyway. I wore light shoes and thin clothes costing less than half as much, although he might think I dressed like a gentleman—which was not the case. In an hour or two I could, if I chose, catch enough fish for two days, or earn enough money for a week’s support, without labor, simply for recreation. If he and his family lived simply, they could all go huckleberry-picking for amusement in summer. John sighed, and his wife stared with her hands on her hips. Both seemed to wonder whether they had enough capital to begin such a life, or enough arithmetic to see it through. To them this was sailing by dead reckoning; they could not see clearly how it would bring them into port. So I suppose they still face life courageously in their own fashion, fighting it tooth and nail. They have not the skill to drive in a fine wedge, split its massive columns, and defeat it piece by piece. They think they must grasp it roughly, as one should grasp a thistle. But the odds against them are overwhelming: John Field, alas! lives without arithmetic, and fails for lack of it.

“Do you go fishing?” I asked. “Oh yes, I get a meal’s worth now and then when I’m taking a rest; I catch good perch.” “What do you use for bait?” “I use worms to catch shiners, then bait the perch with those.” “You’d better go now, John,” his wife said, her face shining with hope. But John held back.

By now the shower had ended, and a rainbow over the woods to the east promised a clear evening, so I took my leave. Once outside, I asked for water, hoping for a look at the bottom of the well to finish my inspection of the place. Alas! it had shallows and quicksands, a broken rope as well, and a bucket beyond recovery. Meanwhile a suitable kitchen vessel was chosen; the water apparently had to be distilled, and after consultation and a long delay it was handed out to the thirsty visitor, without time to cool or to settle. So this gruel sustains life here, I thought. Closing my eyes and keeping out the specks with a carefully managed undercurrent, I drank as heartily as I could to genuine hospitality. Where good manners are involved, I am not squeamish about such things.

Leaving the Irishman’s roof after the rain, I headed back toward the pond. For a moment my hurry to catch pickerel—to wade through secluded meadows, muddy hollows, and bog holes, through wild and desolate places—seemed a trivial pursuit for someone who had attended school and college. But as I ran downhill toward the reddening west, the rainbow over my shoulder, faint tinkling sounds reached me through the washed air from some unknown direction. My Good Genius seemed to tell me: Go fishing and hunting far and wide each day—ever farther and wider—and rest without misgivings beside many brooks and hearths. Remember your Creator while you are young. Rise carefree before dawn and look for adventures. Let noon find you beside different lakes, and let night catch you at home wherever you happen to be. No fields are larger than these; no games are worthier than the ones played here. Grow wild as your nature directs, like these sedges and ferns that will never turn into English hay. Let thunder roll; what if it threatens to destroy the farmers’ crops? That is not its message to you. Find shelter under the cloud while they run to their carts and sheds. Make earning your living a sport instead of a trade. Enjoy the land without owning it. People remain where they are through a lack of enterprise and faith, buying and selling and spending their lives like serfs.
O Baker Farm!

“Landscape whose richest element
Is a little sunshine, innocent.” * *

“No one comes running to revel
On your meadow fenced with rails.” * *

“You argue with no man,
No questions leave you perplexed,
As tame at first sight as now,
In your plain russet gabardine dressed.” * *

“Come, you who love,
And you who hate,
Children of the Holy Dove,
And Guy Faux of the state,
And hang your conspiracies
From the trees’ tough rafters!”

People come meekly home at night from no farther away than the next field or street, where echoes of their households still haunt them. Their lives languish from breathing the same breath over again; morning and evening, their shadows travel farther than their feet do all day. We ought to come home every day from distant places, from adventures, dangers, and discoveries, bringing back fresh experience and character.

Before I reached the pond, some new impulse had drawn John Field out. He had changed his mind and given up “bogging” before sunset. But while I caught a respectable string of fish, the poor man disturbed only a couple of fins. He blamed his luck; then we exchanged seats in the boat, and luck exchanged seats with us. Poor John Field! I hope he does not read this unless he means to learn from it. He thinks he can live in this primitive new country by some secondhand method from the old country—catching perch with shiners. I admit that sometimes they make good bait. Yet, with a whole horizon of his own, he remains a poor man, born to poverty, carrying his inherited Irish poverty or impoverished life, his Adam’s grandmother and his bog-bound ways. Neither he nor his descendants will rise in this world until their wading, webbed, bog-trotting feet grow _talaria_, wings at their heels.

chapters.title: Higher Laws
paragraphs: Walking home through the dark woods with a string of fish and my pole trailing behind, I glimpsed a woodchuck slipping across the path. A strange, savage pleasure thrilled me, and I nearly seized him to eat raw—not from hunger, unless it was hunger for the wildness he embodied. Once or twice during my pond life, though, I roamed the woods like a half-starved hound, strangely abandoned, looking for some venison to devour. No morsel could have been too wild for me. The wildest places had grown inexplicably familiar. Then as now, I felt an instinct toward a higher, or so-called spiritual, life, as most men do, and another toward a primitive, rank, savage life. I honor both. I love the wild no less than the good. Fishing’s wildness and adventure still drew me. Sometimes I like to take a raw grip on life and spend the day more like an animal. Perhaps fishing, and hunting when I was very young, gave me my closest knowledge of Nature. They lead us early into scenery and keep us there when we would otherwise know little of it at that age. Fishermen, hunters, woodchoppers and others who live in fields and woods are themselves, in a special sense, part of Nature. Between their activities they are often better placed to observe her than even poets or philosophers, who approach with expectations. She is unafraid to reveal herself to them. A prairie traveller naturally becomes a hunter, a visitor to the Missouri’s or Columbia’s head waters a trapper, and one at the Falls of St. Mary a fisherman. The mere traveller learns by halves and at second-hand, and makes a poor authority. Science interests us most when it reports what these men already know through practice or instinct. That alone is true _humanity_, an account of human experience.

People are wrong to say the Yankee has few amusements because public holidays are fewer here and men and boys play fewer games than in England. Here the older, solitary amusements—hunting, fishing and their like—have not yet yielded to those others. Nearly every New England boy of my generation shouldered a fowling piece between ten and fourteen. His hunting and fishing grounds were not fenced in like an English nobleman’s preserves, but were more boundless even than a savage’s. Small wonder he did not stay more often to play on the common. This is already changing, however, not because people have become more humane, but because game is scarcer. Perhaps the hunted animals have no greater friend than the hunter, not even in the Humane Society.

Besides, at the pond I sometimes wanted fish to vary my food. I have fished from the same necessity as the earliest fishermen. Any humane objection I summoned was artificial, a matter of philosophy rather than feeling. I am speaking here only of fishing, for I had long felt quite differently about the practice of shooting birds and had sold my gun before I went to live in the woods. I was not less humane than others, but noticed little effect on my feelings. I pitied neither fish nor worms. That was habit. During my last years with a gun I excused bird-shooting as ornithology, seeking only rare or unfamiliar birds. Now, I confess, I think there is a finer way to study them. It requires much closer attention to their habits, reason enough by itself to leave the gun behind. Despite the humane objection, though, I doubt whether sports of equal value ever replace these. When friends have anxiously asked whether to let their sons hunt, I have said yes, remembering how much it taught me. _Make_ them hunters: mere sportsmen initially, perhaps, but mighty hunters eventually, if possible, until no game in this or any leafy wilderness is large enough—hunters as well as fishers of men. To that extent I agree with Chaucer’s nun.

“cared not for the text a plucked hen
That says that hunters are not holy men.”

In an individual’s development, as in mankind’s, there comes a time when hunters are the “best men,” the Algonquins’ name for them. We must pity the boy who has never fired a gun: he is no more humane, only sadly undereducated. That was my answer about boys drawn to hunting, trusting they would soon grow beyond it. No humane person past thoughtless boyhood will deliberately murder a creature whose claim to life is the same as his own. A desperate hare cries like a child. Mothers, I warn you: my sympathies do not always observe the usual phil-_anthropic_ distinctions.

This is how a young man usually first enters the forest and the most original region of himself. He begins as hunter and fisherman. Eventually, if a better life has seeds in him, he discovers his true objects, perhaps as poet or naturalist, and leaves gun and fishing pole behind. Most men remain forever young in this respect. Some countries often display a hunting parson. He might be a good shepherd’s dog, but he is far from the Good Shepherd. I have been astonished to realize that, apart from wood-chopping, ice-cutting or similar business, fishing is the only visible occupation that has ever, to my knowledge, kept any fellow-citizen, parent or child, at Walden for an entire half day—with just one exception. Usually they thought their time poorly rewarded unless they caught a long string, though they had been free to look at the pond throughout. They might visit a thousand times before the sediment of fishing settled and left a clear purpose; still, that clarification would surely be working all along. The governor and his council faintly remember Walden because they fished here as boys. Now too old and dignified to fish, they will know it no more forever. Yet even they expect heaven at last. When the legislature notices the pond, it is mainly to regulate the number of hooks allowed. They know nothing of the hook of hooks with which to fish for the pond itself, using the impaled legislature as bait. So even in civilized society, embryonic man develops through a hunter stage.

In recent years I have repeatedly found that fishing lowers my self-respect a little. I have tried again and again. I am skilled at it and, like many others, have an instinct for it that revives periodically. Yet afterward I always feel I would have done better not to fish. I do not think I am mistaken. The hint is faint, but so are dawn’s first streaks. Undoubtedly this instinct in me belongs to creation’s lower orders. Nevertheless, each year I become less a fisherman, without becoming more humane or even wiser. At present I am no fisherman at all. Yet I know that wilderness living would tempt me to hunt and fish seriously again. There is also something fundamentally unclean about this food and all flesh. I began to understand where housework starts, and why so much effort goes into appearing tidy and respectable daily and keeping a house sweet, without offensive smells or sights. Having served as my own butcher, scullion and cook, and also the gentleman served, I can speak from unusually complete experience. My practical objection to animal food was its uncleanness. Besides, after catching, cleaning, cooking and eating the fish, I felt they had not essentially fed me. The business was small and unnecessary, costing more than it yielded. A little bread or a few potatoes would have served equally well with less dirt and trouble. Like many contemporaries, for years I had seldom taken animal food, tea, coffee, &c., less because of any ill effects I had traced to them than because my imagination disliked them. The aversion to animal food comes from instinct, not experience. A plain, austere life seemed more beautiful in many ways. Though I never fully lived it, I went far enough to satisfy my imagination. I believe anyone seriously intent on keeping his higher or poetic faculties in their best condition has been especially inclined to avoid animal food and excessive food of any kind. Entomologists report a telling fact—I find it in Kirby and Spence—that “some insects in their perfect state, though furnished with organs of feeding, make no use of them;” and give as “a general rule, that almost all insects in this state eat much less than in that of larvæ. The voracious caterpillar when transformed into a butterfly,” . . “and the gluttonous maggot when become a fly,” are content with a drop or two of honey or another sweet liquid. The abdomen beneath a butterfly’s wings still represents its larva. This is the tid-bit that tempts its insect-eating fate. The gross eater is man still in the larval stage. Whole nations live in that condition, without fancy or imagination, betrayed by their enormous abdomens.

It is difficult to obtain and prepare food so simple and clean that it does not offend the imagination. Yet I think the imagination should eat when the body eats; both should sit at one table. Perhaps we can accomplish this. Fruit eaten moderately need neither shame our appetites nor interrupt our highest pursuits. But add an unnecessary condiment and your dish poisons you. Living by elaborate cookery is not worth the trouble. Most people would be ashamed to be caught personally preparing exactly the animal or vegetable dinner that others prepare for them every day. Until that changes, we are not civilized; gentlemen and ladies perhaps, but not true men and women. Surely this points to the necessary reform. Asking why imagination refuses flesh and fat may be useless; I am satisfied that it does refuse them. Is mankind’s meat-eating not a reproach? Certainly man can live, and largely does, by preying on other animals. But anyone snaring rabbits or slaughtering lambs can learn what a miserable way it is. Whoever teaches mankind a more innocent, wholesome diet will be counted a benefactor of the race. Whatever I do myself, I have no doubt that humanity’s gradual improvement will include giving up animal food, just as savage tribes have stopped eating one another after contact with more civilized peoples.

Follow your genius’s faint but persistent suggestions, which are certainly true, and you cannot foresee the extremes, even madness, to which they may lead. Yet that is your road, as you grow more faithful and determined. The slightest definite objection felt by one healthy man will eventually outweigh mankind’s customs and arguments. No man has followed his genius so far that it misled him. Even if physical weakness followed, perhaps nobody could call the consequences regrettable, since they were a life lived by higher principles. If you greet day and night joyfully, if life gives off the fragrance of flowers and sweet herbs, becoming more springy, starry and immortal, that is success. All Nature congratulates you, and every moment gives you reason to bless yourself. The greatest gains and treasures are the least appreciated. We readily doubt they exist and quickly forget them. Yet they are the highest reality. Perhaps men never communicate the most astonishing, real facts to one another. My daily life’s true harvest is as elusive and indescribable as morning and evening colors: a little star-dust caught, a piece of rainbow held in my hand.

For myself, though, I have never been particularly squeamish. If need arose, I could sometimes relish a fried rat. I am glad to have drunk water so long for the same reason I prefer the natural sky to an opium-eater’s heaven. I would like to stay sober always; drunkenness has infinite degrees. Water, I believe, is the wise man’s only drink; wine is less noble. Imagine ruining a morning’s hopes with warm coffee, or an evening’s with tea! Ah, how far I sink when they tempt me! Even music intoxicates. Such seemingly small causes destroyed Greece and Rome and will destroy England and America. Among all kinds of drunkenness, who would not choose intoxication by the air he breathes? My gravest objection to prolonged coarse labor is that it forces me into coarse eating and drinking too. Truthfully, however, I am now somewhat less exacting. I bring less religion to meals and say no blessing—not because I am wiser, but because I must confess that, regrettably, age has made me coarser and less concerned. Perhaps these questions belong only to youth, as people commonly suppose poetry does. My practice is “nowhere”; here is my opinion. Still, I am far from counting myself among those privileged people meant by the Ved when it says “he who has true faith in the Omnipresent Supreme Being may eat all that exists.” Such a person need not inquire what his food is or who makes it. Even for him, however, a Hindoo commentator observes that the Vedant restricts this privilege to “the time of distress.”

Who has not sometimes found food inexpressibly satisfying without appetite having anything to do with it? I have thrilled at realizing that the usually gross sense of taste gave me an insight, that my palate inspired me, that hillside berries nourished my genius. “The soul not being mistress of herself,” says Thseng-tseu, “one looks, and one does not see; one listens, and one does not hear; one eats, and one does not know the savor of food.” Someone who knows his food’s true savor cannot be a glutton; someone who does not can be nothing else. A puritan can attack a brown-bread crust with as gross an appetite as any alderman his turtle. It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a man, but the appetite with which he eats. Neither amount nor quality is the trouble: devotion to sensual flavors is, when food no longer sustains animal life or inspires spiritual life, but feeds the worms possessing us. A hunter relishes mud-turtles, muskrats and such wild tid-bits; a fine lady relishes calf’s-foot jelly or sardines shipped across the sea. They are equal. He visits the mill-pond; she her preserve-pot. The mystery is how they—how you and I—endure this slimy, beastly life of eating and drinking.

Our entire life is astonishingly moral. Virtue and vice never call a moment’s truce. Goodness is the only investment that never fails. What thrills us in the harp music trembling around the world is its insistence on this truth. The harp is the Universe’s Insurance Company’s travelling salesman, recommending its laws; our little goodness is the whole premium we pay. Youth may eventually grow indifferent, but the universe’s laws never do. They always side with the most sensitive. Hear some rebuke in every zephyr: it is certainly there, and whoever misses it is unfortunate. Touch a string or move a stop, and the enchanting moral pierces us. Many an annoying noise, heard far away, becomes music—a proud, sweet satire on our lives’ meanness.

We sense an animal within, waking as our higher nature sleeps. Reptile-like and sensual, it may be impossible to expel entirely, like the worms that inhabit even our living, healthy bodies. Perhaps we can withdraw from it without ever changing its nature. I fear it may possess a health of its own: we may be well without being pure. Recently I picked up a hog’s lower jaw, its teeth and tusks white and sound. It suggested bodily health and vigor quite separate from the spiritual. This creature had prospered by means other than purity and temperance. “That in which men differ from brute beasts,” says Mencius, “is a thing very inconsiderable; the common herd lose it very soon; superior men preserve it carefully.” Who can imagine life after we attained purity? If I knew someone wise enough to teach it, I would seek him at once. “A command over our passions, and over the external senses of the body, and good acts, are declared by the Ved to be indispensable in the mind’s approximation to God.” Yet for a time spirit can fill and govern every bodily member and function, transforming what looks like the grossest sensuality into devotion and purity. Sexual energy dissipates and defiles us when we are loose; restrained, it strengthens and inspires us. Chastity is man’s flowering. Genius, Heroism, Holiness and the rest are the different fruits that follow. Open the channel of purity and man flows straight to God. Our purity lifts us; our impurity casts us down. Blessed is he who knows the animal dies in him each day while the divine takes hold. Perhaps nobody lacks reason for shame over the lower, brutish nature attached to him. I fear we are gods or demigods only like fauns and satyrs: divinity joined to beasts, creatures of appetite, our very life to some degree our disgrace.

“How happy he who has due place assigned
To his beasts and cleared the forest from his mind!
* * * * *
Can use this horse, goat, wolf, and every beast,
And is not ass himself to all the rest!
Else man not only is the herd of swine,
But he’s those devils too which did incline
Them to a headlong rage, and made them worse.”

Sensuality takes many forms but is one thing; purity is one thing too. Sensual eating, drinking, intercourse and sleeping are all the same appetite. Watch someone do any one of them and you know how sensual he is. The impure cannot even stand or sit purely. Attack the reptile at one entrance to its burrow and it emerges from another. To be chaste, be temperate. What is chastity? How can a man know whether he has it? He cannot know. We have heard about this virtue without knowing what it is; we speak according to the rumor reaching us. Earnest exertion gives rise to wisdom and purity; idleness gives rise to ignorance and sensuality. In a student, sensuality is mental sluggishness. An unclean person is invariably idle: sitting by a stove, lying prone in the sun, resting without fatigue. To escape uncleanness and every sin, work earnestly, even at cleaning a stable. Nature is hard to overcome, but overcome her we must. What use is being Christian if you are no purer than the heathen, no more self-denying or religious? I know many religions called heathen whose teachings shame their reader into fresh effort, even if only toward performing rites.

I hesitate to speak of this, not because of the subject—I do not mind how obscene my _words_ may be—but because speaking reveals my own impurity. We discuss one kind of sensuality freely and without shame while keeping quiet about another. Our degradation prevents us from speaking plainly about necessary human functions. In earlier ages and certain countries, every function was reverently discussed and governed by law. However offensive to modern taste, nothing was beneath the Hindoo lawgiver’s notice. He explains eating, drinking, intercourse, the passing of excrement and urine, and similar matters, raising the lowly rather than falsely excusing his silence by calling them trifles.

Each man builds a temple—his body—for the god he worships, in a style entirely his own. Hammering marble instead will not discharge that duty. We are all painters and sculptors, working in our own blood, flesh and bones. Every noble quality immediately refines the features; every mean or sensual one makes them more brutish.

One September evening, after a hard day’s work, John Farmer sat at his door with his thoughts still partly occupied by labor. He had bathed and now sat to re-create his intellectual self. The evening was rather cool; some neighbors feared frost. He had barely begun following his thoughts when someone’s flute reached him, its sound agreeing with his mood. Work still filled his mind. Yet his main thought was that, although planning and scheming went on there against his will, it mattered little to him. It was merely skin scurf, constantly shed. The flute’s notes reached his ears from a sphere different from his working world, suggesting tasks for faculties asleep within him. Gently they dissolved the street, the village, the state he inhabited. A voice asked: Why stay here in this mean life of drudgery when a glorious existence is open to you? The same stars shine over fields beyond these. But how could he leave this condition and truly move there? His only thought was to practise some new austerity, let his mind descend into and redeem his body, and treat himself with ever-growing respect.

chapters.title: Brute Neighbors
paragraphs: Sometimes a friend joined me to fish, walking through the village from the far side of town to my house. Catching our dinner then became as much an occasion for companionship as eating it.

_Hermit._ What can the world be doing now? For three hours I have heard not even a locust above the sweet-fern. Every pigeon sleeps on its roost, without a flutter. Was that a farmer’s dinner horn sounding beyond the woods? The hands are coming home to boiled salt beef, cider and Indian bread. Why must men trouble themselves so? Whoever does not eat need not work. I wonder how much they have harvested. Who would live where Bose’s barking never lets a person think? And O, the housekeeping! Polishing the devil’s door-knobs and scrubbing his tubs on this shining day! Better to have no house. A hollow tree, say—and then consider morning visits and dinner-parties! Just a woodpecker’s knock. O, how they swarm; the sun is too hot there; they are born too far into life for me. I have spring water and a brown loaf on the shelf. Hark! Leaves are rustling. Some underfed village dog obeying the hunting instinct? Or the lost pig said to be roaming these woods, whose tracks I saw after rain? It is coming fast; my sumachs and sweet-briers shake. Ah, Mr. Poet, is that you? How does the world suit you today?

_Poet._ Look how those clouds hang! Nothing I have seen today equals them. No old painting, no foreign land has anything like that—except perhaps when we were off Spain’s coast. A genuine Mediterranean sky. I thought that, since I must make my living and have not eaten today, I might try fishing. That is a poet’s true industry, the only trade I have learnt. Come, let us go.

_Hermit._ I cannot refuse; my brown bread is nearly finished. I shall gladly join you shortly, but I am finishing a serious meditation and think its end is near. Leave me alone a little longer. To save time, you can dig bait meanwhile. Angle-worms are scarce in these parts, where manure has never enriched the soil; their race is nearly extinct. Unless appetite presses too hard, digging bait is almost as good sport as catching fish, and today you may keep that pleasure entirely to yourself. I advise you to begin with your spade down there among the ground-nuts, where you see the johnswort waving. I think I can promise one worm for every three sods turned, if you search among the grass roots as carefully as though weeding. Going farther would also be sensible if you choose: I have found good bait increases almost as the square of the distance.

_Hermit alone._ Let me see, where had I got to? I think my mind was almost in this position; the world lay at about this angle. Shall I go to heaven or go fishing? If I finish this meditation now, will such a sweet chance return? Never in my life have I come closer to dissolving into the essence of things. I fear my thoughts will not return. I would whistle them back if it helped. When they make an offer, is saying We will think of it wise? They have left no tracks, and I cannot find the path. What was I thinking about? It was a very hazy day. I shall try these three sentences of Con-fut-see; perhaps they will restore the state. I cannot tell whether it was low spirits or ecstasy beginning to bloom. Mem. Each kind of opportunity comes only once.

_Poet._ Well, Hermit, am I too early? I have exactly thirteen whole ones, plus some damaged or undersized ones. Those will serve the little fry; they leave more hook exposed. Village worms are altogether too big: a shiner can dine on one without ever meeting the skewer.
_Hermit._ Then away we go. Shall we try the Concord? Fishing is good there, provided the water has not risen too high.

Why should exactly these things we see constitute a world? Why does man have just these animal species for neighbors, as though nothing but a mouse could fill this crack? I suspect Pilpay & Co. have found animals’ finest use. In one sense every animal is a beast of burden, carrying a share of our thoughts.

My house mice were not the usual kind, said to have been imported into the country, but a native wild species absent from the village. I sent one to a noted naturalist, who found it very interesting. While I was building, one nested under the house. Before the second floor was laid and the shavings swept away, it regularly appeared at lunchtime to gather crumbs at my feet. Probably it had never seen a man. Soon it became quite tame, running over my shoes and up my clothes. It climbed the room’s walls in little bursts, easily as a squirrel, whose movements it resembled. One day, as I rested an elbow on the bench, it ran up my clothes and along my sleeve, then circled the paper containing my dinner. I kept the food covered and dodged about, playing bopeep. Finally I held a piece of cheese still between finger and thumb. It came to nibble, sitting in my hand, then washed its face and paws like a fly and walked off.

A phœbe soon nested in my shed, and a robin found shelter in a pine against the house. In June the normally shy partridge (_Tetrao umbellus_) brought her brood past my windows, from the woods behind to the front. She clucked and called like a hen, proving in every action that she was the hen of the woods. Approach them and, at her signal, the young scatter as suddenly as though a whirlwind swept them off. They match dry leaves and twigs so perfectly that a traveller may step among a brood, hear the mother’s wings whir as she takes off, her anxious cries and mewing, or see her drag her wings to draw attention, never guessing the young are nearby. Sometimes she rolls and spins in front of you, so dishevelled that for a moment you cannot identify the creature. The young crouch flat and still, often thrusting their heads beneath a leaf, attending only to their mother’s distant instructions. Your approach will not make them run and expose themselves. You can step on them, or stare at them for a minute, without discovering them. I have held them in my open hand then; obeying their mother and their instinct, they cared only to crouch without fear or trembling. Once I set them back on the leaves and one accidentally fell sideways. Ten minutes later it lay with the others in precisely that position, so perfect was the instinct. Unlike most birds’ helpless young, they are well developed, more precocious even than chickens. Their clear, calm eyes have a memorably adult yet innocent expression. All intelligence seems mirrored there: not just infant purity, but wisdom cleared by experience. Such an eye was not born with the bird; it is as old as the sky it reflects. The woods produce no other jewel like it. Travellers seldom gaze into so clear a well. An ignorant or careless sportsman often shoots the mother at just this time, leaving these innocents for some prowling animal or bird, or to merge slowly into the decaying leaves they so closely resemble. They say that, when hatched by a hen, the chicks scatter at an alarm and are lost, because they never hear the mother’s call that gathers them again. These were my hens and chickens.

How many creatures live free and wild, yet hidden in the woods, maintaining themselves near towns with only hunters suspecting them. How secluded the otter’s life here is! He may grow four feet long, the size of a small boy, without a human ever glimpsing him. I once saw raccoons behind the site of my house, and probably still heard their whinnying at night. After planting, I usually spent an hour or two in the shade at noon, eating lunch and reading beside a spring half a mile from my field. It seeped from beneath Brister’s Hill and fed a swamp and brook. To reach it I descended a series of grassy hollows full of young pitch-pines, entering larger woods around the swamp. In a secluded, shaded spot beneath a spreading white-pine, firm clean turf still offered a seat. I had dug the spring into a well of clear gray water, deep enough to dip a pail without clouding it. Nearly every midsummer day, when the pond was warmest, I went there for water. The wood-cock brought her brood there too to probe the mud for worms. She flew just a foot above them down the bank as they ran together below. On seeing me she left them and circled me, closer and closer until four or five feet away, pretending broken legs and wings to divert my attention and let them escape. Already they would have begun marching single file through the swamp, with thin, wiry peeps, under her direction. Sometimes I heard the young without seeing their mother. Turtle-doves perched over the spring or fluttered between the soft white-pines’ boughs above me. A red squirrel running down the nearest branch might become particularly inquisitive and familiar. Sit quietly long enough in a welcoming woodland place and every inhabitant will show itself in turn.

I also witnessed less peaceful events. One day at my wood-pile—or rather stump-pile—I noticed two large ants fighting fiercely. One was red; the other black, much larger, nearly half an inch long. Once locked together they never released their grip, but wrestled, struggled and rolled endlessly over the chips. Looking farther, I was startled to see combatants covering the chips: not a _duellum_ but a _bellum_, war between two races of ants. Red always fought black, often two reds against one black. Legions of these Myrmidons occupied every hill and valley of my wood-yard. Red and black dead and dying already littered the ground. It was the only battle I have witnessed, the only battlefield I have walked during the fighting: a war of mutual slaughter, red republicans against black imperialists. Deadly combat surrounded me, though without a sound I could hear, and no human soldiers ever fought more stubbornly. I watched one pair locked in an embrace in a little sunny valley among the chips. It was noon; they seemed ready to fight until sunset or death. The smaller red champion gripped his opponent’s front like a vice. Through every tumble he kept gnawing one feeler near its root, having already severed the other. The stronger black ant flung him side to side and, as a closer look showed, had already torn off several of his limbs. Their determination to keep fighting was even more relentless than that of bull-dogs. Neither of these combatants showed even the slightest inclination to retreat from the other. Their cry was plainly Conquer or die. Meanwhile a lone red ant appeared on the valley’s hillside, visibly excited. He had either killed his enemy or had not yet entered the battle—probably the latter, since every limb remained. His mother had told him to return with his shield or upon it. Or perhaps he was Achilles, nursing his anger apart, now come to rescue or avenge Patroclus. From a distance he saw the unequal struggle, for black ants were nearly twice the reds’ size. He hurried up, stopping on guard half an inch from the fighters. Choosing his moment, he sprang on the black warrior and attacked near the root of its right fore-leg, leaving the enemy to select among his own limbs. Now three were joined for life, as though a new attraction had put every lock and cement to shame. By then I would hardly have been surprised to discover military bands on some commanding chip, playing national airs to stir the sluggish and comfort dying fighters. I too grew excited, almost as though watching men. The more you consider it, the smaller the difference. Certainly no battle in Concord’s history, perhaps none in America’s, bears comparison for numbers, patriotism or heroism. In numbers and carnage this was an Austerlitz or Dresden. Concord Fight! Two patriots killed and Luther Blanchard wounded! Here every ant was a Buttrick—“Fire! for God’s sake fire!”—and thousands met Davis’s and Hosmer’s fate. Not one was a hireling. I am certain they fought for a principle as much as our ancestors did, not to escape a three-penny tea tax. For those concerned, this battle’s results will be at least as important and memorable as Bunker Hill’s.

I lifted the chip bearing the three fighters I have described and brought it indoors, placing it beneath a tumbler on the window-sill to watch the outcome. Through a microscope I examined the first red ant. Having severed his enemy’s remaining feeler, he now gnawed persistently at the nearer fore-leg. But his own breast had been torn away, exposing his vitals to the black warrior’s jaws; the black breastplate seemed too thick to pierce. The sufferer’s dark, jewel-like eyes burned with a ferocity only war could kindle. They struggled another half-hour under the glass. When I looked again, the black soldier had cut both enemies’ heads from their bodies. The still-living heads clung to his sides like grisly trophies at a saddle-bow, seemingly as firmly attached as ever. Without feelers, with only a fragment of a leg and unknown other wounds, he struggled feebly to remove them. After another half-hour he succeeded. I lifted the glass and he crawled crippled across the window-sill. Whether he survived and passed his remaining days in some Hotel des Invalides I never learnt, but I doubted his future industry would amount to much. I never discovered the victor or the war’s cause. For the rest of the day, though, my feelings remained stirred and harrowed as if I had watched the struggle, savagery and slaughter of a human battle at my door.

Kirby and Spence report that ant battles have long been famous and their dates recorded, although Huber seems to them the only modern writer who has witnessed one. “Æneas Sylvius,” they say, “after giving a very circumstantial account of one contested with great obstinacy by a great and small species on the trunk of a pear tree,” adds that “‘This action was fought in the pontificate of Eugenius the Fourth, in the presence of Nicholas Pistoriensis, an eminent lawyer, who related the whole history of the battle with the greatest fidelity.’ A similar engagement between great and small ants is recorded by Olaus Magnus, in which the small ones, being victorious, are said to have buried the bodies of their own soldiers, but left those of their giant enemies a prey to the birds. This event happened previous to the expulsion of the tyrant Christiern the Second from Sweden.” My own battle occurred during Polk’s Presidency, five years before Webster’s Fugitive-Slave Bill passed.

Many a village Bose, fit only to chase a mud-turtle in a provision cellar, secretly brought his heavy hindquarters sporting into the woods, sniffing uselessly at old fox dens and woodchuck holes. Perhaps a little cur led him, threading the trees nimbly and still capable of alarming their inhabitants. Far behind his guide, he barked like a canine bull at a squirrel that had climbed up to inspect him, then cantered away, bending bushes beneath his weight and fancying himself on the track of some wandering member of the jerbilla family. Once I was surprised by a cat walking the pond’s stony shore, since cats seldom travel so far from home. She was equally surprised. Yet even the most domestic rug-dwelling cat seems at ease in the forest. Her sly, stealthy movements make her look more native than its regular residents. While berrying once, I met a completely wild mother cat and kittens. All arched their backs like their mother and spat fiercely at me. A few years before I lived here, a “winged cat” stayed at Mr. Gilian Baker’s, one of the Lincoln farm-houses nearest the pond. I visited in June 1842, but she had gone hunting in the woods as usual. (I cannot be certain of her sex, and use the commoner pronoun.) Her mistress said she had arrived in the neighborhood a little over a year earlier, in April, and eventually been taken in. She was dark brownish-gray, with a white throat spot, white feet and a large fox-like bushy tail. In winter her fur grew thick and flattened along her sides into strips ten or twelve inches long and two and a half wide, and beneath her chin like a muff. The upper surface was loose, the underside felted; these appendages fell off in spring. They gave me two “wings,” which I still keep. No membrane is visible in them. Some thought the cat part flying-squirrel or another wild creature—not impossible, since naturalists report fertile hybrids of marten and domestic cat. If I had kept a cat, this would have been the right one. Why should a poet’s cat not be winged like his horse?

In fall the loon (_Colymbus glacialis_) arrived as usual to moult and bathe, filling the woods with wild laughter before I was up. Word of his arrival put every Mill-dam sportsman on alert. By gig or on foot they came in twos and threes, carrying patent rifles, conical balls and spy-glasses. They rustled through the trees like autumn leaves, at least ten men per loon. Some took one side of the pond, others the opposite: the unfortunate bird could not be everywhere; a dive here meant surfacing there. Then the kindly October wind rose, stirring leaves and rippling water until the loon could neither be heard nor seen. His enemies swept the pond with spy-glasses and filled the woods with gunfire. Generous waves rose and dashed angrily, siding with the water-fowl, and the sportsmen had to retreat to town, shops and unfinished work. Too often, though, they succeeded. Early mornings, fetching water, I often saw this stately bird sail from my cove a few rods away. If I followed in a boat to study his maneuvers, he dived and vanished utterly. Sometimes I did not find him again until late that day. On the surface, however, I could more than match him. He usually departed in rain.

One exceptionally still October afternoon, paddling by the north shore, I had searched the pond in vain for a loon. They especially settle on lakes on such days, like milkweed down. Suddenly, a few rods ahead, one sailed toward the middle and gave himself away with his wild laugh. I paddled after him; he dived, but resurfaced closer to me. At the next dive I guessed his direction wrongly and helped widen the distance: now we were fifty rods apart when he rose. Again he laughed loudly and at length, with better reason than before. His cunning maneuvers kept me at least six rods away. Each time he surfaced, he turned his head this way and that, calmly inspected land and water, and apparently chose a route that would bring him up in the broadest open water, farthest from the boat. His speed in deciding and acting was astonishing. He led me straight to the pond’s widest part and would not be driven out. While he formed a thought in his brain, I tried to guess it in mine. It was a pretty game on the smooth pond, man against loon. Suddenly the checker belonging to your opponent vanishes below the board itself, and the problem for you is to set your own piece as close as possible to the spot where his will appear again. Sometimes he appeared unexpectedly on my other side, apparently having swum directly under the boat. His breath and endurance seemed limitless. Even after his longest swim he immediately plunged again, leaving nobody able to guess where, below that smooth surface, he sped fish-like through the deep pond. He had time and capacity to visit its deepest bottom. Loons are reportedly caught in New York lakes on trout hooks eighty feet down, though Walden is deeper. How astonished fish must be by this awkward visitor from another sphere racing through their schools! Yet he seemed as sure of his way underwater as above it, and swam much faster below. Once or twice I saw a ripple as he neared the surface, poked his head out to reconnoitre, and instantly dived. I found resting on my oars and waiting just as useful as calculating his next appearance. Again and again, while I strained my eyes one way, his unearthly laughter startled me from behind. But after such cleverness, why always betray himself on surfacing with that loud laugh? Was his white breast not conspicuous enough? A silly loon indeed, I thought. Usually I could also hear his surfacing splash and locate him that way. After an hour he remained fresh, dived as eagerly and swam even farther than at first. It amazed me how serenely he sailed off on surfacing, breast unruffled, all the labor done by his webbed feet below. His normal call was that demonic laugh, still somewhat like a water-fowl’s. Occasionally, after especially outwitting me and emerging far away, he gave a prolonged, otherworldly howl, more wolf-like than bird-like, like a beast lowering its muzzle and howling deliberately. This was his looning, perhaps the wildest sound heard here, ringing through the woods far and wide. I decided he laughed at my efforts, confident in his own powers. By now clouds covered the sky, but the pond remained so smooth I could see his surfacing even when I missed the sound. White breast, still air and smooth water all worked against him. At last he rose fifty rods off and gave another long howl, as if appealing to the god of loons. Immediately an east wind rippled the water and filled the air with misty rain. I felt his prayer had been answered and his god was angry with me, so I left him vanishing far across the troubled surface.

For hours on autumn days I watched ducks cleverly tack and turn, holding the pond’s middle far from the sportsman—skills less necessary in Louisiana bayous. Forced into flight, they sometimes circled repeatedly high above the pond, black specks against the sky, able from there to see the river and other ponds. Long after I supposed them gone to those waters, they would descend on a slanting quarter-mile flight to a distant, unoccupied part of Walden. What else they gained, apart from safety, by sailing about in the middle of Walden I do not know, unless they love its water for the same reason I do.

chapters.title: House-Warming
paragraphs: In October I went gathering grapes in the river meadows and loaded myself with clusters that were more valuable for their beauty and fragrance than as food. There I also admired, without picking them, the cranberries: small waxy jewels, pearly and red, hanging from the meadow grass. The farmer tears them off with an ugly rake, tangles the smooth meadow, and thoughtlessly measures them only in bushels and dollars. He sells the meadows’ plunder to Boston and New York, where it is destined to be _jammed_ to please the Nature lovers there. In just this way butchers rake bison tongues out of the prairie grass, caring nothing for the torn, drooping plant. The barberry’s brilliant fruit likewise fed only my eyes. But I gathered a small supply of wild apples to stew, overlooked by the owner and travellers. When the chestnuts ripened I stored half a bushel for winter. At that season it was thrilling to wander the then boundless chestnut woods of Lincoln—they now sleep their long sleep beneath the railroad—with a bag over my shoulder and a stick in my hand for opening burrs, for I did not always wait for frost. Leaves rustled, red-squirrels and jays loudly scolded me, and I sometimes stole their half-eaten nuts: the burrs they chose were sure to hold good ones. Sometimes I climbed the trees and shook them. Chestnuts also grew behind my house. One large tree, almost overshadowing it, became a bouquet in flower, perfuming the whole neighborhood. But the squirrels and jays took most of its fruit; the jays came in early-morning flocks and picked nuts from the burrs before they fell. I surrendered these trees to them and went to more distant woods consisting entirely of chestnut. As long as they lasted, the nuts replaced bread very well. Perhaps many other substitutes could be found. One day while digging fishing worms I found the ground-nut (_Apios tuberosa_) on its string, the aborigines’ potato. It had become an almost legendary fruit to me: I had begun to wonder whether I had really dug and eaten it as a child, as I claimed, or had only dreamed it. Since then I had often seen its crinkled, velvety red flower climbing on other plants’ stems without recognizing the plant. Cultivation has almost wiped it out. Its rather sweet taste resembles a frostbitten potato’s, and I found boiling better than roasting it. The tuber seemed a faint promise from Nature that someday she would raise her own children here and feed them simply. In this age of fattened cattle and waving grain-fields, the modest root once chosen as an Indian tribe’s _totem_ is forgotten, or recognized only by its flowering vine. But let wild Nature rule here again: the delicate, pampered English grains will probably fall before countless enemies. Without human care, the crow may even carry the last corn seed back to the Indian’s God’s great cornfield in the south-west, from which he is said to have brought it. Meanwhile the nearly exterminated ground-nut may revive and flourish despite frost and wilderness, show itself native to this soil, and recover its ancient importance and dignity as the hunting tribe’s food. Some Indian Ceres or Minerva must have invented and given it. When poetry’s reign begins here, its leaves and strings of nuts may appear in our works of art.

As early as the first of September, I had seen two or three small maples turn scarlet across the pond. They stood beside the water at the tip of a promontory, below the place where three white aspen trunks branched apart. Ah, how many stories their color told! Week by week each tree gradually revealed its character and admired its reflection in the lake’s smooth mirror. Every morning this gallery’s manager replaced an old picture on the wall with a new one, more brilliantly or harmoniously colored.

In October thousands of wasps arrived at my lodge as if seeking winter quarters. They settled inside my windows and on the walls overhead, sometimes discouraging visitors from coming in. Each morning, while the cold left them numb, I swept a few outside. But I made little effort to drive them away; I was even flattered that they considered my house a desirable refuge. They never seriously bothered me, though they shared my bed. Gradually they vanished into crevices unknown to me, escaping winter and its unspeakable cold.

Before finally settling into winter quarters in November, I behaved like the wasps and often visited Walden’s north-east side. Sunlight reflected from the pitch-pine woods and rocky shore made this the pond’s fireside. Being warmed by the sun, while you still can be, is so much pleasanter and healthier than being warmed by an artificial fire. There I warmed myself at the still glowing embers summer had left behind, like a hunter who had moved on.

When it was time to build my chimney, I learned masonry. The second-hand bricks needed cleaning with a trowel, which taught me more than people usually learn about the qualities of both bricks and trowels. Their mortar was fifty years old and supposedly still hardening. But this is one of those sayings people enjoy repeating whether true or false. Such sayings themselves harden and stick more firmly with age; it would take many trowel blows to scrape them off an old know-it-all. Many Mesopotamian villages are built with excellent second-hand bricks taken from Babylon’s ruins, whose cement is older and probably harder still. Whatever the truth of that, I marvelled at the toughness of steel that survived so many violent blows without wearing out. My bricks had already served in a chimney. Though I found no name of Nebuchadnezzar on them, I selected as many fireplace bricks as possible to save labor and waste. Around the fireplace I packed the spaces between bricks with stones from the pond shore and mixed my mortar with its white sand. I spent the most time over the fireplace, the house’s vital organ. Indeed, I worked so deliberately that, though I began at ground level in the morning, a row of bricks only a few inches above the floor became my pillow that night. I do not remember getting a stiff neck from it; my stiff neck dates further back. About then I took in a poet as a boarder for two weeks, which pressed my space to its limits. He brought a knife, although I owned two, and we cleaned them by thrusting them into the ground. He shared the cooking work. I enjoyed seeing my structure gradually rise so square and solid, reflecting that its slow progress promised a long life. A chimney is partly an independent structure, rooted in the earth and rising through the house toward heaven. Sometimes it remains standing after the house burns, displaying its importance and independence. That building took place near summer’s end. Now it was November.

The north wind had already started cooling the pond, though its depth required many weeks of steady blowing. When I began lighting evening fires, before plastering the house, the many gaps between the boards made the chimney draw particularly well. Yet I spent happy evenings in that cool, airy room, surrounded by rough brown knotty boards, with bark-covered rafters high above. The house never looked so pleasing after I plastered it, though I had to admit it was more comfortable. Shouldn’t every room people live in be high enough to allow some darkness overhead, where evening shadows can flicker among the rafters? Such shapes please fancy and imagination more than frescoes or the costliest furnishings. I might say I only began truly inhabiting my house when I used it for warmth as well as shelter. I had acquired two old fire-dogs to lift the wood off the hearth. Seeing soot gather at the back of my own chimney did me good, and I stirred the fire with unusual satisfaction and a greater right to do so. My dwelling could barely accommodate an echo, so small was it. But having just one room and distant neighbors made it seem larger. Every attraction of a house was gathered into that room: kitchen, bedroom, parlor, and family room. Whatever pleasure a house offers parent or child, master or servant, I enjoyed it all. Cato says a family’s master (_patremfamilias_) must have in his country villa “cellam oleariam, vinariam, dolia multa, uti lubeat caritatem expectare, et rei, et virtuti, et gloriæ erit,” meaning “an oil and wine cellar, many casks, so that it may be pleasant to expect hard times; it will be for his advantage, and virtue, and glory.” My cellar held a firkin of potatoes and about two quarts of peas containing weevils; my shelf held a little rice, a molasses jug, and a peck each of rye and Indian meal.

Sometimes I dream of a bigger house with more people in it, built in a golden age from durable materials, without ginger-bread ornament, yet still containing only one room. It would be an enormous, rough, solid, primitive hall, without ceiling or plaster, its exposed rafters and purlins holding up a lower heaven overhead—useful for keeping out rain and snow. Its king and queen posts would stand prominently to receive your homage after you had honored the fallen Saturn of an older dynasty by stepping across the threshold. In this cavernous house you would need to raise a torch on a pole to see the roof. Some might live in the fireplace, others in a window recess or on benches, some at one end of the hall and some at the other, or, if they preferred, up among the rafters with the spiders. Once you opened the outside door, you would be in the house and the ceremony would be finished. A tired traveller could wash, eat, talk, and sleep without another journey. It would be the shelter you would welcome on a stormy night, containing everything essential to a house and nothing for house-keeping. You could see all its treasures at once, with everything a person needs hanging on its peg. Kitchen, pantry, parlor, bedroom, store-house, and attic would be one. You could see such necessities as a barrel or ladder, such conveniences as a cupboard, hear the boiling pot, and pay your respects to the fire cooking your dinner and the oven baking your bread. Essential furniture and utensils would be the chief ornaments. Neither the washing nor the fire nor the mistress would be put out. Perhaps you would sometimes be asked to move off the trap-door so the cook could enter the cellar, discovering without stamping whether the ground beneath you was solid or hollow. The house’s interior would be as open and visible as a bird’s nest; you could not enter at the front and leave at the back without meeting some inhabitants. A guest would receive the freedom of the house, instead of being carefully barred from seven eighths of it, shut into one cell, and invited to make himself at home—in solitary confinement. Nowadays your host keeps you from _his_ hearth, having hired a mason to build one for you somewhere down his passage. Hospitality has become the art of _keeping_ you as far away as possible. The cooking is conducted with enough secrecy to suggest he means to poison you. I know I have been on many men’s premises, where they could legally have ordered me off; I do not know that I have been inside many men’s houses. If I were passing that way, I might visit in my old clothes a king and queen who lived simply in the house I have described. But if I am ever caught in a modern palace, backing out of it is all I shall want to learn.

Even the language of our parlors seems likely to lose its strength and sink entirely into _palaver_. Our lives are so distant from the things its words represent that its metaphors and figures must be fetched from far away, as if by serving hatches and dumb-waiters. In other words, the parlor is too far from the kitchen and workshop. Even dinner is generally only a parable of a dinner. As though only the savage lived close enough to Nature and Truth to borrow an image from them. How can the scholar living off in the North West Territory or the Isle of Man know what passes for parliamentary language in the kitchen?

Still, only one or two guests ever dared to remain and share a hasty-pudding with me. At the approach of that crisis, most preferred a hasty retreat, as though the meal might rock the house’s foundations. Yet the house survived a great many hasty-puddings.

I waited until freezing weather to plaster. For the job I brought cleaner, whiter sand by boat from the pond’s opposite shore; that mode of transport would have tempted me to travel much further had it been necessary. Meanwhile the house had been shingled to the ground on all sides. While putting up the laths, I enjoyed driving each nail home with one hammer blow. I hoped to move the plaster from board to wall quickly and neatly. I recalled the story of a conceited man who used to lounge around a village in fine clothes, advising workmen. One day he dared to replace words with deeds. Turning up his cuffs, he seized a plasterer’s board, loaded the trowel successfully, and looked complacently at the laths above. He made a bold upward gesture—and, to his complete humiliation, received the entire load down his ruffled shirtfront. I renewed my admiration for plaster’s economy and usefulness: it shuts out cold so effectively and takes such a handsome finish. I also learned the accidents a plasterer risks. The thirsty bricks surprised me, drinking all the moisture from my plaster before I could smooth it; so did the number of pails of water needed to christen a new hearth. The previous winter, as an experiment, I had made a little lime by burning shells of _Unio fluviatilis_ from our river. So I knew the origins of my materials. Had I wished, I could have found good limestone within a mile or two and burned it myself.

Meanwhile a thin skin of ice had formed over the shadiest, shallowest coves, days or even weeks before the pond froze generally. The first ice is especially fascinating and flawless: hard, dark, transparent, and offering the best possible chance to inspect the shallow bottom. You can stretch full-length on ice only an inch thick, like a skater insect on the water, and examine the bottom at leisure. It lies just two or three inches away, like a picture behind glass, and the water must always be smooth then. Many furrows mark the sand where some creature has wandered and doubled back. Scattered wrecks lie there: cadis-worm cases built of tiny grains of white quartz. Perhaps these made the grooves, since some cases lie in them, although the grooves seem too deep and wide for their makers. But the ice itself is most interesting, and you must seize your earliest chance to study it. Look closely on the morning after it forms: most bubbles that seemed to be inside it actually cling to its underside, while more continually rise from the bottom. The ice is still relatively solid and dark—that is, the water shows through. These beautifully clear bubbles range from an eightieth to an eighth of an inch across; through the ice you can see your face reflected in them. A square inch may hold thirty or forty. Already the ice also contains narrow, upright, oblong bubbles about half an inch long, pointed cones with their tips upward. More often, when the ice is very fresh, tiny round bubbles sit directly above one another like beads on a string. These enclosed bubbles are fewer and less visible than those underneath. Sometimes I tested the ice by throwing stones onto it. Those that broke through dragged air along, forming large, conspicuous white bubbles below. Returning to one spot forty-eight hours later, I once found those great bubbles still intact, though another inch of ice had formed; the seam along a broken piece’s edge showed this plainly. But the two days had been very warm, like Indian summer. Instead of being transparent and revealing the bottom and the water’s dark green, the ice was now opaque, whitish or gray. Although twice as thick, it was scarcely stronger. Warmth had greatly expanded the air bubbles, joining them together and destroying their regular arrangement. They no longer sat directly above one another, but often overlapped like silver coins spilled from a bag, or lay in thin flakes as though filling narrow cracks. The ice had lost its beauty, and the chance to study the bottom was gone. Curious about my great bubbles’ position in relation to the new ice, I broke out a piece containing a medium-sized one and turned it upside down. Fresh ice had formed around and beneath the bubble, trapping it between the two layers. The bubble lay entirely in the lower ice, tight against the upper. It was rather flat, perhaps slightly lens-shaped, with a rounded edge, a quarter-inch deep and four inches across. To my surprise, directly beneath it the ice had melted into the very regular shape of an upside-down saucer, rising five eighths of an inch at the center. Only a thin wall, scarcely an eighth of an inch thick, remained there between bubble and water. In many places small bubbles in that wall had burst downward; probably no ice remained beneath the largest bubbles, a foot across. I concluded that the innumerable tiny bubbles first seen clinging underneath had also frozen into the ice, and that each had acted on its own small scale like a burning glass, melting and weakening the ice below. These little air-guns help make the ice crack and whoop.

Winter finally settled in for good just as I finished plastering. The wind began howling around the house as though it had only now received permission. Night after night geese lumbered in through the darkness with clanging cries and whistling wings, even after snow covered the ground. Some landed in Walden; others flew low over the woods toward Fair Haven, on their way to Mexico. Several times, coming home from the village at ten or eleven at night, I heard a flock of geese—or perhaps ducks—walking over dry leaves beside a pond-hole in the woods behind my house. They had come ashore to feed, and I heard their leader’s faint honk or quack as they hurried away. In 1845 Walden first froze completely on the night of December 22d; Flint’s and other shallower ponds, and the river, had already been frozen for ten days or longer. In ’46 it froze on December 16th; in ’49 about the 31st; in ’50 about the 27th; in ’52 on January 5th; and in ’53 on December 31st. Snow had covered the ground since November 25th, abruptly surrounding me with winter scenery. I retreated further into my shell and tried to keep a bright fire in both my house and my breast. My outdoor work now was gathering dead wood, carrying it in my hands or on my shoulders, or dragging a dead pine under each arm to the shed. An old forest fence, past its prime, was a rich haul. I sacrificed it to Vulcan, since it could no longer serve Terminus. How much more interesting is the supper of a man who has just gone into the snow to hunt—or, one might say, steal—the fuel to cook it with! His meat and bread taste sweet. Most towns’ forests contain enough bundles of sticks and waste wood to feed many fires. At present this wood warms nobody, and some believe it obstructs young growth. The pond also supplied drift-wood. During summer I had found a raft of pitch-pine logs, still bark-covered, pinned together by the Irish railroad builders. I pulled it partly ashore. After two years soaking and six months out of water, the logs were perfectly sound, though too waterlogged ever to dry. One winter day I amused myself sliding them piece by piece nearly half a mile across the pond. I skated behind a fifteen-foot log with one end on my shoulder and the other on the ice. Or I bound several logs with a birch withe and dragged them using a longer birch or alder with a hook at its end. Thoroughly waterlogged and almost lead-heavy, they nevertheless burned long and gave intense heat. Indeed, I thought soaking improved their burning, as though the water held the pitch in place and made it burn longer, like oil in a lamp.

Gilpin writes of people living along England’s forests that “the encroachments of trespassers, and the houses and fences thus raised on the borders of the forest” were “considered as great nuisances by the old forest law, and were severely punished under the name of _purprestures_, as tending _ad terrorem ferarum—ad nocumentum forestæ_, &c.” That means frightening the game and harming the forest. Yet I cared more about preserving both venison and vert—the deer and greenery—than the hunters or woodcutters did, and as much as if I had been Lord Warden himself. If any part burned, even through my own accident, my grief lasted longer and resisted consolation more than the owners’ grief. I even grieved when the owners themselves cut it down. I wish our farmers, felling a forest, felt some of the ancient Romans’ awe when thinning a sacred grove or letting light into it (_lucum conlucare_): they should believe some god holds it sacred. The Roman offered atonement and prayed, Whatever god or goddess you are to whom this grove is sacred, look kindly on me, my family, and my children, &c.

Even in this age, in this new country, the value people place on wood is striking—more lasting and universal than gold’s. Despite all our inventions and discoveries, nobody will pass a woodpile without interest. Wood matters as much to us as to our Saxon and Norman ancestors: they made bows from it; we make gun-stocks. More than thirty years ago Michaux wrote that fuel wood in New York and Philadelphia costs “nearly as much as, and sometimes more than, the best wood in Paris, although that enormous capital needs over three hundred thousand cords annually and is surrounded for three hundred miles by cultivated plains.” In this town wood prices rise almost continually; the only question is how much higher they will be this year than last. Mechanics and tradesmen who never personally enter the forest for anything else reliably attend its wood auctions. They even pay dearly for the right to gather what the woodcutter leaves behind. For many years people have sought fuel and the materials of their crafts in the forest. New Englander and New Hollander, Parisian and Celt, farmer and Robinhood, Goody Blake and Harry Gill—in most of the world, prince and peasant, scholar and savage alike still need a few forest sticks to warm themselves and cook their food. I could not dispense with them either.

Everyone feels a kind of affection for his woodpile. I like mine in front of my window; the more chips, the better they recall my pleasant work. I owned an old, unclaimed axe. During intervals on winter days I played with it on the sunny side of the house, among stumps dug from my bean-field. As my driver had predicted while I was ploughing, they warmed me twice: first while I split them, then while they burned. No other fuel could yield more heat. Someone advised me to have the village blacksmith “jump” the axe, renewing its edge. Instead I jumped him, fitted a hickory handle from the woods, and made do. Dull though it was, at least the head sat true on the handle.

A few resin-rich pieces of pine were a treasure. Think how much of this food for fire still hides in the earth’s belly. In earlier years I often went “prospecting” on a bare hillside once covered with pitch-pines, digging out their rich roots. They are nearly indestructible. Stumps at least thirty or forty years old still have sound hearts even when all the sapwood has become vegetable mould. The thick bark’s scales show this, forming a ring flush with the ground four or five inches from the core. Axe and shovel explore this mine, tracing the marrow-like store deep underground, yellow as beef tallow, as though you had struck a gold vein. Usually, though, I lit my fire with dry forest leaves stored in the shed before snowfall. A woodcutter camping in the woods uses finely split green hickory for kindling. Now and then I acquired a little. When the villagers beyond the horizon were lighting their fires, a streamer of smoke from my chimney likewise told Walden vale’s wild inhabitants that I was awake.

Freshly cut green hardwood served me better than anything, though I used little of it. Sometimes I left a good fire burning before a winter afternoon walk; three or four hours later it would still be alive and glowing. My absence did not leave the house empty: I seemed to have left a cheerful housekeeper behind. Fire and I lived there together, and my housekeeper generally deserved my trust. Once, however, while splitting wood, I thought I should glance through the window to make sure the house was not burning. It is the only occasion I remember feeling especially anxious about this. I looked and saw that a spark had ignited my bed. Going inside, I put it out after it had burned a patch the size of my hand. Yet the house stood in so sunny and sheltered a spot, with so low a roof, that I could let the fire die in the middle of almost any winter day.

Moles made their nests in my cellar, nibbling every third potato. Even there they fashioned snug beds from brown paper and hair left over from plastering. The wildest creatures love warmth and comfort as much as people do; they survive winter only by taking such care to secure them. Some friends talked as if I had gone to the woods expressly to freeze. An animal simply builds a bed in a sheltered place and warms it with its body. Man, having discovered fire, encloses air in a roomy chamber and heats that instead of giving up his own warmth. This becomes his bed, where he can move without cumbersome clothing, preserve a sort of summer amid winter, admit daylight through windows, and extend the day with a lamp. He thus advances a step or two beyond instinct and saves a little time for the fine arts. Long exposure to the harshest winds would make my whole body numb, but the welcoming air indoors soon restored my faculties and prolonged my life. Even the most luxuriously housed person has little advantage to boast of here. Nor need we worry over theories of how humanity will finally perish. A slightly sharper blast from the north could cut our threads at any moment. We keep reckoning time from Cold Fridays and Great Snows; a Friday a little colder, or a snowfall a little greater, would put an end to human existence on earth.

The following winter I economized with a small cooking-stove, since the forest was not mine. But it did not hold a fire as well as the open fireplace. Cooking now mostly ceased to be poetry and became mere chemistry. In this age of stoves, people will soon forget how we roasted potatoes in the ashes in the Indian manner. Besides occupying space and filling the house with smells, the stove hid the fire; I felt I had lost a companion. A face is always visible in a fire. Looking into it at evening, the laborer burns from his thoughts the dross and earthiness gathered during the day. I could no longer sit gazing into the flames, and a poet’s fitting words returned to me with fresh force.

“Never, bright flame, may be denied to me
Your dear, life imaging, close sympathy.
What but my hopes shot upward ever so bright?
What but my fortunes sank so low in night?

Why are you banished from our hearth and hall,
You who are welcomed and beloved by all?
Was your existence then too fanciful
For our life’s common light, who are so dull?
Did your bright gleam mysterious converse hold
With our congenial souls? secrets too bold?
Well, we are safe and strong, for now we sit
Beside a hearth where no dim shadows flit,
Where nothing cheers nor saddens, but a fire
Warms feet and hands—nor does to more aspire;
By whose compact utilitarian heap
The present may sit down and go to sleep,
Nor fear the ghosts who from the dim past walked,
And with us by the unequal light of the old wood fire talked.”

chapters.title: Former Inhabitants and Winter Visitors
paragraphs: I rode out some lively snowstorms and spent happy winter evenings beside the fire while snow swirled wildly outside and even the owl’s hooting fell silent. For weeks my walks brought me no company except occasional woodcutters hauling their timber by sled to the village. Yet the weather helped me make a path through the deepest woodland snow. Once I had passed, wind blew oak leaves into my footprints. They settled there, absorbed the sun’s rays, and melted the snow, providing dry footing and a dark line to guide me at night. To find human company, I had to summon these woods’ earlier inhabitants. Many townsmen still remember when laughter and gossip rang along the road near my house. Little gardens and dwellings cut into and dotted the bordering woods, although the forest enclosed the road more closely then. I myself remember places where pines scraped both sides of a chaise at once. Women and children obliged to walk alone this way to Lincoln went fearfully and often ran much of the distance. Though chiefly an unassuming route to neighboring villages or a track for the woodman’s team, its variety once entertained travellers more and stayed longer in their memories. Firm, open fields now extend from village to woods. Formerly the road crossed a maple swamp on logs; their remains doubtless still lie beneath today’s dusty highway, from the Stratton Farm, now the Alms House Farm, to Brister’s Hill.

Across the road east of my bean-field lived Cato Ingraham, enslaved by Duncan Ingraham, Esquire, a Concord village gentleman. Ingraham built Cato a house and allowed him to live in Walden Woods: Cato not Uticensis but Concordiensis. Some describe him as a Guinea Negro. A few people remember his little patch among the walnuts, which he let grow until old age should make him need them. Eventually a younger, whiter speculator acquired them. That man, however, now inhabits a house just as narrow. Cato’s half-erased cellar hole survives, though few know it; a fringe of pines hides it from travellers. Smooth sumach (_Rhus glabra_) fills it now, and an early golden-rod species (_Solidago stricta_) grows abundantly there.

Here at the very corner of my field, still closer to town, stood the little house of Zilpha, a colored woman. She spun linen for the townspeople and filled Walden Woods with piercing songs, for her voice was loud and remarkable. During the war of 1812, English soldiers, prisoners on parole, burned her home while she was away. Her cat, dog, and hens all burned together. Her life was harsh and somewhat inhumane. An old visitor to these woods remembers passing at noon and hearing her mutter to herself over a bubbling pot, “You are all bones, bones!” I have found bricks in the oak thicket there.

Further down the road on the right, on Brister’s Hill, lived Brister Freeman, “a handy Negro,” formerly Squire Cummings’s slave. The apple-trees he planted and tended still grow there.
