They are large and old now, though to me their fruit still tastes wild and fit for cider. Recently I read his epitaph in Lincoln’s old burying-ground, somewhat to one side near the unmarked graves of British grenadiers killed during the retreat from Concord. It calls him “Sippio Brister”—he had some claim to the name Scipio Africanus—and “a man of color,” as though he were discolored. With glaring emphasis it also announced when he died, indirectly informing me that he had once lived. His hospitable wife Fenda lived with him and told fortunes, pleasantly enough. Large, round, and black, blacker than any child of night, she was a dark orb such as Concord never saw rise before or since.

Lower down the hill, to the left along the old woodland road, traces remain of a Stratton family homestead. Its orchard once spread over Brister’s Hill’s whole slope. Pitch-pines killed it long ago, apart from a few stumps whose ancient roots still supply wild stocks for many a flourishing tree in the village.

Closer to town, across the road at the very edge of the woods, you reach Breed’s old place. The ground is famous for the tricks of a demon unnamed in ancient mythology, though he has played a startlingly prominent role in New England life and deserves a biography as much as any mythological being. He arrives as a friend or hired worker, then robs and murders the entire family: New-England Rum. History should not yet relate the tragedies performed here. Let time pass to soften them somewhat and lend them a blue haze. The vaguest and most uncertain tradition puts a tavern here once, with the same well cooling the traveller’s drink and refreshing his horse. Here, then, people greeted one another, exchanged news, and went on their way.

Only a dozen years ago Breed’s hut still stood, though long empty. It was about my house’s size. Mischievous boys burned it, on an Election night if I remember correctly. I then lived at the village’s edge and had just lost myself over Davenant’s Gondibert. That winter I struggled with lethargy. I never decided whether it ran in the family—an uncle falls asleep shaving and must remove sprouts from cellar potatoes on Sundays to stay awake while keeping the Sabbath—or arose from my attempt to read Chalmers’ collection of English poetry without skipping. It thoroughly conquered my Nervii. I had just dropped my head over it when the fire bells rang. Engines hurried off, preceded by a scattered troop of men and boys. I was among the first, having leaped the brook. Those of us experienced at running to fires imagined this one far south beyond the woods: barn, shop, house, or all three. “It’s Baker’s barn,” someone cried. “It is the Codman place,” another insisted. Fresh sparks rose above the trees, as if the roof had collapsed, and we all shouted “Concord to the rescue!” Wagons raced past with crushing loads, perhaps carrying the Insurance Company’s agent among the rest; he was obliged to travel however far it proved. Behind us the engine bell tinkled at intervals, slower and surer. Furthest behind, people later whispered, came the ones who had started the fire and raised the alarm. Like true idealists we pressed on, denying our senses’ evidence, until a bend in the road brought the crackling sound and actual heat across the wall. Then we realized, alas! we had arrived. The fire’s very closeness cooled our zeal. We first considered throwing a frog-pond onto it, then decided to let it burn: it was too far gone and too worthless. We stood around our engine, nudged one another, and voiced our opinions through speaking-trumpets. More quietly we recalled the world’s great conflagrations, including Bascom’s shop. Between ourselves, we believed that, given time to arrive with our “tub” and a full frog-pond nearby, we could turn the threatened final universal fire into another flood. At last we withdrew without doing any harm, back to sleep and Gondibert. Yet I would exempt from my criticism of Gondibert the preface’s passage calling wit the soul’s powder: “but most of mankind are strangers to wit, as Indians are to powder.”

The next night, about the same hour, I happened to cross the fields that way. A low moaning drew me toward the spot in the darkness. There I found the family’s only survivor known to me, heir to its virtues and vices, the only person who cared about this fire. He lay on his stomach, gazing over the cellar wall at the embers still smouldering below and muttering to himself as usual. He had worked all day far away in the river meadows, then used his first free moments to visit his fathers’ home and the home of his youth. In turn he examined the cellar from every side and angle, always lying down to look, as though some remembered treasure lay hidden between stones that held nothing but bricks and ashes. The house was gone; he looked at what remained. The sympathy suggested by my presence comforted him. As well as darkness allowed, he showed me where the well was covered—something, thank Heaven, no fire could burn. He felt around the wall for a long time, seeking the well-sweep his father had cut and mounted. He searched for the iron hook or staple that had fastened a weight to its heavy end, all he could cling to now, to convince me this was no ordinary “rider.” I felt it. Nearly every day on my walks I still notice it, for a family’s history hangs from it.
Again on the left, in what is now an open field, the well and lilac bushes beside the wall mark the home of Nutting and Le Grosse. But let us turn back toward Lincoln.

Deeper in the woods than any of these people, where the road comes closest to the pond, Wyman the potter settled as a squatter, supplied the townspeople with earthenware, and left descendants to carry on. They too possessed little worldly wealth, occupying the land only by tolerance during their lives. The sheriff often came unsuccessfully for taxes and, as his accounts show, “attached a chip” to satisfy legal form; nothing else was available to seize. One midsummer day, as I hoed, a man taking pottery to market halted his horse beside my field and asked about the younger Wyman. He had bought a potter’s wheel from him long before and wanted to know what had happened to him. Scripture had taught me about the potter’s wheel and clay, but somehow I had never considered that our pots might not have survived unbroken from biblical times, or grown somewhere on trees like gourds. It pleased me to discover that such an art of moulding clay had actually been practised in my neighborhood.

The last person to live in these woods before me was an Irishman, Hugh Quoil—if that spelling gives his name enough coil. He occupied Wyman’s house and was known as Col. Quoil. Rumor made him a veteran of Waterloo. Had he lived, I would have asked him to fight his battles again in the telling. Here he worked digging ditches. Napoleon went to St. Helena; Quoil came to Walden Woods. Everything I know of him is tragic. He had the manners of someone who had seen the world and could produce more polite conversation than one could readily absorb. Suffering from delirium tremens, he wore a greatcoat in midsummer; his face was carmine-red. Soon after I moved into the woods he died on the road at Brister’s Hill’s foot, so I have not remembered him as a neighbor. I visited his home before it was demolished, when his companions shunned it as “an unlucky castle.” On the raised plank bed his old clothes lay curled by use, as though they were the man himself. His pipe was broken on the hearth, instead of a bowl broken at the fountain. That latter image could never symbolize his death: he had admitted to me that, though he had heard of Brister’s Spring, he had never seen it. Dirty cards—kings of diamonds, spades, and hearts—littered the floor. A black chicken the administrator could not catch still roosted in the next room, night-black and equally silent, without even a croak, waiting for Reynard. Behind the house a garden’s faint outline remained. It had been planted but never hoed even once because of those terrible shaking fits, although harvest had arrived. Roman wormwood and beggar-ticks overran it; the latter clung to my clothes, its only fruit. A woodchuck skin had recently been stretched on the back of the house, trophy of his last Waterloo. He would need no more warm caps or mittens.

Today only hollows in the earth mark these homes, with buried cellar stones and sunny grass bearing strawberries, raspberries, thimble-berries, hazel-bushes, and sumachs. A pitch-pine or twisted oak stands in the former chimney corner; perhaps a fragrant black-birch waves over the old doorstep. Sometimes you can see the well’s hollow, once fed by an oozing spring, now dry and tearless grass. Or the last of the family covered it deep under the turf with a flat stone, to be discovered only in some distant future. Covering wells must be such a sorrowful act! It happens as wells of tears open. Like abandoned fox burrows, these old cellar hollows are all that survives where human life once bustled and people debated “fate, free-will, foreknowledge absolute” in one form or dialect after another. All I can discover of their conclusions is that “Cato and Brister pulled wool,” about as enlightening as histories of better-known philosophical schools.

The vigorous lilac still lives a generation after door, lintel, and threshold have vanished. Each spring it opens fragrant flowers for a thoughtful traveller to pick. Children’s hands once planted and tended it in a front-yard plot; now it stands beside a wall in a secluded pasture, yielding to a new forest—the last of its line, its family’s sole survivor. The dark children scarcely imagined that the feeble cutting with only two buds, planted in the house’s shadow and watered daily, would take such firm root, outlive them, and find a home behind what had shaded it. It would outlast the grown man’s garden and orchard and tell their story faintly to a solitary wanderer half a century after they had grown up and died. It flowers as beautifully and smells as sweet as that first spring. I notice its still gentle, cultivated, cheerful lilac colors.

Why did this little village, the seed of something larger, fail while Concord holds its ground? Did it lack natural advantages—water privileges, indeed? It had deep Walden Pond and cool Brister’s Spring, with the privilege of long, healthy drinks from both. Yet the inhabitants developed that advantage only to dilute their liquor. They were a thirsty people, every one. Couldn’t basket-making, stable-brooms, mats, corn-parching, linen-spinning, and pottery have prospered here, making the wilderness blossom like the rose, with many descendants inheriting their fathers’ land? At least the barren soil would have guarded against low-land degeneracy. Alas! how little these human memories add to the landscape’s beauty! Perhaps Nature will try again, making me the first settler and my house, built last spring, the hamlet’s oldest.

As far as I know, nobody has built before on my own site. Spare me a city raised over an older city, with ruins for building materials and cemeteries for gardens. Such soil is bleached and cursed; the earth itself will perish before that becomes necessary. With these memories I filled the woods with people again and soothed myself to sleep.

Visitors seldom came in this season. With the snow at its deepest, nobody wandered near for a week or two, while I lived snugly as a meadow mouse. I was like cattle or poultry said to survive long burial in snowdrifts even without food, or the early settler’s family in Sutton, in this state. During his absence the great snow of 1717 buried their cottage completely. An Indian found it only because the chimney’s breath had opened a hole in the drift, and rescued the family. No friendly Indian troubled himself over me, nor was one needed: the house’s master was home. The Great Snow! What a cheerful thing to hear about! Farmers could not take their teams into woods and swamps and had to fell the shade trees by their doors. Later, when the crust hardened, they cut swamp trees ten feet above the ground, as the next spring revealed.

In the deepest snow, the roughly half-mile path from the highway to my house could have been drawn as a winding dotted line, with wide spaces between dots. Through a week of steady weather, I took exactly the same number of equally long steps both ways, deliberately placing my feet in their deep prints with the precision of a pair of dividers. Winter reduces us to such routines; yet heaven’s own blue often filled those hollows. No weather altogether defeated my walks—or rather my excursions. Often I trudged eight or ten miles through the deepest snow to keep an appointment with a beech, yellow-birch, or old friend among the pines. Ice and snow bowed the pines’ limbs and sharpened their outlines, turning them into firs. I waded to the highest hilltops while snow lay nearly two feet deep on level ground, shaking a fresh snowstorm onto my head at every step. Sometimes I crawled and struggled there on hands and knees after the hunters had retired to winter quarters. One afternoon I amused myself observing a barred owl (_Strix nebulosa_) perched near a white-pine’s trunk on a low dead branch. It was broad daylight, and I stood within a rod. He heard me move and crunch the snow but could not see me clearly. At the loudest noises he stretched his neck, raised its feathers, and opened his eyes wide. Soon the lids dropped again and he began nodding. After half an hour watching him sit with half-open eyes like a cat—the cat’s winged brother—I too felt sleepy. Only a narrow slit remained between his lids, preserving a peninsular connection with me. Through half-shut eyes he looked from dreamland, trying to make me out, a vague object or speck interrupting his visions. Eventually a louder noise or my approach made him uneasy. He turned sluggishly on his perch, apparently annoyed by the disturbance of his dreams. When he finally launched himself and flew through the pines, his wings opened astonishingly wide, yet I heard not the slightest sound. Delicately sensing the nearby branches rather than seeing them, as if feeling through twilight with sensitive wings, he found another perch where he could peacefully await his day’s dawn.

Walking the railroad’s long causeway across the meadows exposed me to many blustering, biting winds; nowhere could they range more freely. When frost struck one cheek, heathen though I was, I offered it the other too. The carriage road from Brister’s Hill was scarcely better. Like a friendly Indian I still visited town, even when the broad fields’ contents lay piled between the Walden road’s walls and half an hour erased the previous traveller’s tracks. By my return fresh drifts had formed. I struggled through them where the busy north-west wind deposited powdery snow around a sharp bend, leaving no rabbit trail or even the tiny print, the small type, of a meadow mouse. Yet even in midwinter I almost always found a warm, springlike swamp. Grass and skunk-cabbage still pushed up there in perennial green, and occasionally a hardier bird waited for spring to return.

Sometimes, despite the snow, an evening return from my walk brought me across a woodcutter’s deep footprints leading away from my door. I would find his heap of whittlings on the hearth and his pipe’s smell filling the house. Or, if I was home on a Sunday afternoon, I might hear snow crunch beneath a shrewd farmer’s feet. He had come a long way through the woods for a friendly “crack,” or chat. He was one of the few in his calling who are “men on their farms,” wearing a work-frock instead of a professor’s gown, as ready to draw a moral from church or state as to haul manure from his barn-yard. We talked about rough, simple times when clear-headed people sat around great fires in invigorating cold weather. Lacking other dessert, we tested our teeth on nuts that wise squirrels had long since rejected: the thickest shells are generally empty.

A poet travelled the greatest distance to my lodge, through the deepest snow and dreariest storms. Farmers, hunters, soldiers, reporters, even philosophers may lose courage; nothing stops a poet, moved as he is by pure love. Who can foretell his arrivals and departures? His calling sends him out at any hour, even while doctors sleep. We filled the little house with loud merriment and the low sound of serious conversation, compensating Walden vale for its long silences. Compared with us, Broadway was quiet and deserted. At fitting intervals we fired regular salutes of laughter, equally applicable to the joke just made or the one still coming. Over a thin bowl of gruel we invented many a “bran new” theory of life, combining conviviality’s pleasures with the clear head philosophy demands.

I must remember another welcome guest during my last winter at the pond. Once he made his way through the village in snow, rain, and darkness until my lamp appeared between the trees, and he shared several long winter evenings with me. Connecticut gave this man, one of the last philosophers, to the world. First he peddled her goods; later, he says, his brains. He still peddles them, prompting God and putting man to shame, producing only his brain as fruit, like a nut its kernel. I believe no living man has more faith. His words and bearing always assume a better order of things than other people know. As the ages turn, he will be the last to feel disappointment. He has invested nothing in the present. Little regarded now, he will have his day: laws most people never suspected will take effect, and householders and rulers will seek his counsel.
“How blind are those who cannot see serenity!”

He is a true friend of humanity, almost its only friend of progress. An Old Mortality—or rather an Immortality—he patiently and faithfully restores the image carved in human bodies: the God of whom people are merely defaced, leaning monuments. His welcoming intellect embraces children, beggars, the insane, and scholars. He entertains all their thoughts, usually broadening and refining them. I think he ought to run a caravansary on the world’s highway, lodging philosophers of every nation, with a sign saying, “Entertainment for man, but not for his beast. Enter, you who have leisure and a quiet mind, and earnestly seek the right road.” Perhaps he is the sanest person I know, with the fewest peculiar notions; yesterday and tomorrow he is the same. In earlier days we wandered and talked, effectively leaving the world behind. He owed allegiance to none of its institutions, being freeborn, _ingenuus_. Wherever we turned, heaven and earth seemed joined, for he made the landscape more beautiful. A blue-robed man, he is best roofed by the arching sky that reflects his serenity. I cannot see how he can ever die; Nature cannot afford to lose him.

Each bringing some well-seasoned shingles of thought, we sat whittling them, testing our knives and admiring the pumpkin pine’s clear yellowish grain. We waded so gently and respectfully—or rowed together so smoothly—that the stream’s fish of thought took no alarm and feared no fisherman on its bank. They came and went magnificently, like clouds drifting through the western sky and the mother-o’-pearl flocks that sometimes gather and dissolve there. At our work we revised mythology, rounded off a fable here and there, and built castles in the air too fine for any earthly foundation. Great Looker! Great Expecter! Conversation with him was a New England Night’s Entertainment. Ah! the talk we had—hermit, philosopher, and the old settler already mentioned, we three—stretched and strained my little house. I dare not estimate how many pounds above atmospheric pressure weighed on each circular inch. It opened the seams, which afterward needed caulking with much dulness to stop the leaks. But I already had plenty of that sort of oakum picked and ready.
One other person shared “solid seasons” with me, long remembered, at his village home, and visited me now and then. Apart from these people, I had no further company there.

There, as everywhere, I sometimes awaited the Visitor who never arrives. The Vishnu Purana says, “At evening the house-holder must stay in his court-yard for as long as milking a cow takes, or longer if he wishes, awaiting a guest’s arrival.” I often fulfilled this duty of hospitality, waiting long enough to milk an entire herd. Yet no man appeared on the road from town.

chapters.title: Winter Animals
paragraphs: Once the ponds froze solid, they offered not just shorter new routes to many places but unfamiliar views of the familiar country around them. Crossing snow-covered Flint’s Pond, which I had often paddled and skated on, I found it so strangely and unexpectedly broad that only Baffin’s Bay came to mind. The Lincoln hills rose around the edges of a snowy plain where I could not remember standing before. Far out at an uncertain distance, fishermen moving slowly with wolfish dogs seemed seal-hunters or Esquimaux. In mist they loomed like fabulous beings; I could not tell whether they were giants or pygmies. I took this route to my evening lectures in Lincoln, following no road and passing no house between my hut and the lecture room. On the way lay Goose Pond, where a colony of muskrats built cabins high above the ice, though I saw none out when I crossed. Walden, like the other ponds, was generally snow-free or carried only scattered shallow drifts. It became my yard, letting me walk freely while level ground elsewhere lay under nearly two feet of snow and villagers stayed confined to their streets. Far from the village road and, except at long intervals, the jingle of sleigh-bells, I slid and skated there as in an enormous, well-trodden moose-yard. Oak woods and solemn pines hung above it, bent with snow or bristling with icicles.

On winter nights, and often during the day, I heard the lonely yet musical hoot of an owl at some immeasurable distance. It was the sound frozen earth might give if struck with the proper plectrum, Walden Wood’s own _lingua vernacula_. Eventually it became thoroughly familiar, though I never saw the bird while it uttered it. I rarely opened the door on a winter evening without hearing that resonant _Hoo hoo hoo, hoorer, hoo_, the first three syllables stressed rather like _how der do_; sometimes it was only _hoo hoo_. One night early in winter, before the pond froze, a loud goose-honk startled me around nine o’clock. At the door I heard wings roaring like a storm in the woods as the geese flew low over the house. They crossed the pond toward Fair Haven, apparently put off landing by my light, while their commodore honked in steady rhythm. Suddenly, very close by, an unmistakable cat-owl answered the goose at regular intervals. Its voice was harsher and more tremendous than any woodland creature’s I had ever heard. It seemed determined to shame and expose this intruder from Hudson’s Bay by demonstrating a native’s greater vocal range and volume, and to _boo-hoo_ him beyond Concord’s horizon. What do you mean by alarming the citadel at this hour of night, sacred to me? Do you imagine you can catch me napping now, or that I lack lungs and a larynx equal to yours? _Boo-hoo, boo-hoo, boo-hoo!_ I have seldom heard a more thrilling discord. Yet a discerning ear could find in it the ingredients of a concord these plains had never seen or heard.

I also heard the pond’s ice whooping—my great bed-fellow in that part of Concord—as though it lay restless, wanting to roll over, troubled by wind and dreams. Or frost splitting the ground would wake me with a crash as though somebody had driven a team into my door. Next morning I would discover a crack in the earth a quarter-mile long and a third of an inch wide.

On moonlit nights I sometimes heard foxes searching the snow crust for partridges or other game, barking hoarsely and demonically like forest dogs. They seemed anxious, or straining to express themselves, struggling toward the light and toward becoming full-fledged dogs free to run in the streets. If we reckon in ages, might civilization not be developing among beasts as well as men? To me they resembled primitive, burrowing people, still on guard, waiting for their transformation. Occasionally my lamp attracted one close to the window. He would bark a fox’s curse at me, then withdraw.

Usually a red squirrel (_Sciurus Hudsonius_) woke me at dawn, racing across the roof and up and down the house’s sides as though the woods had commissioned him to do it. During winter I scattered half a bushel of unripe sweet-corn ears on the snow crust by my door and enjoyed watching the various animals they attracted. Rabbits regularly arrived at twilight and during the night for a hearty meal. Red squirrels came and went all day, entertaining me with their manœuvres. One would first creep cautiously through the shrub-oaks, then dash across the snow in fits and starts like a windblown leaf. He sped a few paces one way, extravagantly wasting energy, hurrying his “trotters” beyond belief as though racing for a wager; then he took as many paces another way, never advancing more than half a rod at once. Suddenly he would stop with a ridiculous expression and perform an unnecessary somersault, as if every eye in the universe watched him. Even deep in the loneliest forest, a squirrel’s movements imply an audience as surely as a dancing girl’s. His delays and precautions took longer than walking the whole distance would have done—though I never saw one walk. Then, before you could say Jack Robinson, he would be atop a young pitch-pine, winding his clock and scolding imaginary spectators, talking to himself and the whole universe simultaneously. I could never discover a reason, and suspect he knew none himself. At last he reached the corn, chose a suitable ear, and frisked along the same uncertain geometrical angles to the highest stick of my woodpile before the window. There he faced me and sat for hours, fetching fresh ears now and then. At first he ate greedily, tossing half-stripped cobs aside; later he became choosier and played with his food, tasting only each kernel’s inside. An ear balanced over the stick with one paw slipped from his careless grip and fell. He looked down with comical uncertainty, as though suspecting it of being alive, unable to decide whether to retrieve it, fetch another, or leave. One moment he thought of corn; the next he listened for news on the wind. The impudent little fellow could waste many ears in a morning. Finally he seized a longer, plumper one, much bigger than himself, balanced it expertly, and headed for the woods like a tiger carrying a buffalo. He followed the same zig-zag route with frequent stops, scratching along as if the load were too heavy and continually falling. Its descent traced a diagonal between vertical and horizontal; he was determined to get it through regardless. Such a frivolous, whimsical creature. Somehow he carried it home, perhaps to a pine’s top forty or fifty rods away. Later I found the cobs scattered through the woods in all directions.

Eventually the jays arrived. Their harsh screams had announced them long before, as they approached cautiously from an eighth of a mile away. They slipped furtively from tree to tree, drawing closer, and gathered kernels the squirrels had dropped. Perched on a pitch-pine branch, they hurriedly tried to swallow a kernel too large for their throats and choked. After a great struggle they brought it up again, then spent an hour trying to break it with repeated blows of the bill. Plainly they were thieves, and I respected them little. The squirrels, by contrast, though shy at first, set to work as if reclaiming their own property.

Flocks of chickadees came meanwhile, picking up the squirrels’ crumbs and flying to the nearest twig. They pinned the fragments beneath their claws and hammered them with tiny bills, as if working on insects in bark, until the pieces fitted their narrow throats. A small flock of these tit-mice visited daily to find dinner in my woodpile or crumbs at my door. Their faint, fleeting, lisping notes resembled icicles tinkling in the grass; at other times they gave a lively _day day day_, or, more rarely on springlike days, a thin, wiry, summery _phe-be_ from the woods’ edge. They became so trusting that one finally landed on an armful of wood I was carrying inside and pecked fearlessly at the sticks. Once, while hoeing a village garden, I had a sparrow rest briefly on my shoulder. I felt that honor distinguished me more than any epaulet I might have worn. The squirrels too eventually grew quite familiar and sometimes stepped on my shoe when it offered the shortest route.

Before snow fully covered the ground, and again toward winter’s end when it melted from my southern hillside and around the woodpile, partridges came out morning and evening to feed. Wherever you walk in the woods, a partridge bursts away on whirring wings, dislodging snow from dry leaves and high twigs. It sifts through the sunbeams like gold dust; this brave bird does not let winter frighten it. Drifts often cover it, and people say it “sometimes dives straight from flight into soft snow, staying hidden there for a day or two.” I also startled them in open country, where they emerged from the woods at sunset to “bud” wild apple-trees. They return every evening to certain trees where the crafty hunter waits, and distant orchards adjoining the woods suffer considerably. At least I am glad the partridge eats. It is Nature’s own bird, living on buds and diet-drink.

On dark winter mornings or in the brief afternoons, I sometimes heard hounds weaving through the entire woods with yelps and hunting cries, helpless against the chase’s instinct. Intermittent hunting-horn notes showed that men followed. The woods echoed again, yet no fox broke onto the pond’s open level, nor any pack chasing its Actæon. Perhaps that evening I would see the hunters heading to their inn, one fox’s brush trailing from their sleigh as a trophy. They tell me a fox would be safe if he stayed within the frozen earth, or that no fox-hound could catch him if he ran straight away. Instead, after leaving his pursuers far behind, he stops to rest and listen until they catch up. When he runs again, he circles toward his familiar haunts, where hunters wait. Sometimes, though, he runs along a wall for many rods and leaps far aside. He seems to understand that water holds no scent. A hunter told me he once saw a pursued fox rush onto Walden when shallow puddles covered the ice, run partway across, then double back to the same shore. The hounds soon arrived but lost the trail there. Sometimes a pack hunting alone passed my door, circled the house, and yelped and bayed without noticing me, as though possessed by a madness nothing could distract from the pursuit. They kept circling until they found a fresh fox trail, for a sensible hound abandons everything else for that. Once a Lexington man visited my hut to ask about his large-footed hound, which had been hunting alone for a week. I doubt my information made him any wiser: whenever I tried to answer, he interrupted with “What do you do here?” He had lost a dog but found a man.

An old hunter with a dry tongue used to bathe in Walden once a year, when the water was warmest, and call on me then. He told me that years earlier he had taken his gun for an afternoon cruise in Walden Wood. On the Wayland road he heard approaching hounds. Soon a fox leaped the wall into the road and instantly cleared the opposite wall; the hunter’s swift bullet missed him. Some distance behind came an old hound and her three pups, hunting on their own, in full pursuit. They too vanished into the trees. Late that afternoon, resting in dense woods south of Walden, he heard them far away toward Fair Haven, still chasing the fox. Their cries rang through the woods, coming nearer, now from Well-Meadow, now from Baker Farm. He stood listening a long time to that music, so sweet to a hunter, until the fox suddenly appeared. He ran easily through the solemn woodland aisles, swift and silent, close to the ground, his footfalls hidden by a sympathetic rustle of leaves, his pursuers far behind. Springing onto a rock among the trees, he sat upright listening, his back to the hunter. For an instant pity held the man’s arm. The mood passed quickly; as fast as thought follows thought, he aimed, and _whang!_ The fox tumbled from the rock and lay dead. The hunter stayed where he was, listening. The hounds kept coming, until their demonic cries filled every aisle of the nearby woods. Finally the old hound appeared, muzzle down, snapping at the air as though possessed, and ran straight to the rock. At the sight of the dead fox she stopped baying, seemingly struck speechless with amazement, and circled him silently. One by one her pups arrived and, like her, fell silent before the mystery. Then the hunter stepped forward among them, explaining everything by his presence. They waited quietly while he skinned the fox, followed the brush for a while, and eventually turned back into the woods. That evening a Weston Squire came to the Concord hunter’s cottage asking after his hounds. He said they had been hunting independently out of Weston woods for a week. The hunter told his story and offered the skin, but the visitor refused and left. He did not find his dogs that night. The next day he learned they had crossed the river and lodged at a farm-house overnight; well fed, they had departed early the following morning.

This hunter remembered Sam Nutting, who hunted bears on Fair Haven Ledges and traded their skins for rum in Concord village. Nutting even claimed to have seen a moose there. His celebrated fox-hound, Burgoyne—he pronounced it Bugine—was one my informant used to borrow. In the “Wast Book” of a former local trader, also a captain, town-clerk, and representative, I found this entry: Jan. 18th, 1742–3, “John Melven Cr. by 1 Grey Fox 0—2—3;” no gray foxes are found here now. His ledger for Feb. 7th, 1743, credits Hezekiah Stratton “by ½ a Catt skin 0—1—4½;” naturally a wild-cat, since Stratton served as a sergeant in the old French war and would scarcely have earned credit hunting less noble quarry. Deer skins also appear as credits and were sold daily. One man still keeps the antlers of the last deer killed nearby; another has described to me the hunt in which his uncle took part. Once hunters formed a large, merry company here. I clearly remember a lean Nimrod who would snatch a roadside leaf and play on it a tune wilder and, if memory is right, sweeter than any hunting-horn.
At moonlit midnight I sometimes came upon hounds prowling along my woodland path. They would slip aside as if frightened and wait silently among the bushes until I had gone past them.

Squirrels and wild mice fought over my stored nuts. Scores of pitch-pines around the house, one to four inches thick, had been gnawed by mice the winter before. It had been a Norwegian winter for them, with deep snow lingering long, forcing them to add a large share of pine bark to their diet. By midsummer the trees were alive and apparently thriving; many had gained a foot despite having their bark stripped in a complete ring. After another winter every such tree was dead. Remarkable that a single mouse should be allowed an entire pine for dinner, eating around it instead of up and down. Perhaps this is needed to thin these trees, which tend to grow in dense stands.

The hares (_Lepus Americanus_) grew very familiar. One spent the whole winter in a resting place beneath my house, separated from me only by the floor. Every morning when I stirred, her sudden departure startled me: thump, thump, thump, as she hurriedly struck her head against the floor timbers. At dusk they came around my door to nibble discarded potato peelings. Their color matched the ground so closely that a motionless hare was almost invisible. Sometimes in twilight I repeatedly lost and rediscovered one sitting still below the window. Opening my door in the evening sent them squeaking and bounding away. Close up they inspired only pity. One evening a hare sat two paces from my door, initially trembling with fear but reluctant to move. It was a poor little thing, thin and bony, with ragged ears, pointed nose, meager tail, and slender paws. Nature seemed to have exhausted her nobler bloodlines and to be standing on her last toes. The large eyes looked immature and unhealthy, almost swollen with dropsy. I stepped forward, and suddenly it bounded elastically over the snow crust, stretching body and limbs into graceful length. Soon the forest stood between us: free, wild venison affirming its vigor and Nature’s dignity. Its slenderness had a purpose. This, then, was its true nature. (_Lepus_, _levipes_, light-foot, some think.)

What would a country be without rabbits and partridges? They are among its simplest native animal growths: ancient, venerable families familiar to antiquity and to our own time, made of Nature’s very color and substance. Their closest relatives are leaves and earth—and each other; one goes by wings, the other by legs. When a rabbit or partridge darts away, you scarcely feel you have seen a wild creature, only a natural one, as expected as rustling leaves. Whatever revolutions come, these true natives of the soil will keep thriving. Cut down the forest, and the shoots and bushes that follow give them hiding places, multiplying their numbers. A country must be poor indeed if it cannot support a hare. Our woods abound in both. Around every swamp you can see partridge or rabbit paths, lined with twig fences and horse-hair snares tended by some boy who watches cattle.

chapters.title: The Pond in Winter
paragraphs: After a quiet winter night I woke feeling that someone had asked me a question I had struggled unsuccessfully to answer in sleep: what—how—when—where? Yet Nature at dawn, within whom every creature lives, looked through my broad windows with a calm, satisfied face and no question on _her_ lips. I woke into an answer, into Nature and daylight. Deep snow over the earth, dotted with young pines, and even the slope beneath my house seemed to say, Forward! Nature asks no questions and answers none of ours. Long ago she made her decision. “O Prince, our eyes admire and convey to the soul this universe’s wonderful and varied spectacle. Night doubtless hides part of this glorious creation, but day arrives to reveal the great work stretching from earth into the plains of the ether.”

Then I turn to my morning work. First, axe and pail in hand, I look for water—unless that too is a dream. After a cold, snowy night, finding it calls for a divining rod. Each winter the pond’s trembling liquid surface, responsive to every breath and reflecting every shadow and light, freezes a foot or a foot and a half deep. It can bear the heaviest teams. Snow may cover it just as deeply, making it indistinguishable from a level field. Like the marmots in the nearby hills, it shuts its eyes and sleeps three months or more. Standing on the snowy plain as in a hillside pasture, I chop through a foot of snow, then a foot of ice, opening a window beneath me. Kneeling to drink, I look into the fishes’ quiet parlor. Light softens through it as through ground glass, and its bright sandy floor remains just as in summer. A lasting, unruffled calm rules there, like the amber twilight sky, matching the inhabitants’ cool, even temper. Heaven lies beneath our feet as well as above our heads.

Early in the morning, when frost makes everything crisp, men arrive with fishing reels and scant lunches. Through the snowy field they lower fine lines for pickerel and perch. These are wild men, instinctively following fashions and trusting authorities different from those of their townsmen. Their journeys stitch towns together where they would otherwise tear apart. Wearing thick fear-naught coats, they sit on dry oak leaves along the shore to eat, as wise in Nature’s ways as the citizen is in artificial ones. They never consult books; what they know and can explain is much less than what they have done. The things they practise are considered still unknown. Here one uses full-grown perch as pickerel bait. You peer into his pail in amazement, as into a summer pond, as if he kept summer locked away at home or knew her hiding place. How did he obtain these in midwinter? Why, after the ground froze he found worms in rotten logs and caught the perch with them. His actual life goes deeper into Nature than the naturalist’s investigations; he himself is material for the naturalist. The latter gently lifts moss and bark with a knife to find insects; the former splits logs to their hearts with an axe, scattering moss and bark everywhere. Stripping bark earns his living. Such a man has some claim to fish, and I enjoy seeing Nature fulfilled in him. Perch eats grub-worm, pickerel eats perch, fisherman eats pickerel: every gap in the scale of being is filled.

Walking around the pond in mist, I sometimes enjoyed the simple methods of an unsophisticated fisherman. He might lay alder branches across narrow ice holes spaced four or five rods apart, equally far from shore. He would fasten a line’s end to a stick to keep it from being pulled through, drape the slack over an alder twig a foot or more above the ice, and attach a dry oak leaf. When a fish pulled the leaf down, it signalled a bite. For half a circuit of the pond, those alders appeared at regular intervals through the fog.

Ah, Walden’s pickerel! Whether lying on the ice or in a well a fisherman has cut into it, with a small hole to let water in, they always astonish me with their extraordinary beauty. They seem fabulous fish, as foreign to our streets—even to the woods—as Arabia is to Concord life. Their dazzling, almost otherworldly beauty sets them far apart from the corpse-like cod and haddock advertised so loudly in our streets. They are neither pine-green, stone-gray, nor sky-blue. To my eyes their colors are rarer still, like flowers and gemstones, as though they were Walden water’s pearls, its living _nuclei_ or crystals. Naturally they are wholly Walden, inside and out: little Waldens in the animal kingdom, Waldenses. Amazing that one catches them here, that this great golden and emerald fish swims in the deep, ample spring far below the rattling teams and chaises and jingling sleighs on Walden road. I have never seen its like in a market, where every eye would be drawn to it. With a few convulsive twists they easily surrender their watery ghosts, like a mortal transported too soon into heaven’s thin air.

Wanting to recover Walden Pond’s long-lost bottom, I carefully surveyed it early in ’46, before the ice broke, using compass, chain, and sounding line. Many stories about its bottom—or lack of one—have circulated without any foundation of their own. Remarkable how long people believe a pond bottomless without bothering to sound it. In one neighborhood walk I have visited two such Bottomless Ponds. Many supposed Walden went right through the globe. People lying flat on its ice for a long time, staring through the deceptive medium, perhaps with watering eyes as well, and hurrying to conclusions for fear of chest colds, have seen immense holes “into which a load of hay might be driven”—if anyone would drive it. Surely here, they think, are the Styx’s source and our local entrance to the Infernal Regions. Others brought a “fifty-six” and a wagonload of inch-thick rope from the village and still found no bottom. While the fifty-six-pound weight rested along the way, they kept paying out rope, vainly trying to sound their own truly limitless capacity for marvels. I assure readers, however, that Walden has a fairly watertight bottom at an unusual but reasonable depth. A cod-line and a stone of about a pound and a half easily sounded it. The extra pull needed before water could get underneath and help told me precisely when the stone left the bottom. The deepest spot measured exactly one hundred and two feet. Add its subsequent five-foot rise, and the depth becomes one hundred and seven. For so small an area this is remarkable, yet imagination cannot spare a single inch. What if every pond were shallow? Wouldn’t that affect people’s minds? I am grateful this pond was made deep and pure to serve as a symbol. As long as people believe in infinity, some ponds will be thought bottomless.

A factory owner doubted my measured depth. His experience with dams, he said, showed that sand would not rest at such a steep angle. Yet even the deepest ponds are shallower in proportion to their area than most people imagine; drain them and the remaining valleys would be unremarkable. They are not cups among hills. Even this pond, exceptionally deep for its size, looks in a vertical section through its centre no deeper than a shallow plate. Empty most ponds and you would reveal meadows no more hollow than many familiar ones. William Gilpin, admirable on landscape and usually accurate, stood at the head of Scotland’s Loch Fyne, which he calls “a salt-water bay, sixty or seventy fathoms deep and four miles wide,” about fifty miles long and ringed by mountains. He remarks, “Had we seen it just after the flood’s crash, or whatever upheaval of Nature caused it, before water rushed in, what a dreadful chasm it must have seemed!

As high as rose the swelling hills, so low
Down sank a hollow bottom broad and deep,
Capacious bed of waters—.”

But take Loch Fyne’s shortest diameter and apply its proportions to Walden, which already looks like a shallow plate in vertical section: our pond would appear four times shallower. So much for the _increased_ horror of an emptied Loch Fyne. Doubtless many a pleasant valley spreading with cornfields fills exactly such a “horrid chasm” after its waters have withdrawn. Convincing unsuspecting residents of this takes a geologist’s penetrating, long view. An inquisitive observer can often recognize an ancient lake’s shores in the low hills along the horizon; no later raising of the plain was needed to hide their story. Still, road workers know the easiest way to locate hollows is to look for puddles after rain. The point is that imagination, allowed the least freedom, dives deeper and flies higher than Nature. The ocean’s depth, too, will probably prove very small beside its breadth.

Sounding through ice let me trace the bottom more accurately than one can survey harbors that never freeze, and its overall regularity surprised me. Several acres at the deepest part are flatter than almost any field subject to sun, wind, and plough. Along one arbitrarily chosen line, the depth changed by no more than a foot in thirty rods. Near the centre I could generally predict the variation over each hundred feet in any direction within three or four inches. People often mention dangerous deep holes even in quiet sandy ponds like this, but here water works to smooth away irregularities. The bottom’s regularity, and its agreement with the shoreline and neighboring hills, were so exact that a distant promontory registered in soundings clear across the pond. Its direction could be found by studying the opposite bank. A cape becomes a bar, a plain a shoal, a valley deep water, and a gorge a channel.

After drawing the pond at ten rods to the inch and entering more than a hundred depth measurements, I noticed an extraordinary coincidence. The greatest depth’s number seemed to lie at the map’s centre. I laid a ruler lengthwise on the map, then crosswise, and discovered to my surprise that the greatest length crossed the greatest breadth _exactly_ at the deepest point. This held although the middle was nearly level, the shoreline far from regular, and the maximum dimensions included measurements into the coves. I asked myself whether this clue might also lead to an ocean’s deepest point, as well as a pond’s or puddle’s. Doesn’t the same rule govern mountains’ heights, if mountains are valleys’ opposites? We know a hill’s highest part is not its narrowest.

Of the five coves, the three I had sounded all had a bar stretching across the mouth, with deeper water inside. Each bay thus expanded into the land vertically as well as horizontally, forming a basin or separate pond; the two capes’ direction indicated the bar’s course. Every coastal harbor likewise has an entrance bar. The wider a cove’s mouth in relation to its length, the deeper the water over its bar in relation to the basin’s depth. Give us a cove’s length and breadth and the nature of the surrounding shore, then, and we have almost enough information to formulate a rule covering every case.

To test how closely this experience let me predict a pond’s deepest point from only its surface outline and shores, I mapped White Pond. It covers about forty-one acres and, like Walden, has neither an island nor any visible inlet or outlet. Its greatest-width line lay very close to its narrowest-width line, where opposite capes approached each other and opposite bays drew back. I ventured to mark the deepest point a short distance from that narrowest line, still along the greatest-length line. Sounding found the deepest part within a hundred feet of my mark, a little further in the direction I had chosen. At sixty feet, it was only a foot deeper. Naturally, an island or a stream flowing through the pond would greatly complicate the problem.

If all Nature’s laws were known to us, one fact, or the description of one real phenomenon, would suffice to infer every particular result at that point. We know only a few laws, so our conclusions are flawed—not because Nature is confused or irregular, but because our calculations lack essential information. We generally restrict our ideas of law and harmony to the cases we recognize. Yet the harmony produced by many more undiscovered laws, seemingly conflicting but actually working together, is more wonderful still. Individual laws resemble our viewpoints: a mountain changes its outline with every step a traveller takes, offering infinitely many profiles while having only one actual shape. Even cutting it open or boring through it does not reveal its entirety.

These observations about the pond apply equally to ethics. They express the law of average. The rule of two diameters points not only toward the solar system’s sun and the human heart. Draw lines across the length and breadth of someone’s combined daily actions, through life’s waves into his coves and inlets: their crossing marks his character’s height or depth. Perhaps knowing the direction of his shores and the country or circumstances beside them is enough to infer his depth and hidden bottom. Mountainous circumstances, an Achillean shore whose peaks overshadow his breast and reflect in it, suggest matching depths within. A low, smooth shore shows shallowness on that side. In the body, a boldly projecting brow slopes away and suggests a corresponding depth of thought. Across every cove or particular inclination of ours lies a bar. Each cove serves for a time as our harbor, holding us partly enclosed by land. These inclinations are seldom arbitrary. Their shape, size, and direction follow the shore’s promontories, its ancient axes of elevation. Suppose storms, tides, or currents gradually build the bar, or the water falls until it emerges. What began as a bend in the shore sheltering a thought becomes a separate lake, cut off from the ocean. There the thought establishes its own conditions, perhaps changing from salt to fresh, becoming a sweet sea, dead sea, or marsh. Might each individual’s entrance into life mean that somewhere such a bar has risen to the surface? Admittedly we navigate so poorly that most of our thoughts tack back and forth along a coast without harbors. They know only the bends in poetry’s bays, or steer for public ports of entry and enter science’s dry docks. There they merely refit for this world; no natural currents combine to give them individuality.

I have found no inlet or outlet for Walden apart from rain, snow, and evaporation. Perhaps a thermometer and line could locate one: water entering should be coldest in summer and warmest in winter. During the ice harvest of ’46–7, workers loading and stacking blocks on the shore once rejected those arriving because they were too thin to fit alongside the others. The cutters discovered that the ice over a relatively small patch of water was two or three inches thinner than elsewhere and suspected an inlet below. Elsewhere they showed me what they called a “leach hole,” through which they thought the pond drained beneath a hill into a neighboring meadow. They pushed me out on an ice block to inspect it. It was a small hollow under ten feet of water; I think I can guarantee the pond needs no soldering until they find a worse leak. Someone suggested testing any such hole’s connection to the meadow by placing colored powder or sawdust at its mouth, then covering the meadow spring with a strainer. The strainer would catch any particles the current carried through.

During my survey the sixteen-inch ice rose and fell like water beneath a light wind. Everyone knows that a level cannot be used on ice. I set one on land and aimed at a graduated staff a rod offshore. Although the ice seemed firmly fastened to the bank, its greatest movement there was three quarters of an inch, probably more toward the middle. Perhaps delicate enough instruments would detect waves in the earth’s crust itself. With two legs of my level ashore and the third on ice, its sights aimed across the pond, an almost imperceptible rise or fall shifted the reading several feet on a tree opposite. When I began cutting sounding holes, deep snow had pressed the ice down enough to leave three or four inches of water on top. This water immediately drained into the holes and kept flowing for two days in deep streams, eroding ice on every side. The process helped substantially, perhaps chiefly, to dry the pond’s surface: as water ran underneath, it lifted and floated the ice. It resembled cutting a hole in a ship’s bottom to let water out. When these holes freeze, followed by rain and then another freeze laying smooth new ice across everything, beautiful dark patterns appear within. Shaped rather like spider webs—ice rosettes, one might call them—they come from channels worn by water flowing inward from all directions. Sometimes, too, with shallow puddles on the ice, I saw my shadow doubled, one figure standing on the other’s head: one on ice, the other on trees or hillside.

While January is still cold and snow and ice lie thick and solid, the prudent landlord comes from town to harvest ice for his summer drinks. Such impressive, almost touching foresight: anticipating July’s heat and thirst in January, wearing a thick coat and mittens! Yet so much else goes unprovided for. Perhaps he stores no earthly treasures that will cool his summer drink in the next world. He chops and saws the solid pond, takes the roof off the fishes’ house, and carts away their very element and air. Like stacked firewood, it is secured with chains and stakes and carried through the helpful winter air into wintry cellars, to lie beneath summer there. From afar, as it passes through the streets, it looks like solid blue sky. These merry ice-cutters joke and play. When I visited, they liked to invite me to join their pit-sawing—with me underneath.

One winter morning in ’46–7, a hundred men of Hyperborean origin swooped onto our pond with many carloads of awkward-looking farm implements: sleds, ploughs, drill-barrows, turf-knives, spades, saws, and rakes. Each carried a double-pointed pike-staff of a kind neither the New-England Farmer nor the Cultivator describes. Were they sowing winter rye, I wondered, or some new Icelandic grain? Seeing no manure, I supposed they intended to skim the soil as I had, believing it deep and long enough fallow. They said a gentleman farmer behind the operation wished to double his money—already half a million, as I understood. To put another dollar over each he owned, however, he stripped Walden of its only coat, indeed its very skin, in a hard winter’s midst. They immediately began ploughing, harrowing, rolling, and furrowing in splendid order, apparently determined to create a model farm. While I watched closely for the seed they would drop, a nearby gang abruptly hooked up the untouched soil itself with a special jerk. They took it clean down to sand—or rather water, for this soil was very springy—all the _terra firma_ there was, and hauled it away on sleds. Then I supposed they must be cutting peat in a bog. Every day, with a peculiar locomotive shriek, they travelled to and from what seemed some polar destination, like a flock of arctic snow-birds. Sometimes Squaw Walden took revenge. A hired man following his team slipped through a crack toward Tartarus; the formerly brave fellow abruptly became only the ninth part of a man, nearly surrendered his animal heat, and gladly sheltered in my house, admitting a stove had its merits. At other times the frozen ground broke steel from a ploughshare, or trapped a plough in its furrow so firmly that it had to be cut free.

Literally, a hundred Irishmen supervised by Yankees came daily from Cambridge to harvest ice. Their familiar methods of dividing it into blocks need no explanation. Sleds brought the blocks ashore, where they were quickly hauled onto an ice platform, then lifted by grappling irons and horse-powered block and tackle into a stack, as securely as barrels of flour. They laid them neatly side by side and row upon row, like the solid foundation of an obelisk meant to pierce the clouds. They told me a good day yielded a thousand tons, about an acre’s worth. Repeated sled traffic wore deep ruts and “cradle holes” into the ice as into _terra firma_. The horses always ate oats from ice blocks hollowed into buckets. Outdoors the pile rose thirty-five feet on one side and measured six or seven rods square. Hay between the outer layers excluded air: wind, however cold, finds passages and eats great cavities, leaving scattered slender supports or studs until the stack collapses. At first it resembled a huge blue fort or Valhalla. Then coarse meadow hay stuffed into its crevices acquired frost and icicles, turning it into an ancient, mossy, hoary ruin of blue-tinted marble. It was Winter’s dwelling—the old man in the almanac—his shanty, as though he planned to spend summer with us. They estimated that less than twenty-five per cent would reach its destination and two or three per cent would be lost in the cars. Yet still more of the pile met an unintended fate. Perhaps the ice contained more air than usual and kept worse than expected, or perhaps another reason intervened; it never reached market. Built in the winter of ’46–7 and estimated at ten thousand tons, the heap was finally covered with boards and hay. They removed the roof the following July and carried some away, leaving the remainder in the sun. It lasted through that summer and the next winter, not completely melting until September 1848. Thus the pond reclaimed most of it.

Close up, Walden ice looks greenish like its water; from a distance it is beautifully blue. Even a quarter-mile away you can distinguish it from the river’s white ice or some of the other ponds’ merely greenish ice. Sometimes a great block slips off an ice-man’s sled in the village street and lies there a week like an enormous emerald, intriguing everyone who passes. I have seen green Walden water turn blue when frozen, viewed from exactly the same place. Similarly, nearby hollows sometimes fill in winter with greenish water resembling the pond’s, then freeze blue by the next day. Perhaps the blue of water and ice comes from the light and air they hold; the clearest is also the bluest. Ice rewards contemplation. I was told Fresh Pond’s ice-houses held five-year-old ice as good as ever. Why does a pail filled with water quickly turn foul, while freezing keeps it sweet forever? This, people commonly say, is the difference between the affections and the intellect.

For sixteen days, then, my window framed a hundred men working like busy farmers, with teams, horses, and apparently every farming tool: a scene from an almanac’s first page. Each glance recalled the fable of the lark and reapers, the parable of the sower, or something similar. Now they have all left. Probably thirty days from now the same window will show pure sea-green Walden water reflecting trees and clouds, lifting its vapors in solitude, with no sign that a person ever stood there. Perhaps I shall hear one loon laughing as it dives and preens, or see a solitary fisherman in his boat, like a floating leaf, gazing at his reflection in the waves where a hundred men so recently worked in safety.

So the sweltering people of Charleston, New Orleans, Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta apparently drink from my well. Each morning I bathe my mind in the Bhagvat Geeta’s immense philosophy of the universe’s creation. Ages measured in gods’ years have passed since its composition; beside it our modern world and literature seem tiny and trivial. Its sublimity is so far from our conceptions that I suspect it belongs to an earlier state of existence. I put down the book and fetch water from my well, and lo! I meet the servant of the Bramin, priest of Brahma, Vishnu, and Indra, still reading the Vedas in his Ganges temple, or living at a tree’s root with crust and water jug. His servant comes to draw the master’s water, and our buckets seem to scrape together in one well. Walden’s pure water mingles with the Ganges’ sacred stream. Favorable winds carry it past the legendary sites of Atlantis and the Hesperides, along Hanno’s voyage around the coast, past Ternate, Tidore, and the Persian Gulf’s mouth. It melts in the tropical winds of Indian seas and reaches ports Alexander knew only by name.

chapters.title: Spring
paragraphs: Ice-cutters usually hasten a pond’s breakup by opening large areas: wind-stirred water erodes the surrounding ice even in cold weather. Walden did not respond that way that year, however; she soon put on a thick new garment in place of the old. This pond opens later than every other pond in the neighborhood, partly because her water is much deeper and partly because no stream runs through her to melt the ice or wear it away. I have never known her to open during winter, even in ’52–3, which severely tested the ponds. She generally opens around April first, a week or ten days after Flint’s Pond and Fair-Haven. Melting begins on the north side and in the shallows where freezing began. Less affected by brief temperature changes, she marks the season’s real progress better than any nearby water. A few severely cold March days may greatly delay those other ponds’ opening, while Walden’s temperature rises almost without interruption. On March 6th, 1847, a thermometer placed in Walden’s middle read 32°, the freezing point; near shore it read 33°. That same day, in Flint’s Pond’s middle it showed 32½°, but in shallow water a dozen rods offshore, beneath a foot of ice, 36°. That three-and-a-half-degree difference between Flint’s deep and shallow water, together with its large proportion of shallows, explains its much earlier opening. Its shallowest ice was then several inches thinner than its central ice. In midwinter the centre had been warmest, with the thinnest ice. Anyone wading a pond’s shores in summer likewise notices how much warmer water is close to shore, only three or four inches deep, than a little further out, and how much warmer deep water is at the surface than near the bottom. In spring the sun does more than raise air and ground temperatures. Its heat passes through ice a foot or more thick and reflects from the shallow bottom, warming the water and melting the ice underneath while directly melting the upper surface. This makes it uneven and stretches its air bubbles upward and downward until the whole is honeycombed, finally vanishing suddenly in one spring rain. Ice, like wood, has a grain. When a block starts rotting or “combing,” taking on a honeycomb appearance, its air cells always stand at right angles to the former water surface, whatever the block’s position. Above a rock or log close to the surface, the ice is much thinner and often melts entirely through this reflected warmth. I am told that Cambridge’s experiment in freezing water in a shallow wooden pond allowed cold air underneath, exposing both sides, yet sunshine reflected from its bottom more than cancelled that advantage. When warm midwinter rain removes Walden’s snow-ice and leaves hard, dark or transparent ice in the middle, a band of rotten white ice, thicker though it is, remains around shore, a rod or more wide, produced by this reflected heat. As I have also said, bubbles inside the ice act as burning-glasses, melting the ice below.

Every day a pond repeats the year’s events in miniature. Generally its shallow water warms faster each morning than the deep water, though it may not finally become as warm; each evening it also cools faster until morning. A day condenses a year. Night is winter, morning and evening are spring and fall, noon is summer. Ice cracking and booming announces a change of temperature. On February 24th, 1850, a pleasant morning following a cold night, I went to spend the day at Flint’s Pond. Striking the ice with my axe-head, I was surprised to hear it ring like a gong for many rods around, or like a tightly stretched drum. About an hour after sunrise the pond began booming as slanting rays reached it over the hills. It stretched and yawned like a waking man, its growing clamor continuing three or four hours. After a short midday siesta it boomed again toward night as the sun’s influence receded. In the appropriate weather a pond fires its evening gun very punctually. But at midday, riddled with cracks, with the air less elastic too, it had lost all resonance. A blow could probably no longer stun fish or muskrats. Fishermen say the “thundering of the pond” frightens fish and stops them biting. It does not thunder every evening, and I cannot reliably predict it. Yet it notices differences in weather that escape me. Who would expect such a large, cold, thick-skinned thing to be so sensitive? Still it follows a law, thundering its obedience at the proper time as surely as buds open in spring. Earth is alive everywhere and covered with papillæ. The greatest pond responds to atmospheric changes as sensitively as the bead of mercury in a thermometer’s tube.

Part of what drew me to live in the woods was the leisure and opportunity to watch spring arrive. Finally the pond’s ice grows honeycombed, soft enough for my walking heel to sink in. Fog, rain, and warmer suns gradually melt the snow. Days are noticeably longer; I see I can finish winter without adding to the woodpile, because large fires are no longer needed. I watch for spring’s earliest signals: a newly arrived bird’s stray note, the striped squirrel’s chirp—his stores must be nearly spent—or the woodchuck venturing from winter quarters. On March 13th, after hearing bluebird, song-sparrow, and red-wing, I still found nearly a foot of ice. Warming weather did not visibly erode it by water, or break it up and float it away as happens in rivers. Though a strip half a rod wide had melted completely alongshore, the centre merely became honeycombed and soaked. You could step through ice still six inches thick. Yet by the following evening, perhaps after warm rain and fog, it would all be gone, carried off with the fog, spirited away. One year I crossed the middle just five days before the ice entirely vanished. Walden first opened completely on April 1st in 1845; March 25th in ’46; April 8th in ’47; March 28th in ’51; April 18th in ’52; March 23d in ’53; and about April 7th in ’54.

For those of us in a climate of such extremes, everything connected with rivers and ponds breaking open and weather settling is especially interesting. With warmer days, riverside residents hear night-time ice crack in startling, artillery-loud whoops, as though icy chains had snapped from end to end. Days later they watch it rush away. So an alligator rises from mud amid trembling earth. An old man told me a story. He had observed Nature closely and seemed to understand her workings as thoroughly as if, when he was a boy, she had been set on shipbuilders’ stocks and he had helped lay her keel. He had reached his full growth in knowledge and could scarcely acquire any further understanding of Nature’s operations even if his life lasted to the great age of Methuselah. I was astonished to hear this man express wonder at anything Nature did, for I had supposed that she had no secrets left to keep from him. One spring day, he said, he took his boat and gun to try the ducks. Ice still covered the meadows, but the river was clear, and he drifted freely from his home in Sudbury to Fair-Haven Pond. Unexpectedly, most of it remained under a solid field of ice. On so warm a day its extent astonished him. No ducks appeared. He hid the boat on an island’s north or back side and concealed himself among bushes on its southern side to wait. Ice had melted three or four rods out from shore, leaving smooth warm water over mud, just what ducks like. He expected some to arrive soon. After about an hour lying still, he heard a low sound, apparently very distant, yet extraordinarily grand and impressive, unlike anything he knew. It swelled gradually as though building toward some universal, unforgettable conclusion, a brooding rush and roar. Suddenly he took it for a vast gathering of birds coming down to settle, snatched his gun, and sprang up excitedly. To his surprise, the entire ice field had moved while he waited, drifting shoreward. What he heard was its edge grinding against the bank. At first it nibbled and crumbled gently; finally it rose and scattered its wreckage to a considerable height along the island before coming to rest.

At last sunlight strikes at the right angle. Warm winds bring mist and rain, melting the snowbanks; then the sun scatters the mist and smiles on a russet-and-white patchwork smoking with incense. Travellers choose paths from islet to islet, cheered by the music of a thousand tinkling streams and rivulets. Their veins run with winter’s blood, which they are carrying away.

Few sights pleased me more than thawing sand and clay flowing down a deep railroad cutting that I passed on my way to the village. One seldom sees this spectacle on such a large scale, though since railroads were invented the number of newly exposed banks containing the right material must have increased enormously. This was sand of every fineness and many rich colors, usually mixed with a little clay. As frost leaves in spring, or even on a thawing winter day, the sand flows down like lava. Sometimes it bursts through snow and floods over it where previously no sand showed. Countless little streams cross and overlap, producing a hybrid form half governed by flowing currents and half by vegetation. Moving, it assumes the shapes of juicy leaves or vines, piling pulpy sprays a foot or more deep. Viewed from above, these resemble certain lichens’ thalluses, cut into fringes, lobes, and overlapping scales. Or they recall coral, leopards’ paws, birds’ feet, brains, lungs, bowels, and every sort of excrement. This is truly _grotesque_ vegetation, its shapes and colors imitated in bronze: architectural foliage older and more fundamental than acanthus, chiccory, ivy, vine, or any plant’s leaves. Under some conditions it might puzzle future geologists. The whole cutting struck me as a stalactite cave opened to daylight. Its sands have remarkably rich, pleasing shades, the various colors of iron: brown, gray, yellowish, reddish. Reaching the drain at the bank’s foot, the flowing mass spreads into flatter _strands_. Separate streams lose their half-cylinder shape, slowly broadening and flattening, merging as they grow wetter until they form an almost level _sand_. It remains beautifully varied in shade, with the first vegetation-like shapes still traceable. Finally, in the water itself, these become _banks_ like those off river mouths, and the plant forms disappear into ripple marks along the bottom.

Sometimes, in a single spring day, this sandy eruption or foliage blankets a bank twenty to forty feet high for a quarter-mile along one or both sides. Its sudden emergence makes these sand leaves remarkable. Seeing the lifeless bank on one side—the sun reaches one side first—and on the other this lush growth made within an hour, I feel I have entered the laboratory of the Artist who made the world and me. Here he still works, playing on the bank, scattering fresh designs in a surplus of energy. I seem closer to the globe’s vital organs, for this overflow resembles the leafy mass of an animal’s entrails. Sand itself anticipates the plant leaf. No wonder earth expresses herself outwardly through leaves: inwardly she labors so intensely with the idea. Her atoms already know this law and are pregnant with it. The overhanging leaf can see its prototype below. _Inside_ globe or animal, the form is a moist, thick _lobe_, a word especially fitting liver, lungs, and _leaves_ of fat (?e?ß?, _labor_, _lapsus_, flowing or slipping down, a lapsing; ??ß??, _globus_, lobe, globe; also lap, flap, and many other words). _Outside_ it is a dry, thin _leaf_, just as _f_ and _v_ are pressed, dried forms of _b_. The root letters of _lobe_ are _lb_: the soft mass of _b_—one lobe, or B with two—with liquid _l_ behind, pushing it forward. In globe, _glb_, the throaty _g_ adds the throat’s capacity to the meaning. Birds’ feathers and wings are thinner, drier leaves still. Similarly, the earth’s lumpish grub becomes an airy, fluttering butterfly. The globe itself continually surpasses and transforms itself, taking wings in its orbit. Even ice starts in delicate crystal leaves, as though poured into moulds left by water plants’ fronds on the watery mirror. An entire tree is only one leaf; rivers are larger leaves still, their pulp the earth between them, their axils holding towns and cities like insect eggs.

When sunlight withdraws, sand stops flowing. Morning starts the streams again, branching and rebranching into countless others. Perhaps you are watching how blood vessels form. Look closely: a current of softened sand first pushes from the thawing mass with a rounded, drop-shaped tip like a fingertip’s pad. It feels its way slowly, blindly downward. As the rising sun adds warmth and moisture, the most liquid part tries to obey the same law as the most inert, separates from it, and makes a winding channel or artery within it. A little silver stream flashes like lightning from one tier of pulpy leaves or branches to another, periodically vanishing into sand. Wonderful how swiftly and perfectly the moving sand organizes itself, choosing its best material for the channel’s sharp edges. Rivers begin like this. Perhaps the water’s deposits of silicious material form the skeleton, while finer soil and organic matter become muscle fibre or cellular tissue. What is a human being but thawing clay? A fingertip’s pad is simply a hardened drop. Fingers and toes stream out to their limits from the body’s melting mass. Who knows how far a human body might spread and flow beneath a kinder heaven? Isn’t the hand a spreading _palm_ leaf, lobes and veins complete? Imagination may see the ear as an _umbilicaria_ lichen on the head’s side, with its lobe or drop. The lip—_labium_, from _labor_ (?)—laps or slips from the cavernous mouth’s sides. Plainly the nose is a congealed drop, a stalactite. The chin is a bigger drop, the face’s drippings joining together. Cheeks slide from the brows into the face’s valley, meeting resistance and spreading over cheek bones. Every rounded lobe of a plant leaf likewise is a thick drop, large or small, now pausing. Lobes are the leaf’s fingers. For every lobe there is a direction in which it tends to flow; more warmth or another kindly influence would have drawn it further.

This single hillside seemed to display the principle behind all Nature’s workings. Earth’s Maker merely patented a leaf. What Champollion will read this hieroglyphic for us, so we may finally turn over a new leaf? To me this sight is more invigorating than rich, fertile vineyards. Admittedly it has an excremental quality, endless heaps of livers, lungs, and bowels, as though the globe were turned inside out. At least that suggests Nature has bowels, and once again is humanity’s mother. Here frost leaves the ground; here is Spring. It comes before the green, flowering spring as mythology comes before formal poetry. Nothing better purges winter’s fumes and indigestion. It persuades me that Earth remains in swaddling clothes, reaching baby fingers everywhere. New curls sprout on the baldest brow. Nothing is inorganic. Leafy heaps line the bank like furnace slag, showing Nature is “in full blast” inside. Earth is more than dead historical debris, layer on layer like book leaves for geologists and antiquaries chiefly to study. She is living poetry, like tree leaves before flower and fruit: living earth, not fossil earth. Beside her great central life, all animal and vegetable life is merely parasitic. Her convulsions will lift our cast-off remains, our exuviæ, from their graves. Melt metals and pour them into your loveliest moulds; they will never move me like the shapes this molten earth flows into. Nor is earth alone malleable: her institutions too are clay in the potter’s hands.

Soon frost emerges not only from these banks but from every hill, plain, and hollow, like a hibernating four-footed beast leaving its burrow. With music it seeks the sea, or travels in clouds to other climates. Thaw’s gentle persuasion is stronger than Thor’s hammer: one melts, while the other merely breaks things apart.

When snow had partly cleared and several warm days had somewhat dried the surface, I enjoyed comparing the infant year’s first tender shoots with the stately remains of plants that had survived winter. Life-everlasting, golden-rods, pinweeds, and graceful wild grasses often showed more clearly and interested me more than in summer, as though their beauty ripened only now. Even cotton-grass, cat-tails, mulleins, johnswort, hard-hack, meadow-sweet, and other strong-stemmed plants remained unemptied granaries feeding the earliest birds—at least respectable mourning weeds for widowed Nature. The wool-grass’s arching, sheaf-like crown especially attracts me. It recalls summer to our winter memory and offers one of the shapes art loves copying. Such plant forms relate to patterns already in the human mind as astronomy does. This antique style predates both Greek and Egyptian. Many of Winter’s displays suggest tenderness beyond expression and a fragile delicacy. We usually hear this king called a rough, blustering tyrant; yet he ornaments Summer’s hair with a lover’s gentleness.

As spring neared, red-squirrels gathered two at a time beneath my house, directly under my feet while I read or wrote. They produced the strangest chuckles, chirrups, gurgles, and vocal pirouettes imaginable. Stamping only made them chirrup louder, as though their wild play had carried them beyond fear or respect and they dared humanity to stop them. No you don’t—chickaree—chickaree. Either my arguments fell on wholly deaf ears or their force escaped the squirrels, who launched into an irresistible stream of abuse.

Spring’s first sparrow! A year opening with hope younger than ever!
