Across damp fields only partly cleared of snow, blue-bird, song-sparrow, and red-wing send faint silvery warbles, like winter’s final flakes tinkling as they fall! What do histories, chronologies, traditions, and written revelations matter at such a moment? Brooks sing spring’s carols and glees. The marsh-hawk sailing low over the meadow already hunts the first slimy creatures to awaken. In every dell comes the sinking sound of melting snow; pond ice quickly dissolves. Grass flares on the hillsides like a spring fire—“et primitus oritur herba imbribus primoribus evocata”—as though earth sent her own warmth outward to welcome the returning sun. Its flame is green, not yellow. The grass-blade, everlasting youth’s emblem, streams like a long green ribbon out of the turf into summer. Frost checks it, but soon it pushes forward again, fresh life beneath lifting last year’s spear of hay. Its growth is as steady as a small stream oozing from the ground. The two are almost one: during June’s growing days, when the streams dry, grass-blades become their channels. Year after year herds drink from this perennial green current, and the mower draws their winter supply from it in good time. So human life merely dies back to its root, sending its green blade onward into eternity.

Walden thaws quickly. A channel two rods wide follows its north and west sides, broadening further at the east end. A large ice field has split from the main sheet. From shoreline bushes I hear a song-sparrow: _olit_, _olit_, _olit,_—_chip_, _chip_, _chip_, _che char_,—_che wiss_, _wiss_, _wiss_. He too helps crack the ice. How beautiful its edge’s broad, sweeping curves, answering the shoreline’s curves but more regular! A recent severe, brief cold spell has made it unusually hard, with watered or wavy patterns like a palace floor. Wind slides uselessly eastward over this opaque surface until it reaches living water beyond. That sun-sparkling ribbon is glorious: the pond’s bare face young and joyful, seeming to speak the delight of fish within and sand alongshore. Its silver gleam resembles a _leuciscus_’s scales, as though the whole were one lively fish. Here is winter’s contrast with spring. Walden was dead and lives again. Yet this spring, as I have said, its breakup was steadier.

The turn from winter storms to mild, serene weather, from dark, sluggish hours to bright, springy ones, is a memorable turning point announced by everything. In the end it seems instantaneous. Suddenly light flooded my house, although evening approached, winter clouds still hung above, and sleety rain dripped from the eaves. Through the window, lo! where cold gray ice lay yesterday, the transparent pond was already peaceful and hopeful as a summer evening. Its breast reflected a summer evening sky invisible overhead, as though it had news from some distant horizon. Far away a robin sang, the first I thought I had heard in thousands of years, with a note I would remember for thousands more: the same old sweet, powerful song. O the evening robin at a New England summer day’s end! If only I could find his twig! I mean _him_; I mean _the twig_. This, at least, is no mere _Turdus migratorius_. Pitch-pines and shrub-oaks around the house, so long drooping, abruptly recovered their individual characters. They looked brighter, greener, straighter, more alive, as though rain had truly washed and restored them. I knew the rain was over. Any forest twig, even your woodpile, can tell you whether its winter has passed. As darkness gathered, geese _honking_ low over the trees startled me. Like tired travellers late from southern lakes, they finally indulged in unrestrained complaints and mutual comfort. At my door I heard their rushing wings. Heading toward the house, they suddenly noticed my lamp, quieted their clamor, wheeled, and settled on the pond. I went inside, closed the door, and spent my first spring night in the woods.

Next morning I watched the geese from the doorway through mist as the geese sailed fifty rods away in the pond’s middle. They seemed so large and noisy that Walden looked like a man-made pond provided for their amusement. When I reached the shore, their commander signalled; they rose with a great beating of wings, formed ranks, and circled overhead, twenty-nine in all. Then they headed straight for Canada, their leader _honking_ regularly, trusting to find breakfast in muddier pools. A “plump” of ducks rose with them and followed their noisier cousins northward.

For a week, on foggy mornings, I heard a lone goose circling and crying as it searched for its mate, still filling the woods with a sound of life larger than they could support. April brought small flocks of pigeons flying express. In time martins twittered above my clearing, though I had doubted the township possessed enough to spare me any. I imagined these especially belonged to the ancient race that lived in hollow trees before white men arrived. In nearly every climate tortoise and frog precede and announce this season. Birds fly singing in flashing plumage, plants rise and flower, and winds blow, correcting the poles’ slight oscillation and keeping Nature in balance.
Just as each season seems best when its turn comes, spring’s arrival resembles the making of Cosmos from Chaos and the Golden Age becoming real.

“Eurus ad Auroram Nabathæaque regna recessit,
Persidaque, et radiis juga subdita matutinis.”

“The East-Wind withdrew to Aurora and the Nabathæan kingdom,
And the Persian realm, and the ridges beneath the morning rays.

Man was born, whether that Maker of things,
The source of a better world, made him from divine seed;
Or earth, being new and lately parted from the high
Ether, kept some seeds of kindred heaven.”

One gentle rain deepens grass’s green by many shades. Better thoughts entering us brighten our prospects just so. What a blessing to live always in the present, using every chance event as grass responds to the lightest dew, instead of spending our days making amends for missed opportunities and calling it duty. We linger in winter after spring has arrived. A lovely spring morning pardons everyone’s sins; such a day makes a truce with vice. While such a sun still burns, the vilest sinner may return. Our own renewed innocence lets us recognize our neighbors’ innocence. Yesterday you may have known your neighbor as a thief, drunkard, or sensualist, pitied or despised him, and despaired of the world. But on this first spring morning the bright, warm sun creates the world anew. You find him at some peaceful task, see his exhausted, debauched veins widen with quiet joy and bless the day, feeling spring as innocently as a baby, and forget every fault. Good will surrounds him, with even a hint of holiness struggling for expression, perhaps blindly and ineffectively like a newborn instinct. For a brief hour no coarse joke echoes on the southern hillside. You see lovely, innocent shoots preparing to burst from his gnarled bark and try another year’s life, as tender and fresh as the youngest plant. He too has entered his Lord’s joy. Why won’t the jailer open his prison doors, the judge dismiss his case, the preacher release his congregation! Because they ignore God’s hint and reject the pardon he freely offers everyone.

“The calm and kindly breath of each new morning brings a daily return to goodness. In loving virtue and hating vice, one comes a little closer to humanity’s original nature, like new shoots in a felled forest. Likewise, the evil one does during the day stops the seeds of virtue that have begun sprouting again from developing, and destroys them.

“Once these seeds of virtue have been prevented many times from growing and developing, the kindly breath of evening is no longer enough to preserve them. When that breath no longer suffices to keep them alive, human nature becomes little different from a beast’s. Seeing this person’s beastlike nature, people imagine he never had an inborn capacity to reason. But are these humanity’s true and natural feelings?”

“First came the Golden Age, which without any avenger
Freely, without law, cherished faithfulness and uprightness.
Punishment and fear were absent; no threatening words were read
On hanging brass; nor did the pleading crowd fear
Their judge’s words; they were safe without an avenger.
Not yet had the pine felled on its mountains descended
To the liquid waves to see a foreign world,
And mortals knew no shores but their own.
* * * *
There was eternal spring, and peaceful zephyrs with warm
Breaths soothed the flowers born without seed.”

On April 29th I fished beside the river near Nine-Acre-Corner bridge, standing on trembling grass and willow roots where muskrats hide. I heard an odd rattle, rather like sticks boys play between their fingers. Looking up, I saw a slim, graceful hawk resembling a night-hawk. It alternately rose like a ripple and tumbled over and over for a rod or two, revealing wing undersides that shone like satin ribbon in sunlight or a shell’s pearly interior. The sight recalled falconry and the nobility and poetry belonging to that sport. Perhaps it was called the Merlin; I care little for its name. No flight I have seen was more ethereal. It neither merely fluttered like a butterfly nor soared like larger hawks, but played with proud confidence in the fields of air. Rising repeatedly with a strange chuckle, it renewed that lovely, unconstrained fall, turning like a kite, then recovering from its lofty somersaults as if its feet had never touched _terra firma_. It seemed alone in the universe, playing there, needing no companion beyond the morning and the ether it played with. It was not lonely; it made the whole earth beneath seem lonely. Where was the parent that hatched it, its family, its father in heaven? This air-dweller seemed linked to earth only by an egg once hatched in a rocky crevice. Or was its first nest in a cloud’s corner, woven from rainbow trimmings and sunset sky, lined with soft midsummer haze lifted from earth? Now some cliff-like cloud was its eyry.

Besides this I caught a splendid meal of gold, silver, and shining copper-colored fish, like a string of jewels. Ah! on many an early spring morning I have entered those meadows, leaping between hummocks and willow roots, when the wild valley and woods lay in light so clear and brilliant it would have woken the dead, had they been sleeping in their graves as some believe. Immortality needs no stronger proof. Everything must live in such light. O Death, where was your sting? O Grave, where then was your victory?

Without the unexplored woods and meadows around it, our village life would stagnate. We need wildness’s tonic: sometimes to wade marshes where bittern and meadow-hen hide, hear snipe booming, smell the whispering sedge where only a wilder, lonelier bird nests and a mink creeps belly-close to earth. Eager as we are to explore and know everything, we also need everything to remain mysterious and beyond exploration. Land and sea must be endlessly wild, unmeasured and unfathomed by us because they cannot be fathomed. Nature can never be enough for us. Inexhaustible vigor must refresh us: vast, Titanic shapes, wreck-strewn coasts, wilderness with living and rotting trees, thunderclouds, and rains lasting three weeks and bringing floods. We need to see our limits exceeded, life grazing freely beyond our own wanderings. It heartens us to watch a vulture draw strength and health from a meal of carrion that sickens and dispirits us. A dead horse lay in a hollow beside my homeward path. I sometimes had to detour, especially at night in heavy air; compensation came in its assurance of Nature’s powerful appetite and unassailable health. I love seeing her so abundant in life that countless creatures can be sacrificed or allowed to eat one another; delicate living structures calmly crushed like pulp out of existence—tadpoles swallowed by herons, tortoises and toads run over on roads—and sometimes flesh and blood raining down! Though accidents are possible, we must see how little importance to give them. A wise observer receives an impression of universal innocence. Poison, after all, is not poisonous, and no wound is fatal. Compassion offers no secure standing ground. It must act quickly; its appeals cannot be cast into fixed formulas.

Early May brought new growth to the oaks, hickories, maples, and other trees among the pines around the pond. Their leaves brightened the landscape like sunshine, especially on cloudy days, as though sun broke through mist and shone faintly on scattered hillsides. On May third or fourth I saw a loon. During that first week I heard whippoorwill, brown-thrasher, veery, wood-pewee, chewink, and other birds. The wood-thrush had sung long before. Already the phœbe had returned to inspect my door and window, testing whether the house was enough like a cave for her. Humming wings held her aloft, claws clenched as though grasping the air, while she surveyed it. Soon pitch-pine pollen, yellow as sulphur, coated the pond, shoreline stones, and decaying wood in quantities enough to fill a barrel. Here were the “sulphur showers” we hear about. Even Calidas’ play Sacontala speaks of “rills dyed yellow with the golden dust of the lotus.” Thus the seasons rolled onward into summer as a walker enters grass growing taller and taller.
That completed my first year of woodland life. My second followed much the same course. I finally departed from Walden on September 6th, 1847.

chapters.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: Doctors wisely advise the sick to seek different air and scenery. Thank Heaven, this place is not the whole world. Buck-eye does not grow in New England; mocking-birds seldom sing here. A wild-goose is a better citizen of the world than we are: breakfast in Canada, lunch in the Ohio, feathers preened for night in a southern bayou. Even bison partly follow the seasons, grazing Colorado pastures only until sweeter, greener grass waits by the Yellowstone. Yet once we take down rail-fences and build stone-walls on our farms, we imagine our lives bounded and our destinies fixed. Elected town-clerk, you supposedly cannot visit Tierra del Fuego this summer; you can still reach the country of infernal fire. The universe extends beyond our vision of it.

We ought to look more often over our vessel’s stern rail like curious passengers, instead of travelling like dull sailors picking oakum. The globe’s far side is simply where our correspondent lives. Our voyages merely follow great circles, and doctors treat only skin complaints. Someone rushes to Southern Africa to hunt giraffes; surely that cannot be his true quarry. How long would anyone chase giraffes if free to do so? Snipe and woodcock offer fine sport too, yet I trust shooting oneself would be a nobler kind of hunting.

“Turn your eye right inward, and you’ll find
A thousand regions in your mind
Still undiscovered. Travel them, and be
Expert in home-cosmography.”

What does Africa represent, or the West? Isn’t our own interior blank white on the map, however black it may prove, like the coast, once explored? Do we really seek the Nile’s source, the Niger’s, the Mississippi’s, or a North-West Passage around this continent? Are these humanity’s most pressing questions? Is Franklin the only lost man, that his wife should search so earnestly? Does Mr. Grinnell know where he himself stands? Become the Mungo Park, the Lewis and Clarke, the Frobisher of your own rivers and oceans. Explore your higher latitudes, taking shiploads of preserved meat if necessary, and pile the empty cans to the sky as a marker. Was preserving meat invented only to preserve meat? Better, become Columbus to entire new continents and worlds within, opening channels of thought rather than trade. Everyone rules a realm beside which the Czar’s earthly empire is a petty province, an ice-left hummock. Yet some patriots lack _self_-respect and sacrifice the greater realm to the smaller. They cherish the soil that forms their graves but feel no kinship with the spirit that may still animate their clay. Patriotism is a maggot in their brains. What did the costly, showy South-Sea Exploring Expedition mean, if not an indirect admission that the moral world has continents and oceans still unexplored, each person an isthmus or inlet to them? It is easier to sail thousands of miles through cold, storms, and cannibals aboard a government ship, helped by five hundred men and boys, than to explore alone one’s private sea, the Atlantic and Pacific of one’s own being.

“Erret, et extremos alter scrutetur Iberos.
Plus habet hic vitæ, plus habet ille viæ.”

Let them roam and examine the outlandish Australians.
I have more of God, they more of the road.

Circling the earth merely to count Zanzibar’s cats is hardly worthwhile. Still, do even that until you can do better; perhaps you will find a “Symmes’ Hole” leading inward at last. England, France, Spain, Portugal, the Gold Coast, and the Slave Coast all border this private sea. Yet none of their ships has ventured beyond sight of land, though this surely is the direct route to India. To speak every language, follow every nation’s customs, out-travel every traveller, belong in every climate, and make the Sphinx dash her head against a stone, follow the old philosopher’s command: Explore yourself. That task needs both vision and nerve. Only the defeated and deserters go to war, cowards who run away to enlist. Set out now on the furthest westward course, which stops at neither Mississippi nor Pacific and leads to no worn-out China or Japan. It runs straight off at a tangent from this sphere, through summer and winter, day and night, sun down, moon down, and finally earth down too.

Mirabeau reportedly became a highway robber “to discover how much resolve one needs to put oneself openly against society’s most sacred laws.” He said “a soldier fighting in the ranks needs less than half a highway robber’s courage,” and “honor and religion have never obstructed a firm, carefully considered resolution.” By the world’s standard this was manly, but pointless, if not desperate. A sounder man, obeying laws more sacred still, would often find himself “in formal opposition” to what people call “the most sacred laws of society.” He could test his determination without making a detour. Our task is not to strike such a pose toward society, but to hold whatever position obedience to our own being’s laws brings us to. That position will never oppose a just government, should we happen to encounter one.

My reason for leaving the woods was as good as my reason for going. Perhaps I felt several other lives remained to be lived and could give this one no more time. How easily and unknowingly we settle into one route and wear ourselves a track. Within my first week there my feet had made a path from the doorway to the pond. Five or six years after I last used it, it remains clear. Admittedly, I suspect others have followed it and helped keep it open. Earth’s soft surface takes the imprint of human feet; the mind’s paths do likewise. How dusty and worn, then, the world’s highways must be, how deep tradition’s and conformity’s ruts! I wanted no cabin passage, preferring to work before the mast on the world’s deck, where I could best watch moonlight among mountains. I have no wish to go below now.

My experiment taught me at least this: confidently moving toward your dreams and trying to live the life you have imagined brings success you would not expect in ordinary hours. You leave things behind and cross an unseen boundary. New, universal, freer laws establish themselves within and around you; or existing laws widen and receive a more generous interpretation in your favor. You live with the freedom of a higher order of beings. As life grows simpler, the universe’s laws seem less complicated; solitude ceases to be solitude, poverty poverty, weakness weakness. Building castles in the air need not waste your work: that is their proper place. Now build their foundations beneath them.

England and America make an absurd demand: speak so they can understand. Neither people nor toad-stools grow that way. As though their understanding mattered, or there weren’t enough others to understand you. As though Nature could nourish only one kind of mind, not birds as well as four-footed beasts, fliers as well as crawlers; as though _hush_ and _who_, understood by Bright, were the finest English. As though stupidity alone were safe. My chief fear is that my language may not be _extra-vagant_ enough, may not stray sufficiently beyond daily experience’s narrow confines to match the truth I have come to believe. _Extra vagance!_ It depends on the yard fencing you in. A migrating buffalo seeking new pasture at another latitude is not extravagant in the same way as a cow that kicks over the milk pail, jumps the fence, and runs after her calf at milking time. Somewhere I want to speak _without_ limits, as an awake man to others in their waking moments. I believe no exaggeration of mine can even adequately prepare the ground for truthful expression. Who, after hearing music, still feared ever speaking extravagantly again? Facing the possible and the future, we should live loosely, with our forward edges undefined, dim and misty, as shadows show an imperceptible vapor rising toward the sun. The escaping, volatile truth of our words should continually expose the inadequacy of the statement left behind. Their truth is instantly _translated_; only its literal monument remains. Words expressing faith and piety are indefinite, yet to higher natures they carry meaning and the fragrance of frankincense.

Why always reduce ourselves to our dullest understanding and praise it as common sense? The commonest sense belongs to sleeping people and speaks through snores. We sometimes put the one-and-a-half-witted among the half-witted because we grasp only a third of their intelligence. Some would criticize dawn’s red if they ever rose early enough. I hear that “they claim Kabir’s verses have four meanings: illusion, spirit, intellect, and the Vedas’ exoteric doctrine.” Yet in this part of the world people complain if a writer permits more than one reading. While England struggles to cure potato-rot, will nobody try curing the much more widespread and deadly brain-rot?

I do not imagine I have achieved obscurity. Still, I would be proud if my pages faced no worse objection on that score than Walden ice did. Southern buyers disliked its blue, the very proof of purity, as though it signalled mud. They preferred Cambridge’s white ice, which tastes of weeds. The purity people love resembles earth-enveloping mist rather than the blue ether beyond.

People keep drumming into our ears that Americans, and modern people generally, are intellectual dwarfs beside the ancients or even the Elizabethans. What does that settle? A living dog is better than a dead lion. Should someone hang himself for belonging to a race of pygmies instead of becoming the largest pygmy he can? Let each person attend to his own business and try to become what he was made to be.

Why this desperate rush toward success, these desperate undertakings? Someone out of step with his companions may be hearing another drummer. Let him follow the music reaching him, however measured or distant. It does not matter whether he matures as quickly as an apple-tree or oak. Must he force his spring into summer? If the condition we were made for has not arrived, what value has any substitute reality? We refuse shipwreck on a hollow reality. Should we labor to erect a blue-glass heaven overhead when, once it is finished, we will certainly keep gazing at the true ethereal heaven far above, as though our construction did not exist?

In Kouroo lived an artist determined to pursue perfection. One day he thought of making a staff. Reflecting that time enters imperfect work but has no place in perfect work, he told himself: It must be perfect in every respect, even if I accomplish nothing else in life. He immediately entered the forest to find wood, determined to use no unsuitable material. As he examined and rejected one stick after another, his friends gradually left him: they aged at their work and died, while he grew not a moment older. Unknowingly, his single purpose, resolve, and lofty devotion gave him lasting youth. Because he made no bargain with Time, Time stayed out of his way, sighing at a distance at his inability to defeat him. Before he found wood entirely fit for the purpose, Kouroo had become an ancient ruin. He sat on one of its mounds to strip his stick. Before he shaped it properly, the dynasty of the Candahars ended. With the stick’s point he wrote the name of the last of their line in sand, then returned to work. By the time he had smoothed and polished the staff, Kalpa had ceased to be the pole-star. Before he fitted its ferrule and jewel-decorated head, Brahma had woken and slept many times. Why pause to mention these things? At the finishing stroke the staff suddenly expanded before its maker’s astonished eyes into Brahma’s most beautiful creation. Making a staff, he had made a new system, a world in complete and lovely proportion. Though ancient cities and dynasties had vanished, finer, more glorious ones had replaced them. Now the fresh shavings at his feet showed him that, for himself and his work, all that elapsed time had been illusion. No more time had passed than a single spark from Brahma’s mind needs to fall upon and kindle a mortal mind’s tinder. His material was pure, his art was pure; how could the result be anything but wonderful?

No appearance we give a matter serves us as well in the end as truth. Truth alone wears well. Mostly we occupy a false position instead of the place where we actually are. A weakness in our nature makes us invent a situation and put ourselves inside it. Now we are in two situations at once, and escape is twice as hard. In sane moments we attend only to facts, the case that exists. Say what you have to say, not what you ought to say. Any truth beats make-believe. On the gallows Tom Hyde the tinker was asked for last words. “Tell the tailors,” he answered, “to remember to knot their thread before taking the first stitch.” His companion’s prayer has been forgotten.

However lowly your life, face it and live it; do not avoid it or insult it. It is less bad than you are. When you are richest it looks poorest. A fault-finder discovers faults even in paradise. Love your life, however poor. Even a poor-house may offer pleasant, thrilling, glorious hours. Sunset shines just as brightly from alms-house windows as from a rich man’s home, and spring snow melts as early at its door. A peaceful mind, I think, can live there as contentedly and think as cheerfully as in a palace. The town’s poor often seem its most independent people. Perhaps they are simply great enough to accept help without uneasiness. Most people think themselves above town support, yet often are not above supporting themselves dishonestly, which ought to bring greater disgrace. Tend poverty as you would a garden herb, as sage. Do not strain to acquire new things, clothes or friends. Turn the old, return to them. Things stay as they are; we change. Sell clothes, keep thoughts. God will make sure you do not lack company. Were I confined like a spider to an attic corner all my life, the world would remain as large so long as my thoughts stayed with me. The philosopher said: “You can remove the general from an army of three divisions and throw it into disorder; you cannot remove thought from even the humblest and most ordinary man.” Do not anxiously pursue development by exposing yourself to a multitude of influences to play upon you; it all scatters your strength. Like darkness, humility reveals heaven’s lights. Poverty’s and lowliness’s shadows gather, “and lo! creation widens to our view.” We are often told that even Crœsus’s wealth would leave our aims unchanged and our means essentially the same. Moreover, poverty’s restrictions—being unable to buy newspapers or books, for example—merely confine you to the most vital, meaningful experiences. You must work with material yielding the most sugar and starch. Life close to the bone tastes sweetest. You are protected from becoming a trifler. Greatness of spirit on a higher level never causes a loss on a lower one. Excess wealth buys only excess. None of the soul’s necessities costs money.

I live in a corner of a leaden wall containing a little bell-metal alloy. Often during my midday rest, a confused _tintinnabulum_ reaches me from outside: the noise of my contemporaries. Neighbors describe encounters with famous gentlemen and ladies, the distinguished people at their dinners. Such matters interest me no more than the Daily Times. Dress and manners supply most of the fascination and talk; dress a goose however you like, it remains a goose. They recount California and Texas, England and the Indies, the Hon. Mr. —— of Georgia or Massachusetts, all passing, fleeting sights, until I could leap from their court-yard like the Mameluke bey. I delight in finding my true bearings: walking, if I may, beside the Builder of the universe rather than conspicuously marching in a pompous procession; thoughtfully standing or sitting while the restless, nervous, bustling, trivial Nineteenth Century passes rather than living inside it. What are people celebrating? All serve on an arrangements committee, expecting somebody’s speech at any hour. God merely presides over the day, with Webster as his orator. I like to weigh, settle, and gravitate toward what most strongly and rightly draws me—not cling to the scale’s beam to make myself lighter; take the actual case, not an invented one; travel my only possible path, where no power can stop me. Beginning to spring an arch before laying a sound foundation gives me no satisfaction. Let us stop playing kittly-benders on thin ice. Solid bottom exists everywhere. We read of a traveller asking a boy whether the swamp ahead had a firm bottom. Yes, the boy replied. Soon the horse sank to its girths. “I thought you said this bog had a hard bottom,” the traveller objected. “It does,” said the boy, “but you haven’t reached halfway to it.” Society’s bogs and quicksands are like that, but it takes an old boy to know it. Only thought, speech, or action at a certain rare convergence is good. I refuse to be one of those foolish enough to drive a nail into nothing but lath and plaster; it would keep me awake at night. Give me a hammer to feel for the supporting furring. Trust no putty. Drive the nail home and clinch it so truly that you can wake at night satisfied with your work, unashamed to call on the Muse for it. Only so will God help you. Every nail should become another rivet in the universe’s machine, with you continuing the work.

Give me truth before love, money, or fame. I once sat at a table loaded with fine food and wine, attended with servile eagerness, yet lacking honesty and truth. I left that unwelcoming table hungry. Its hospitality was as cold as its ices; I thought no ice was needed to freeze the hosts. They spoke of the wine’s age and celebrated vintage. I thought of wine older, newer, purer, from a more glorious vintage, which they neither owned nor could buy. Style, house, grounds, and “entertainment” count for nothing with me. I visited the king; he left me waiting in his hall and behaved like someone incapable of hospitality. A neighbor of mine lived in a hollow tree. His manners were truly royal. Visiting him would have served me better.

How long will we sit on porches practising stale, idle virtues that any real work would render irrelevant? As though one began a day in long-suffering while hiring someone to hoe one’s potatoes, then went out after lunch to practise Christian meekness and charity with goodness aforethought! Consider humanity’s China pride and stagnant self-satisfaction. This generation rather congratulates itself on coming last in an illustrious line. In Boston, London, Paris, and Rome it recalls its ancestry and complacently discusses its progress in art, science, and literature. Behold the Records of the Philosophical Societies, the public Eulogies of _Great Men!_ Good Adam admires his own virtue. “Yes, we have performed great deeds and sung divine songs that will never die”—meaning while _we_ can still remember them. Where are Assyria’s learned societies and great men? What young philosophers and experimenters we are! Not a single reader of mine has yet lived an entire human life. Perhaps these are merely spring months in our race’s lifetime. We may have had the seven-years’ itch, but Concord has yet to see the seventeen-year locust. We know only a thin skin of our globe. Most people have neither dug six feet down nor leaped that far up. We do not know where we are. Besides, nearly half our time we sleep soundly. Yet we consider ourselves wise and have established an order on the surface. Truly we think deeply and aspire high! Standing above an insect crawling among forest-floor pine needles, trying to hide from me, I wonder why it clings to such humble thoughts. Why hide its head from someone who might benefit it and give its race encouraging news? Then I remember the greater Benefactor and Intelligence above me, the human insect.

Newness streams into the world without pause, yet we put up with unbelievable dulness. I need only mention the sermons still heard in the most enlightened countries. Words like joy and sorrow become merely a psalm’s refrain, sung through the nose, while our faith stays with the ordinary and mean. We think only our clothes can change. People call the British Empire great and respectable, the United States a first-rate power. We cannot believe that behind each person a tide rises and falls strong enough to float that empire like a wood chip, if he ever admitted it into his mind. Who knows what seventeen-year locust will emerge next? The government of my world was not devised, like Britain’s, in after-dinner talk over wine.

Our inward life resembles a river’s water. This year it may rise beyond anything people have known and flood the dry uplands; this very year may be the memorable one that drowns out all our muskrats. Our dwelling place was not always dry land. Far inland I see banks washed by the ancient stream before science recorded its floods. Everyone knows the story told throughout New England of a strong, beautiful insect emerging from the dry leaf of an old apple-wood table. It had stood in a farmer’s kitchen for sixty years, first in Connecticut, later in Massachusetts. Counting the growth rings beyond the egg showed it had been laid in the living tree many years earlier still. For weeks people heard the insect gnawing its way out, perhaps hatched by an urn’s heat. Whose faith in resurrection and immortality does this not strengthen? Who knows what beautiful winged life may have its egg buried for ages under concentric layers of woodenness in society’s dry, dead life—first laid in the alburnum, or sapwood, of a green, living tree, gradually transformed into the semblance of its well-seasoned tomb, perhaps heard gnawing out for years by the astonished human family seated at its festive table—and may unexpectedly emerge from society’s most ordinary, well-used furniture to enjoy its perfect summer at last!

I do not claim John or Jonathan will experience all this. Yet such is the tomorrow that time’s mere passing can never bring to dawn. Light that blinds our eyes becomes darkness for us. Day dawns only where we are awake to it. More daylight waits to break. The sun is only a morning star.
